topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Division as equal sharing
topic.description: Understand division as sharing equally into groups or as grouping (how many groups of a given size can be made)
evidence: Share 10 counters equally between 2 plates
Group 12 objects into sets of 3 and count 4 groups
Use concrete objects to solve 'How many groups of 2 in 8?'
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has 12 grapes to share equally between 3 friends, can they work out that each friend gets 4 — and explain what they did?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 4–6 (UK Reception–Y1, US K–Grade 2, formalised Grade 3). Division as equal SHARING (partitive: share 12 among 3 → how many each?) and equal GROUPING (quotitive: how many groups of 3 in 12?) — the domain's most central concept (centrality 0.43, highest in Maths).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y1 'solve one-step problems involving multiplication and division, by calculating the answer using concrete objects, pictorial representations and arrays with the support of the teacher'; non-statutory 'through grouping and sharing small quantities, pupils begin to understand … division'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): concept seeded in K–Grade 2; formalised at 3.OA.2 'interpret whole-number quotients — e.g. 56 ÷ 8 as the number of objects in each share when 56 are partitioned into 8 equal shares, OR as the number of shares when partitioned into groups of 8'.
• Operational details: teach BOTH structures explicitly — sharing (deal out one-to-each) meets children's fairness intuition first; grouping (make groups of a fixed size) links division to repeated subtraction and to the multiplication tables/inverse. Same equation, two different pictures. Keep quantities small, concrete, and initially remainder-free.
• Checkpoint: model and distinguish the two meanings. Tier A (4–5): fairly share a small set one-to-each and say how many each got. Tier B (5–6): solve both a sharing and a grouping story for the same numbers with counters. Tier C (6): explain that 12÷3 can mean '3 equal shares' OR 'groups of 3', and that both give 4.
bestPractices: Teach BOTH division structures deliberately, not just sharing: sharing (partitive — 'share 12 among 3 plates, how many each?') and grouping (quotitive — 'how many groups of 3 can I make from 12?'). Children default to sharing; grouping must be taught because it is the bridge to repeated subtraction and to reading a times-table fact as a division.
Start fully concrete with a 'one for you, one for me' dealing action for sharing, and a 'scoop groups of n' action for grouping, before any symbol — the physical act carries the meaning.
Show the SAME numbers under both stories so children see one division fact (12÷3=4) can be pictured two ways — this prevents them treating sharing and grouping as unrelated.
Link division to multiplication as its inverse from the start using the array/equal groups (3 groups of 4 is 12, so 12 shared into 3 is 4) — builds the fact-family idea early.
Use fair-sharing language to connect to early fractions (sharing 1 cake among 2 = a half), and keep first examples exact (no remainder) so the core idea is secure before remainders complicate it.
keyRepresentations: Equal-sharing model — dealing counters one-at-a-time into plates/hoops (partitive)
Equal-grouping model — scooping a set into groups of a fixed size (quotitive)
Arrays and equal groups linking division to its inverse multiplication
Bar model (whole split into equal parts) and number line (equal jumps back for grouping/repeated subtraction)
commonMisconceptions: Believing division only means sharing-out (partitive), so a 'how many groups of 3?' problem is not recognised as division at all.
Treating sharing and grouping as different operations rather than two meanings of the same ÷ — not seeing they give the same answer.
Thinking division is commutative: that 12÷3 and 3÷12 are the same (they are not).
Confusing which number is shared and which is the number of groups/size of group (dividend vs divisor) when moving to symbols.
Assuming every sharing must come out exactly and being thrown by leftovers, or sharing unequally and still calling it 'fair'.

learn.summary: For ages 4–6 (roughly UK Reception–Y1, US Pre-K–Grade 1; division with symbols is formalised later, e.g. US Grade 3), build division from two concrete meanings on the same quantity: equal SHARING (partitive: share 12 among 3 plates → how many each?) and equal GROUPING (quotitive: how many groups of 3 fit in 12?). Children default to sharing, so grouping must be taught deliberately — it is the bridge to repeated subtraction and to reading a times-table fact as a division. Keep quantities small, concrete, and initially remainder-free, and show the same numbers under both stories so children see one division fact (12÷3=4) pictured two ways.

activities.title: Share-and-group the same pile
feedback: If a learner makes groups of 3 when asked to share among 3 plates, act out both situations separately side by side — 'share between 3 plates' (3 shares) versus 'make groups of 3' — and name the difference out loud.
If shares come out unequal, model round-robin dealing ('one for you, one for you'), then count both piles and compare, so 'fair' is pinned to 'equal'.
When a total does not divide evenly, simply name 'there's one left over, it won't share fairly' and move on — do not treat the leftover as an error to reteach; remainders come later.
Reinforce the link to multiplication: '3 groups of 4 make 12, so 12 shared into 3 gives 4' — the actions are inverses.
activities.rationale: The curriculum expects division to be met through both grouping and sharing of small quantities using concrete objects, pictorial representations and arrays, and standards describe interpreting a quotient as either the number in each share or the number of equal groups. Enacting both structures on one quantity makes the two meanings concrete and comparable.
sourceClaims: Y1: solve one-step problems involving multiplication and division using concrete objects, pictorial representations and arrays; through grouping and sharing small quantities pupils begin to understand division.
3.OA.2 interpret whole-number quotients as the number in each share (partitive) OR the number of equal groups (quotitive) — the two structures of division.
Division should be taught through both sharing (partitive) and grouping (quotitive) structures; grouping links division to repeated subtraction and to multiplication facts.
learnerActions: Take 12 counters and 3 plates (or hoops). Deal counters out one at a time — 'one for this plate, one for this plate, one for this plate' — until the pile is gone, then count how many each plate got (4).
On the SAME 12 counters, now scoop them into groups of 3, setting each group aside until none remain, then count how many groups you made (4).
Say the matching division sentence for both actions: 12÷3=4. Notice the same answer arrived from two completely different actions — sharing among 3, and making groups of 3.
Try a total that will not share evenly (e.g. 13 counters among 3 plates): deal fairly until you cannot give everyone one more (4 each), and name the leftover (1 left over).

Optional with an interactive counters tool: toggle between a SHARE mode (choose number of plates, tap 'deal', watch counters distribute one at a time) and a GROUP mode (choose a group size, lasso groups); flip modes on the identical pile to see the same equation form on screen.
activities.intendedInsight: Division has two meanings — equal shares and equal groups — and the same numbers can be pictured both ways, giving the same answer; this is the twin meaning children most often miss.

activities.title: Fair-share check with teddies
feedback: Correct full answer for the 2-teddy share: '6 each — it's fair because both teddies have the same number with none left over; I gave them out one at a time until they were gone.'
If a learner offers unequal piles and is untroubled by the difference, model one-for-you dealing, then count and compare both piles so equality becomes the test of fairness.
If a learner shares equally but never checks the piles match, prompt them to count both and confirm they are the same before calling it fair.
With an odd total (e.g. 13 between 2), name the leftover plainly rather than reteaching; noticing 'one left over, won't share evenly' is the goal, not resolving the remainder.
activities.rationale: A 'share fairly and justify' prompt discriminates children who use equality as the governing idea (deal one-to-one, verify equal shares) from those who split unevenly or call it fair without checking. Asking 'how do you know it's fair' surfaces whether 'equal' rather than 'everyone got some' is the constraint. The share-among-3 and groups-of-3 follow-ups revisit 12÷3 under both meanings.
learnerActions: Share 12 counters fairly between 2 teddies so each gets the same. Say how many each teddy gets (6) and explain how you know it is fair.
Count each teddy's pile and compare — are they the same, with none left over?
Describe your method: 'I gave them out one at a time to each teddy until they were gone.'
Now share the same 12 counters among 3 teddies and say how many each gets (4); then answer the matching grouping question: how many groups of 3 can you make from 12? (4) — both are 12÷3.
Try 13 counters: can you still share them fairly between the 2 teddies? What happens? (6 each with 1 left over — it won't share evenly).
activities.intendedInsight: Fairness here means everyone gets an equal amount. When the total shares evenly there are none left over, and when it does not (e.g. 13 between 2), the leftover is simply named. A child shows understanding by checking the groups match, not just by giving everyone 'some'.

activities.title: Sort the stories: sharing or grouping?
feedback: If a learner does not recognise a 'how many groups of 3?' problem as division, act it out with counters alongside a sharing version and name both as division.
If a learner thinks 12÷3 and 3÷12 are the same, show with counters that sharing 12 among 3 differs from sharing 3 among 12 — division is not commutative.
This sorting and matching can check whether the child holds both meanings; it checks classification rather than eliciting the physical dealing/scooping, so use it after hands-on sharing and grouping.
activities.rationale: Categorising stories and matching a division sentence to both picture types can verify that a learner holds both meanings and does not treat sharing and grouping as unrelated operations. It checks classification and is best used after concrete work; it does not itself elicit the physical handling that builds the concept.
sourceClaims: 3.OA.2 interpret whole-number quotients as the number in each share (partitive) OR the number of equal groups (quotitive) — the two structures of division.
Division should be taught through both sharing (partitive) and grouping (quotitive) structures; grouping links division to repeated subtraction and to multiplication facts.
learnerActions: Read or hear short word problems and sort each into 'sharing' (share a total among a number of people/plates) or 'grouping' (make groups of a fixed size).
Match a division sentence like 12÷3=4 to BOTH a shared picture (3 plates with 4 each) and a grouped picture (4 groups of 3).
Fill in the answer to simple remainder-free division sentences, using counters to check.
activities.intendedInsight: Both wordings — 'share among 3' and 'how many groups of 3' — are division, and a single division fact matches both a sharing picture and a grouping picture.

activities.title: Correct the unfair sharer
feedback: If a learner accepts the unequal shares, hand them the counters and have them redeal one-to-one, then count each friend's share.
Use fair-sharing language to connect to early fractions — sharing 1 cake between 2 is a half — keeping first examples exact with no remainder.
A talking partner cannot move the counters for the child, so make sure the child physically redistributes the quantity rather than only talking about it.
activities.rationale: A fair-share dilemma can prompt reasoning about equality, but a talking character cannot let the child manipulate the quantity, so dialogue works best paired with hands-on dealing. Fair-sharing language also seeds early fraction ideas.
learnerActions: A puppet or story character shares a set unfairly on purpose (gives one friend 'a lot'). Fix it so every friend gets an equal share.
Explain to the character why the new sharing is fair and the old one was not.
Pose and solve a fair-share dilemma aloud: 'We have 12 sweets and 4 friends — what's fair?' (3 each).
activities.intendedInsight: Talking through fairness reinforces that equal shares are the rule, while actually moving the counters is what lets the child make and check the equal shares.

constraints: Keep totals small, concrete, and initially remainder-free so the core idea is secure before leftovers complicate it.

Teach BOTH structures deliberately: sharing meets the fairness intuition first, but grouping must be explicitly taught because children default to sharing and grouping is the bridge to repeated subtraction and to multiplication facts.
Treat leftovers gently at this age: name 'there's one left over' and move on; do not reteach remainders as a misunderstanding — remainder work comes later.
Start fully concrete (dealing and scooping actions) before introducing symbols; the physical act carries the meaning.
Sorting/matching and fill-in-the-answer tasks can check classification but do not themselves elicit the physical dealing/scooping — use them after hands-on sharing and grouping, not instead of it.
A talking character or puppet cannot let the child manipulate quantity, so keep dialogue as a supplement to concrete dealing.

Watch for the dividend/divisor confusion as symbols appear: be clear which number is the total being shared and which is the number of groups or the size of each group; division is not commutative (12÷3 ≠ 3÷12).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source claims for 3.OA.2 and NCETM are marked unverified in the source row; the DfE National Curriculum claim is marked verified. Confidence levels were not independently re-checked.

The optional interactive counters tool (share/group mode toggle, tap-to-deal, lasso grouping, live recompute, highlighted leftover) is offered as one way to make the mechanism concrete, not as a required medium; equivalent learning can occur with physical counters and plates.

The original research rated a 3D environment as adding no conceptual gain and a static picture as unable to deliver the 'same answer, two pictures' moment; these are presented as scoped design preferences, not evidence of necessity. A fixed picture can still introduce vocabulary even if it cannot be re-manipulated.

Activity 2 (diagnostic fair-share) and Activity 4 (puppet dialogue / fair-sharing dilemma) have empty sourceClaims: the available source claims support the division topic and concrete sharing/grouping method, but no cited claim directly backs activity 2's diagnostic-discrimination principle or activity 4's dialogue-supplement and early-fraction rationale (the fraction connection comes from pedagogy best-practice notes, not a source claim).

probeDeeper: Count each teddy's pile — are they the same?
Now share the same 12 between 3 teddies — how many each?
How many groups of 3 can you make from 12?
What if you had 13 counters — could you still share them fairly?
assess.correctAnswer: 6 each — it's fair because both teddies have the same number with none left over. I gave them out one at a time to each teddy until they were gone.

errorPatterns.pattern: shares unequally — makes two piles that aren't equal or hands 'a lot' to one teddy; equality isn't yet the constraint
errorPatterns.nextMove: model round-robin dealing ('one for you, one for you'), then count both piles and compare so 'fair' is pinned to 'equal'
errorPatterns.distractor: One teddy gets more because that pile looks big.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: offers unequal piles as the answer and is untroubled by the difference

errorPatterns.pattern: confuses sharing-between with grouping-into — asked to share between 2 teddies, instead makes groups of 2
errorPatterns.nextMove: act out the two situations separately — 'share between 2 teddies' (2 groups) versus 'make groups of 2' — and name the difference
errorPatterns.revealedBy: builds sets of 2 rather than 2 equal shares

errorPatterns.pattern: mishandles a leftover — with a number that won't share evenly, quietly gives one teddy extra
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT treat as a misunderstanding to reteach — remainder understanding comes later; simply name 'there's one left over, it won't share fairly' and move on
errorPatterns.revealedBy: with an odd total, produces unequal piles without noticing the remainder

responseLevels.gap: Splits into unequal piles or stops before all are shared; equality is not the governing idea.
responseLevels.full: Deals out one-to-one into equal groups, verifies the shares are equal with none left over, and handles both sharing-between and grouping-into forms.
responseLevels.partial: Shares equally by dealing but doesn't check the groups match, or handles sharing-between but not the 'how many groups of' form.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are 12 counters. Share them out fairly between these 2 teddies so each teddy gets the same. How many does each teddy get — and how do you know it's fair?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands equal sharing deals out one-to-one and checks the two groups are equal, justifying fairness by equal amounts. A child without it splits unevenly (a big pile and a small one), stops before all are shared, or calls it fair without checking. The 'how do you know it's fair' tier surfaces whether 'equal' is the governing idea rather than just 'everyone got some'.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Arrays for multiplication
topic.description: Use arrays to represent multiplication and division situations
evidence: Build an array of 3 rows of 4 objects to show 3 × 4
Read an array and state the total
Use an array to solve a simple division problem (e.g. 12 objects in rows of 4 → 3 rows)
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees eggs arranged in 3 rows of 4 in a box, can they use that grid layout to work out both '3 × 4 = 12' and '12 ÷ 3 = 4'?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 5–6 (UK Y1–Y2, US Grade 2). Using ARRAYS (rows and columns) to represent both multiplication and division — the canonical model that carries commutativity, the ×÷ inverse, and later the area model.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y1 'calculating the answer using … arrays with the support of the teacher'; Y2 'solve problems … using materials, arrays, repeated addition …'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.OA.4 'use addition to find the total number of objects arranged in rectangular arrays with up to 5 rows and up to 5 columns; write an equation to express the total as a sum of equal addends'; feeds 3.OA.1/3.
• Operational details: an array is a rectangle of objects in equal rows and columns. Read it two ways (3 rows of 4 = 4 columns of 3) to see COMMUTATIVITY; read it as repeated addition (each row is a group); cover part to see DIVISION (total ÷ rows = columns). The array is the single most reusable representation in the domain — it becomes the area model for written multiplication.
• Checkpoint: build and read arrays. Tier A (5): make a 2×3 array and count the total. Tier B (5–6): write the multiplication for an array (3 rows of 4 = 12) and rotate it. Tier C (6): from one array write two multiplications and a division (3×4=12, 4×3=12, 12÷4=3).
bestPractices: Build arrays physically in equal rows and columns and describe them precisely as 'rows of' and 'columns of' before recording — the regular structure is what makes the total computable without counting every object.
Rotate the array a quarter turn to reveal commutativity concretely: 3 rows of 4 becomes 4 rows of 3, same total — the array makes 3×4=4×3 obvious rather than asserted.
Read the SAME array as repeated addition (row by row) and as multiplication, so the array ties the two together.
Use the array to introduce division as the inverse: cover the total and ask 'if 12 objects make 3 equal rows, how many in each row?' — one picture yields the whole fact family.
Treat the array as the seed of the area model — keep rows/columns aligned in a rectangle so the later transition to area and the grid/expanded written methods is continuous.
keyRepresentations: The rectangular array of counters/dots (rows × columns)
The array rotated 90° to show commutativity
Fact-family link: one array → two × facts + two ÷ facts
The array as precursor to the area model / grid method for written multiplication
commonMisconceptions: Confusing rows with columns and so mis-describing the array (though the total is the same, the language matters for later).
Counting every object one-by-one instead of using the row/column structure (missing the point of the array).
Not seeing that a rotated array has the same total — treating 3×4 and 4×3 as needing separate counts.
Building arrays with unequal rows (ragged rectangles) — breaking the equal-groups structure.
Not recognising the array as a division picture as well as a multiplication one.

learn.summary: For ages 5–6 (roughly UK Year 1 into early Year 2; US Kindergarten–Grade 1, noting that US standards formally introduce arrays in Grade 2, ages 7–8), use rectangular arrays (equal rows and columns) as a central model for multiplication and division. Learners build arrays, read them two ways to see commutativity, read them as repeated addition, and cover part to reveal division — so one picture yields a whole fact family and seeds the later area model.

activities.title: Build and read an array
feedback: If a learner counts all 12 by ones, model skip-counting each row aloud ('4, 8, 12') and point to each row as you go; the structural view develops with repeated exposure to equal grouping, so do not drill it.
If rows are different lengths (a ragged arrangement), line up the columns and check every row has the same number before reading it — only then is it a true array.
Prompt: 'How could you count the total quickly using the rows?'
activities.rationale: Describing arrays precisely as 'rows of' and 'columns of' before recording makes the regular structure explicit, which is what lets the total be computed from the factors rather than counted individually. If using physical counters, note the counters sit in a flat grid: the array represents a 2D arrangement.
sourceClaims: Y1 use arrays (with teacher support); Y2 solve problems using materials, arrays and repeated addition.
2.OA.4 find the total of objects in rectangular arrays (up to 5×5) and express as a sum of equal addends.
The array is the key representation linking repeated addition, commutativity and the inverse relationship, and is the precursor to the area model for formal multiplication.
learnerActions: Lay out counters (or draw dots) in equal rows and columns to make an array, e.g. 3 rows of 4.
Say aloud exactly what you made: '3 rows of 4' — then also read it as columns: '4 columns of 3'.
Find the total WITHOUT counting every object: skip-count each row, '4, 8, 12'.
Write the multiplication the array shows: 3 × 4 = 12.
Try building another array to order as an extension, e.g. 'Show me 2 × 5 as an array', and state its total.
activities.intendedInsight: An array has a regular row/column structure, so you can find the total by using the rows rather than counting every object one by one.

activities.title: Rotate the array to see commutativity
feedback: If a learner re-counts from scratch after rotating and is surprised the total matches, revisit that the same counters were only turned, none added or removed.
If a learner treats 3×4 and 4×3 as needing separate counts, have them physically rotate the same array rather than build a new one.
Prompt: 'If I turned the array on its side, what multiplication would it show then?'
activities.rationale: Physically rotating one array a quarter turn demonstrates commutativity concretely rather than asserting it, because the same objects are rearranged and the total is preserved. In a screen model this can be an interactive rotate control with the product shown updating live; on paper, physically turning the layout serves the same purpose.
sourceClaims: The array is the key representation linking repeated addition, commutativity and the inverse relationship, and is the precursor to the area model for formal multiplication.
learnerActions: Build 3 rows of 4 and record the total (12).
Turn the whole array a quarter turn so it becomes 4 rows of 3.
Count or check the total again and notice it is still 12.
Write both multiplications from the one array: 3 × 4 = 12 and 4 × 3 = 12.
activities.intendedInsight: Rotating an array turns 3 rows of 4 into 4 rows of 3 while the total stays the same — so 3 × 4 = 4 × 3 is something you can see, not just a rule to remember.

activities.title: Find the division in the same array
feedback: If a learner builds rows of 4 but can't name a division, point to each 'group of 4', count the groups, and name that as 12 ÷ 4 = 3 — bridging both operations on one array.
Prompt: 'What division does your rows-of-4 array show?'
activities.rationale: Using the array to introduce division as the inverse — covering the array, stating the total and the number of rows, and asking how many are in each row — lets a single picture yield the whole fact family, linking multiplication and division. A cover action (physical card or an interactive mask) makes the 'unknown' concrete.
sourceClaims: Y1 use arrays (with teacher support); Y2 solve problems using materials, arrays and repeated addition.
The array is the key representation linking repeated addition, commutativity and the inverse relationship, and is the precursor to the area model for formal multiplication.
learnerActions: Start from a total, e.g. 12 loose counters.
Arrange them into an array with rows of 4; count how many rows you made.
State the division the array shows: 12 ÷ 4 = 3 (12 grouped into rows of 4 makes 3 rows).
Cover the array, tell a partner the total (12) and the number of rows (3), and ask how many are in each row (12 ÷ 3 = 4); then uncover to check.
activities.intendedInsight: One array is a division picture as well as a multiplication picture: the rows and columns are the two factors, and reading the total the other way reveals the inverse fact.

activities.title: Write the whole fact family from one array
feedback: If a learner writes only one multiplication, have them rotate (or re-read) the array to find the second.
If the division facts are missing, link each factor to a dimension: 'how many rows?' and 'how many in each row?'

A tap-to-reveal reference array (callouts for rows, columns, total and the facts) can support learners as a check — but reading and writing the facts themselves, not just recognising them, is the goal.
activities.rationale: Reading the SAME array as repeated addition and as multiplication, and deriving both × and ÷ facts, connects the representations so one picture supports the whole fact family and keeps the rows/columns aligned for the later area/grid method.
sourceClaims: The array is the key representation linking repeated addition, commutativity and the inverse relationship, and is the precursor to the area model for formal multiplication.
learnerActions: Look at a single array (e.g. 3 rows of 4).
Write both multiplication facts: 3 × 4 = 12 and 4 × 3 = 12.
Write both division facts: 12 ÷ 4 = 3 and 12 ÷ 3 = 4.
Also write the array as repeated addition, row by row: 4 + 4 + 4 = 12.
activities.intendedInsight: A single array ties together repeated addition, two multiplication facts and two division facts — it is a key, highly reusable representation, and the same rectangle later becomes the area model for written multiplication.

constraints: Keep rows and columns equal and aligned in a rectangle; ragged arrangements break the equal-groups structure the array depends on.

Learners should construct and build arrays (from counters, drawing, or a drag-to-set builder), not only recognise or match pre-made ones — recognition/matching tasks check array-reading but do not elicit independent construction.
Keep the rows/columns aligned as a rectangle so the transition to the area model and grid/expanded written methods stays continuous.

Checkpoint tiers: Tier A (age 5) make a 2×3 array and count the total; Tier B (5–6) write the multiplication for an array and rotate it; Tier C (6) from one array write two multiplications and a division.

A static labelled array (e.g. a fixed on-screen image) is a useful reference and can show the fact family, but the learner cannot resize or rebuild it, and a fixed screen image cannot be rotated. Pair it with building/rotating work when the commutativity-by-rotation insight is the aim.

An array is a flat 2D rectangular arrangement; distinguish the grid from any physical counters used to build it. A 3D rendering is not required for this 2D objective and adds handling cost — this is a design judgement for this task, not a claim that 3D provides no learning value in general.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source rated a 'conversation/dialogue' artefact as poor-fit on the grounds it 'adds little' and 3D as adding 'no insight'; these are catalog fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws. They have been softened throughout to scoped notes about the 2D representation and the value of construction; comparative efficacy of any medium is not asserted.

The original pedagogy called the array 'the single most reusable representation in the domain'; this superlative exceeds the cited source claims (which say 'key representation') and has been reduced to a sourced 'key, highly reusable representation' framing.
Source worked examples use 3 rows of 4 = 12 (3×4=12, 4×3=12, 12÷4=3, 12÷3=4) and 2×3=6; arithmetic checked and correct.
Source marks CCSS-M 2.OA.4 and the NCETM claim as verified:false; treat those citations as unverified. The DfE NC claim is marked verified:true in the source but has not been re-checked here.

sourceClaims in Activity 1 attach the DfE and CCSS-M curriculum claims (building arrays with materials; equal-addend/repeated-addition basis) alongside the NCETM structural claim; the NCETM claim most directly supports the precise-structure rationale, while DfE/CCSS support the array-and-repeated-addition basis rather than the specific language principle.

probeDeeper: How could you count the total quickly using the rows?
What division does your rows-of-4 array show?
If I turned the array on its side, what multiplication would it show then?
Show me 2 × 5 as an array.
assess.correctAnswer: The array shows 3 × 4 = 12 (3 rows of 4). Arranging 12 into rows of 4 makes 3 rows — that same picture shows 12 ÷ 4 = 3. The rows and columns match the two factors.

errorPatterns.pattern: doesn't use the array structure — counts every counter one at a time instead of rows × per-row
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT drill — model skip-counting each row ('4, 8, 12'); the structural view of arrays develops with repeated exposure to equal grouping
errorPatterns.revealedBy: counts all 12 by ones with no use of the rows

errorPatterns.pattern: builds a non-rectangular arrangement — makes rows of different lengths so it isn't a true array
errorPatterns.nextMove: align the columns and check every row has the same number before reading it
errorPatterns.revealedBy: ragged, unequal rows when building

errorPatterns.pattern: can't read the division from the array — reads 3 × 4 but doesn't see 12 ÷ 4 = 3 in the same picture
errorPatterns.nextMove: point to the 'groups of 4', count the groups, and name that as 12 ÷ 4 — bridging both operations on one array
errorPatterns.revealedBy: builds rows of 4 but can't state the number of rows as a division

responseLevels.gap: Miscounts arrays by counting one-by-one and cannot build an equal-rows arrangement; rows/columns aren't linked to the factors.
responseLevels.full: Reads an array as a multiplication and total, builds an array to match a grouping/division situation, and connects the same array to both operations.
responseLevels.partial: Reads or builds an array for multiplication but doesn't connect it to the matching division, or needs support to keep the rows equal.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is an array — 3 rows with 4 counters in each row. Tell me a multiplication this array shows and what the total is. Now here are 12 loose counters — arrange them into an array with rows of 4, and tell me how many rows you made.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who reads arrays maps rows-and-columns to the factors and the total, both when reading a given array and when building one from a situation. A child without it counts one-by-one (missing the row structure and often mis-totalling), says only 'lots' rather than 3×4, or builds a ragged arrangement with unequal rows. Requiring both an INTERPRET (read the array) and a TRANSLATE (build from a grouping) exposes exactly where the mapping breaks.

topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to count 4 bags with 3 apples in each, can they see that instead of counting all 12 one by one, they could add 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 — or say '4 groups of 3'?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 5–6 (UK Y1–Y2, US K–Grade 2). Multiplication as repeated addition of EQUAL groups — the entry model for ×, built directly on the equal-groups skip counting from Counting & Cardinality.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y1 non-statutory 'make connections between arrays, number patterns, and counting in 2s, 5s and 10s'; Y2 'solve problems involving multiplication … using materials, arrays, repeated addition, mental methods and multiplication facts'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.OA.4 'use addition to find the total number of objects arranged in rectangular arrays … express the total as a sum of equal addends'; 3.OA.1 'interpret products — 5×7 as the total in 5 groups of 7 objects each'.
• Operational details: multiplication starts as 'a groups of b' — 3 groups of 4 = 4+4+4. Anchor in the skip-counting bridge (count 4, 8, 12 = one, two, three fours). IMPORTANT caveat for later: repeated addition is the entry MODEL, not the whole meaning (scaling and continuous quantities come later) — but for this age equal-groups/repeated addition is the correct foundation.
• Checkpoint: connect groups, repeated addition and count. Tier A (5): make 3 groups of 2 and count the total. Tier B (5–6): write 4+4+4 for '3 groups of 4' and give the total. Tier C (6): say '3 groups of 4 is 12' and skip-count 4, 8, 12 to match, recognising it as three fours.
bestPractices: Introduce × as 'groups of' with equal groups the child physically makes, and always stress the groups must be EQUAL — the defining feature children most often drop.
Bridge explicitly from the skip counting already mastered: counting 4, 8, 12 IS one four, two fours, three fours — so multiplication is met as something familiar (equal jumps) not brand new.
Move along the concrete–pictorial–abstract path: real objects in groups → pictures/arrays → the repeated-addition sentence 4+4+4 → later the × symbol; keep the group structure visible at each step.
Use the number line with equal jumps alongside grouped objects so repeated addition and skip counting are seen as the same thing in two representations.

Distinguish the two numbers in 'a groups of b' (number of groups vs size of group) with consistent language, so children don't muddle 3 groups of 4 with 4 groups of 3 even before commutativity is formalised.
keyRepresentations: Equal groups of concrete objects ('3 groups of 4')
Number line with equal jumps (linking to skip counting)
Repeated-addition number sentence (4 + 4 + 4)
Arrays (rows of equal size) as the bridge to the × symbol
commonMisconceptions: Adding groups that are not equal and still calling it multiplication — losing the 'equal groups' defining property.
Reading 3 × 4 as 3 + 4 (confusing multiplication with a single addition).
Counting the number of groups when asked for the total, or vice versa — muddling the two roles.

Believing multiplication is ONLY repeated addition (a seed of later trouble with fractions/decimals/scaling) — at this age fine, but teachers should model equal-groups language, not 'times means add lots'.
Miscounting the total by losing track of which groups have been counted (no systematic skip count).

learn.summary: For 5–6 year olds (roughly UK Y1, US K–Grade 1), introduce multiplication as repeated addition of EQUAL groups ('a groups of b'): 3 groups of 4 = 4+4+4. Build on the skip counting children are learning at this age (counting in 2s, 5s and 10s, e.g. 2, 4, 6 = one, two, three twos); when using groups of 4, introduce counting in fours alongside the groups (4, 8, 12 = one, two, three fours) rather than assuming it is already known. Keep the group structure visible from real objects → pictures/arrays → the repeated-addition sentence → later the × symbol. Stress that the groups must be equal (the defining feature children most often drop) and keep the two numbers distinct (how many groups vs how many in each). Repeated addition is the correct entry model at this age, but it is a model, not the whole meaning of multiplication.

activities.title: Equal-groups builder: watch groups, sentence and number line move together
feedback: When the jumps land on 4, 8, 12, point out that these are the numbers we say when counting in fours, so 'three fours' and 'count in fours three times' coincide; with groups of 2, 5 or 10, point out that the landing numbers are the skip-count numbers already learned.
If a learner adds an unequal group, note that this isn't multiplication yet: multiplication needs the SAME number in every group; help them make the groups equal again.
Ask which number says how many groups and which says how many in each group, to keep the two roles separate.
activities.rationale: Building the groups and watching the repeated-addition sentence, number-line jumps and total update in lockstep makes the equivalence of grouping, repeated addition and skip counting concrete and lets the child vary the number of groups and feel the pattern. Live sentence growth, number-line jumps, the collapse control and the unequal-group flag are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism visible, not required features.
sourceClaims: Y1 connect arrays and number patterns to counting in 2s, 5s and 10s; Y2 solve multiplication problems using materials, arrays, repeated addition, mental methods and facts.

Multiplication is introduced via equal groups/repeated addition and connected to skip counting; repeated addition is the entry model but multiplication is more than repeated addition (scaling comes later).
learnerActions: Set a group size, e.g. 4.

Add groups one at a time. With each group added, watch three things update together: a new '+4' joins a running repeated-addition sentence (4, then 4+4, then 4+4+4), a jump advances along a number line (4→8→12), and a total counter climbs.

Notice where each number-line jump lands (4, 8, 12) and say these numbers as counting in fours; also try a group size of 2, 5 or 10 and compare where the jumps land with the skip counting you already know.
Use a collapse control to fold '4+4+4' into '3 groups of 4', then expand it back.
Try adding an unequal group (e.g. a group of 3 among the fours) and see it flagged as 'not equal groups yet'; fix it so all groups match.
activities.intendedInsight: '3 groups of 4', '4+4+4', and 'counting in fours three times' are three views of one and the same thing, and the groups must be equal for it to be multiplication.

activities.title: Make the groups yourself with real objects
feedback: Have the learner map each addend back to a specific group ('point to where this 2 is').
If the child counts by ones without grouping, separate the groups physically and count each group, writing one addend per group.
activities.rationale: Concrete, child-made equal groups anchor the concrete–pictorial–abstract path and keep the group structure visible as the repeated-addition sentence is written.
sourceClaims: Y1 connect arrays and number patterns to counting in 2s, 5s and 10s; Y2 solve multiplication problems using materials, arrays, repeated addition, mental methods and facts.
learnerActions: Physically make, for example, 3 groups of 2 counters.
Count the total.
Write the matching repeated-addition sentence 2+2+2 and point to where each '2' is in your groups.
Rebuild with a different number of groups (e.g. 4 groups of 2) and write the new sentence.
activities.intendedInsight: Each addend in the repeated-addition sentence corresponds to one equal group of objects.

activities.title: Number line and grouped objects side by side
feedback: If jumps are unequal, note that equal jumps correspond to equal groups; help resize them.
Ask the child to connect the last number landed on to the total of all the groups.
activities.rationale: Showing equal jumps alongside grouped objects links the two representations the Y1 curriculum connects (arrays/number patterns and counting in 2s, 5s, 10s).
sourceClaims: Y1 connect arrays and number patterns to counting in 2s, 5s and 10s; Y2 solve multiplication problems using materials, arrays, repeated addition, mental methods and facts.
learnerActions: Place grouped objects (e.g. three groups of 4) next to a number line.
Draw equal jumps of 4 on the number line, landing on 4, 8, 12.
Say the totals as you jump and match each jump to a group.
activities.intendedInsight: Skip counting on a number line and repeated addition of equal groups are the same idea shown two ways.

activities.title: Match, sequence and fill in — a companion check
feedback: For the unequal-groups item, confirm that multiplication needs equal groups and ask the child to say why the offered picture fails.
If a match is wrong, return to grouped objects and rebuild the sentence addend by addend.
activities.rationale: Matching, sequencing and fill-in-the-blank crisply test the picture–sentence–total connection and the equal-groups property; this checks understanding rather than constructing and varying the groups, so use it alongside the hands-on work.
learnerActions: Match an equal-groups picture to its repeated-addition sentence (e.g. three groups of 4 ↔ 4+4+4).
Put skip-count totals in order (4, 8, 12).
Fill in the blank: 4+4+4 = ?
Spot and reject a picture of unequal groups offered as if it were '3 groups of 4'.
activities.intendedInsight: A matching/sequencing/fill-in task shows whether the picture–sentence–total link holds and whether unequal groups are correctly rejected; recognition here does not by itself build or vary the concept.

activities.title: Talk it through: 'how many wheels on 3 cars?'
feedback: When the partner makes groups unequal, prompt the child to notice and fix it.
Encourage the full phrase '3 groups of 4 is 12', not just the total.
activities.rationale: Spoken, responsive discussion rehearses equal-groups language; because the insight is visual and quantitative, pair talk with objects or the builder rather than using it alone.
learnerActions: Answer an equal-groups question such as 'how many wheels on 3 cars with 4 wheels each?' by counting groups aloud.
Correct a partner who 'forgets' to keep the groups equal (e.g. gives one car 3 wheels).
Say the matching sentence, e.g. 4+4+4, and give the total.
activities.intendedInsight: Equal-groups language ('3 groups of 4') describes real situations and must keep every group the same size.

constraints: Groups must always be EQUAL; adding unequal groups and calling it multiplication is the defining error to prevent.
Keep the two numbers in 'a groups of b' distinct: how many groups vs how many in each group. Do not let '3 groups of 4' blur into '4 groups of 3' even before commutativity is formalised.
Do not read 3 × 4 as 3 + 4; multiplication is repeated addition of equal groups, not a single addition of the two numbers.

Repeated addition is the entry model for this age, not the full meaning of multiplication; avoid 'times just means add lots'. Scaling and continuous quantities come later. Model equal-groups language instead.
Matching/sequencing/fill-in tasks check the connection but do not by themselves have the child construct and vary equal groups; keep hands-on building central.
A static picture or tap-to-reveal caption can introduce equal groups but does not let the child vary the number of groups; treat it as an introduction or scaffold, not the main concept-builder.
Interaction examples (live sentence growth, number-line jumps, collapse control, unequal-group flag) are illustrative options, not mandatory mechanisms.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic/logic: 3 groups of 2 = 2+2+2 = 6 ✓; 4+4+4 = 12 with number-line landing on 4,8,12 ✓; 3 cars of 4 wheels = 4+4+4 = 12 ✓; 4 groups of 2 = 2+2+2+2 = 8 ✓. The diagnostic distractor '5 cakes' arises from erroneously doing 3+2 (groups + size) and is presented only as an error pattern, never as a valid answer.

Among the listed curriculum/professional standards, the CCSS-M (2.OA.4/3.OA.1) and NCETM claims carry verified:false in the original; the DfE claim is marked verified. All are treated as unverified in this rewrite since sources were not re-checked, and the specific US standard codes were not reproduced in the learner guidance.
The original cites 3.OA.1, a Grade 3 standard, alongside the stated 5–6 / US K–Grade 2 scope; this pre-existing tension is left unaltered as an original-row framing rather than rewritten.

The original 'equal groups and repeated addition are planar... a 3D environment adds no conceptual value' was a catalog fit judgement; it has been dropped rather than asserted as a universal law. A flat representation is sufficient here, but this is a scoped design preference, not evidence that 3D can teach nothing.

The original curriculum objective 'recognise an array as showing equal rows' is carried only lightly (via the CPA progression and matching pictures); an explicit array-focused activity could strengthen coverage but was not present as a separate scaffold in the original.

The original's age-tiered checkpoint (Tier A/B/C) is covered informally across activities (make groups and count → write the sentence → say and skip-count) but its explicit per-age tiering was condensed out; reinstating differentiated tiers could aid assessment.

probeDeeper: Which number tells us how many plates, and which tells us how many cakes on each?
Can you point to where each '2' in 2 + 2 + 2 is on the plates?
If there were 4 plates with 2 cakes, what would the adding-up look like?
What if one plate had 3 cakes and another had 1 — could we still say 2 + 2 + 2?
assess.correctAnswer: 6 cakes. A child reasoning correctly sees the three plates as three EQUAL groups of 2 and connects '3 groups of 2' to the repeated addition 2 + 2 + 2 = 6 — explaining that each plate contributes one 2 to the sum.

errorPatterns.pattern: counts all the cakes by ones with no sense of the equal groups — cannot connect to 2 + 2 + 2
errorPatterns.nextMove: physically separate the plates and count each group of 2, writing 2 + 2 + 2; make each addend a plate.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child gets 6 by counting each cake but, asked to show 2+2+2, cannot map each 2 to a plate

errorPatterns.pattern: adds the numbers seen rather than repeating the group — does 3 + 2 = 5
errorPatterns.nextMove: clarify 3 is HOW MANY groups, 2 is HOW MANY in each; act out three lots of two, not 'three and two'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answer of 5; child adds the count of plates to the count on a plate

errorPatterns.pattern: does not require the groups to be EQUAL — accepts unequal plates as the same kind of situation
errorPatterns.nextMove: contrast equal vs unequal plates; repeated addition of the SAME number is what multiplication captures.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child treats plates with 2, 3, 1 cakes as also '3 groups' for multiplication

responseLevels.gap: counts by ones only, or adds 3 + 2; no equal-groups structure.
responseLevels.full: identifies the equal groups, maps each addend to a group, connects '3 groups of 2' to 2 + 2 + 2 = 6, and recognises the groups must be equal.
responseLevels.partial: gets 6 and links it to 2 + 2 + 2 for this case but doesn't clearly require the groups to be equal or generalise to a new number of groups.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are 3 plates with 2 cakes on each. How many cakes altogether? After the child answers, ask: can you show me why that's the same as 2 + 2 + 2?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child can count 6 by ones without grasping the equal-groups structure. Asking them to connect it to 2 + 2 + 2 reveals whether they see multiplication as repeated addition of EQUAL groups, or merely counted a pile. The reason tier separates counting from grouping structure.
