topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Sharing and grouping on screen
topic.description: Represent practical equal-sharing and grouping situations with virtual materials (dragging on-screen objects onto plates or into groups) as well as physical objects, using counting or subitising to check each share
evidence: Share 10 on-screen strawberries equally onto 2 plates by dragging them and say each plate has 5
Drag 12 virtual blocks into groups of 3 and count the groups
Share 6 real crackers between 3 teddies, then repeat the share on screen and check it matches
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} uses a tablet game to share 10 strawberries between 2 plates, can they make the shares equal — and share real crackers between teddies the same way?

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Commutative Multiplication
topic.description: Understand and apply the commutative property of multiplication and recognise that division is not commutative
evidence: Explain that 3 × 5 = 5 × 3 and show this with an array rotated
Use commutativity to choose the easier calculation
Demonstrate that 12 ÷ 3 ≠ 3 ÷ 12
topic.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} know that 4 × 7 gives the same answer as 7 × 4 — so they can choose whichever order is easier to remember from their times tables?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 6–7 (UK Y2, US Grade 3). The COMMUTATIVE property of multiplication (a×b = b×a) and the recognition that division is NOT commutative.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y2 'show that multiplication of 2 numbers can be done in any order (commutative) and division of 1 number by another cannot'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 3.OA.5 'apply properties of operations as strategies to multiply and divide — e.g. if 6×4=24 is known, then 4×6=24 is also known (Commutative property of multiplication)'.
• Operational details: prove commutativity with the ROTATED ARRAY (3 rows of 4 = 4 rows of 3), which both convinces and halves the fact-learning load. Equally important: teach the counterexample that division is NOT commutative (12÷3 ≠ 3÷12) so children don't over-generalise. Use commutativity as a strategy to derive and check facts.
• Checkpoint: apply and bound the property. Tier A (6): agree 2×5 = 5×2 using a rotated array. Tier B (6–7): use commutativity to state an unknown fact from a known one (know 3×8 → 8×3). Tier C (7): explain WHY multiplication is commutative (rotate the array) and give a counterexample showing division is not.
bestPractices: Prove commutativity concretely by rotating an array a quarter turn — same objects, same total, different reading — rather than stating it as a rule; the array makes it self-evident.
Explicitly use commutativity to lighten fact learning: knowing 3×8 gives 8×3 for free, so the multiplication square is nearly halved by its diagonal symmetry.

Teach the boundary firmly: division is NOT commutative — have children test 12÷3 vs 3÷12 with counters and see they differ, so the property isn't wrongly generalised (a very common error, also later applied wrongly to subtraction).
Connect to context: 3 bags of 4 and 4 bags of 3 are different situations but the SAME product — distinguishing 'same answer' from 'same story'.
Use commutativity as a checking strategy (compute both ways, compare) to build self-correction.
keyRepresentations: The array rotated 90° (the proof of commutativity)
The multiplication square's diagonal symmetry
Counters showing 12÷3 ≠ 3÷12 (the non-commutative counterexample)
Paired context pictures (3 groups of 4 vs 4 groups of 3)
commonMisconceptions: Over-generalising commutativity to division and subtraction (thinking 12÷3 = 3÷12, or 8−3 = 3−8).
Believing 3×4 and 4×3 are different facts needing separate memorisation.
Accepting commutativity as a stated rule without being able to justify it (no array reasoning).
Confusing 'same product' with 'same situation' — not seeing that different stories can share an answer.
Applying commutativity correctly to × but then assuming order never matters in any calculation.

learn.summary: For ages 6–7 (UK Year 2; in the US this content is formally taught in Grade 3, usually ages 8–9): teach that multiplication is commutative (a×b = b×a) by rotating an array so the same objects give the same total read two ways, use this to nearly halve fact-learning, and firmly teach the boundary that division is NOT commutative (12÷3 ≠ 3÷12) to prevent over-generalising. Learners should predict then prove commutativity by action, use it as a strategy to derive and check facts, and refute the claim that order never matters.

activities.title: Predict then rotate the array to prove 3×4 = 4×3
feedback: If you predicted the total would change, compare your prediction with what you counted — turning the array does not add or take away any objects, so the total must stay the same.
Strong answer: 'It's the same counters turned on their side, so there are still 12.' That reasons from the array, not just from working both sums out.
If a learner only says 'I worked them both out', push for the structural reason: show them the rotation so commutativity is seen, not just checked.
activities.rationale: Committing to a prediction and then proving commutativity concretely by a quarter-turn of the array makes the property self-evident and distinguishes 'same answer' from an unjustified rule; this reflects standards and mastery guidance on using the rotated array.
sourceClaims: Y2: show that multiplication of two numbers can be done in any order (commutative) and division of one number by another cannot.
Commutativity is best proven with the rotated array and used to reduce fact-learning load; children must be taught explicitly that division is not commutative to prevent over-generalisation.
learnerActions: Build an array of 3 rows of 4 counters (or dots) and count the total: 12.
Before you turn the array, predict whether the total will change if you turn it, and give your reason.
Rotate the whole array a quarter turn so it becomes 4 rows of 3 — do not add or remove any counters.
Count again and confirm the total is still 12; record 3×4 = 4×3.
Repeat with another pair you choose (e.g. 2×5 and 5×2) and state the matching fact.
Explain in your own words WHY the total cannot change when you turn the array.
activities.intendedInsight: The same set of objects, read in two directions, gives the same product, so multiplication can be done in either order — this is predicted and then seen by rotating, not merely stated as a rule.

activities.title: Use commutativity to get facts for free
feedback: If a learner recomputes the partner fact, remind them the array proof means the answer must be identical — they already know it.
Encourage them to point to the diagonal mirror on the square to justify why the facts pair up.
Note the facts that sit on the diagonal (like 3×3) have no separate partner, which is why commutativity nearly halves, rather than exactly halves, the facts to learn.
activities.rationale: Explicitly using commutativity as a strategy lightens fact learning and supports self-correction, as highlighted in the standards and mastery guidance.
sourceClaims: 3.OA.5 apply the commutative property of multiplication as a strategy (know 6×4=24 → 4×6=24).
Commutativity is best proven with the rotated array and used to reduce fact-learning load; children must be taught explicitly that division is not commutative to prevent over-generalisation.
learnerActions: Given a known fact (e.g. 3×8 = 24), state its commuted partner (8×3 = 24) without recomputing.
Look at a multiplication square and find the diagonal line of symmetry; notice that facts on either side of it mirror each other.
Decide which of a pair is easier to work out (e.g. 2×9 vs 9×2) and explain why using the easier order helps.
Use 'compute both ways and compare' to check one of your own answers.
activities.intendedInsight: Because order doesn't matter for multiplication, each known fact gives its partner free, nearly halving the facts to learn, and you can pick the easier order or check your work.

activities.title: Test the boundary: division does not swap
feedback: If a learner says 12÷3 = 3÷12 'because order doesn't matter in maths', have them physically share both ways; the different outcomes make the difference felt.
Good distinction: '12÷3 gives 4, but 3÷12 gives less than one — division can't be turned round.'
Note that subtraction also does not commute (8−3 ≠ 3−8), so 'order never matters' is the mistaken rule to avoid.
activities.rationale: Teaching the counterexample firmly heads off the very common over-generalisation of commutativity to division and subtraction, which the curriculum and mastery guidance call out explicitly.
sourceClaims: Y2: show that multiplication of two numbers can be done in any order (commutative) and division of one number by another cannot.
Commutativity is best proven with the rotated array and used to reduce fact-learning load; children must be taught explicitly that division is not commutative to prevent over-generalisation.
learnerActions: Act out 12 ÷ 3 with counters: share 12 counters into 3 equal groups and count one group (4).
Now act out 3 ÷ 12: try to share 3 counters among 12 — you cannot give everyone a whole counter, so each would get less than one.
Compare the two results and state clearly that 12÷3 ≠ 3÷12 (4 is not the same as less than one).
Try to 'rotate' the sharing the way you rotated a multiplication array, and describe why it does not work.
Decide for each pair whether order can swap: sort statements (mixing × and ÷) into 'order can swap' and 'order matters'.
Consider whether swapping works for subtraction too (e.g. 8−3 vs 3−8) and say what you find.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplication's array can be turned freely without changing the total, but swapping the two numbers in a division (or subtraction) usually changes the answer (it only stays the same when the two numbers are equal) — so the swapping shortcut has a precise stopping point.

activities.title: Same product, different story
feedback: If a learner thinks the stories must be identical because the totals match, point to the different group sizes — 3 bags of 4 is a different arrangement from 4 bags of 3.
If a learner thinks the totals differ because the stories differ, have them count both to 12.
activities.rationale: Connecting commutativity to context distinguishes 'same product' from 'same situation', addressing a listed misconception.
learnerActions: Draw or set out '3 bags of 4' and '4 bags of 3' as two separate situations.
Confirm both give 12, then explain how the stories differ even though the answer is the same.
Match a context picture to the fact it shows, and to its commuted partner.
activities.intendedInsight: Different real situations can share the same product; 'same answer' is not the same as 'same story'.

activities.title: Refute the character who says division swaps too
feedback: A convincing refutation does the sharing: 12 shared into 3 is 4 each, but 3 shared among 12 is less than one.
If the learner just says 'no' without evidence, ask them to show it with counters.
activities.rationale: A character over-generalising invites Socratic refutation; the disproof is more convincing when the learner manipulates quantities and produces a worked counterexample rather than merely asserting, so this works as a supplement to hands-on testing.
learnerActions: Listen to a character claim 'division works both ways, like multiplication — 12÷3 is the same as 3÷12'.
Disagree and give a counterexample, backing it up by sharing counters both ways.
State the correct rule: multiplication can be swapped, division cannot.
activities.intendedInsight: You can justify and defend the boundary of commutativity by producing a worked counterexample, not just asserting it.

constraints: Prove commutativity by action (rotating the array) rather than stating it as a rule; a static paired image or captioned diagram is a useful reference but cannot itself let the learner perform the rotation or test the division counterexample.
Always teach the division (and subtraction) boundary alongside commutativity so learners do not over-generalise 'order doesn't matter'.
True/false, matching and sort tasks check whether the learner holds the property and its boundary, but do not by themselves elicit the structural proof-by-rotation; pair them with hands-on building.

The dialogue/character task is a supplement: the actual disproof should be done by sharing quantities, not by bare assertion alone — a worked counterexample is valid reasoning; an unsupported 'no' is not.
Distinguish 'same product' from 'same situation': commutativity gives the same total, not the same story.
A learner who gets both facts right numerically but justifies only by 'I worked them both out' has not yet reached the structural insight; prompt for the array reason.
Commutativity nearly halves (not exactly halves) the facts to learn, because facts on the diagonal of the multiplication square (e.g. 3×3) have no separate partner.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Of the cited sources, only the DfE National Curriculum claim is marked verified in the row; the CCSS 3.OA.5 and NCETM claims are marked unverified. Do not treat them as confirmed.
Arithmetic checked: 3×4=12 and 4×3=12; 3×5=15 and 5×3=15; 3×8=24 and 8×3=24; 2×9=18 and 9×2=18; 12÷3=4; 3÷12=0.25 (<1); 8−3=5 and 3−8=−5; these are consistent across the activities.

Acting out 3÷12 yields a fractional result (1/4) that sits beyond typical Y2 scope and is awkward with whole counters; it is preserved from the original assessment and used only as an observable 'each gets less than one' contrast, not as formal fraction work.

The original Predict–Observe–Explain assessment task (predict 'more/fewer/same' and why, then build and count) has been reintegrated into Activity 1 as a prediction step so the discriminating commitment is not lost.

The original noted a 3D interactive 'adds nothing conceptual'; this comparative/necessity claim is not established by the sources and has been omitted rather than asserted as a universal law. Planar rotation is sufficient to show the proof, which is retained as a scoped point.

assess.poeTask: Set out 3 groups of 5 counters. Before building the comparison, ask the child to PREDICT: 'If I make 5 groups of 3 instead, will the total be more, fewer, or the same — and why?' They commit to a reason, then build 5 groups of 3 and count. Predicting 'the same' with a rotate/rearrange reason shows commutative understanding; predicting 'different' reveals the order-changes-the-total misconception.
probeDeeper: Show me with an array why 3 × 5 = 5 × 3.
Which is easier to work out, 2 × 9 or 9 × 2? Why does that help?
Draw 12 ÷ 3 and 3 ÷ 12 — do they look the same?
Does swapping work for adding? For subtracting?
assess.correctAnswer: 3 × 5 = 5 × 3 (both 15) — it's the same array turned on its side, so multiplication can be done in either order. But 12 ÷ 3 (= 4) is NOT the same as 3 ÷ 12 (less than one) — division can't be swapped round.

errorPatterns.pattern: over-generalises commutativity to division — thinks 12 ÷ 3 = 3 ÷ 12 because 'order doesn't matter in maths'
errorPatterns.nextMove: act out 12 ÷ 3 (4 each) versus 3 ÷ 12 (sharing 3 among 12) with counters so the difference is felt; contrast with the rotate-the-array move for ×
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says division can be swapped just like multiplication

errorPatterns.pattern: denies 3 × 5 = 5 × 3 — thinks '3 groups of 5' and '5 groups of 3' give different totals because the order changes the meaning
errorPatterns.nextMove: build both sets, count each to 15, then rotate one array onto the other to show the total is identical
errorPatterns.distractor: No, 3 groups of 5 is different from 5 groups of 3.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says they are different amounts

errorPatterns.pattern: accepts 3 × 5 = 5 × 3 numerically but has no structural reason
errorPatterns.nextMove: rotate a 3 × 5 array to 5 × 3 — same counters, same total — so commutativity is seen, not merely checked
errorPatterns.revealedBy: correct answer justified only by 'I worked them both out'

responseLevels.gap: Thinks multiplication order changes the total, or swaps division freely.
responseLevels.full: Explains multiplication commutes using a rotated array, uses it to pick the easier calculation, and shows division does not commute.
responseLevels.partial: Accepts 3 × 5 = 5 × 3 (and that division differs) but justifies only by computing, not by the array structure.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Is 3 × 5 the same as 5 × 3? And is 12 ÷ 3 the same as 3 ÷ 12? For each one, tell me yes or no and how you know.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Pairing × (which commutes) with ÷ (which doesn't) tests whether the child has a REASON — the rotated array, the different meanings of ÷ — rather than an over-general rule 'order doesn't matter'. A child who swaps both has a rule without understanding; one who only checks numerically misses the structural insight.

sources.claim: Y2: show that multiplication of two numbers can be done in any order (commutative) and division of one number by another cannot.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study, Year 2 Multiplication and division

sources.claim: 3.OA.5 apply the commutative property of multiplication as a strategy (know 6×4=24 → 4×6=24).
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 3 Operations & Algebraic Thinking

sources.claim: Commutativity is best proven with the rotated array and used to reduce fact-learning load; children must be taught explicitly that division is not commutative to prevent over-generalisation.
sources.source: NCETM — Primary Mastery Professional Development (Multiplication and Division)

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Multiplication as repeated addition (age 6+)
topic.description: Solve problems involving multiplication and division using arrays, repeated addition, mental methods, and known facts
evidence: Solve 'There are 5 bags with 2 apples in each. How many apples?' using repeated addition or known fact
Solve 'Share 15 sweets equally among 3 children' using grouping
Draw an array to solve a multiplication problem in context
topic.assessmentPrompt: If you tell {{name}} 'you have 5 bags with 4 marbles in each — how many altogether?', can they figure it out using objects, a drawing, or mental adding?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 6–7 (UK Y2, US Grade 2–3). Solving multiplication and division PROBLEMS using arrays, repeated addition, mental methods and known facts — the application layer that ties the early representations to real contexts.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y2 'solve problems involving multiplication and division, using materials, arrays, repeated addition, mental methods, and multiplication and division facts, including problems in contexts'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.OA.4 (array totals via equal addends) building toward 3.OA.3 'use multiplication and division within 100 to solve word problems in situations involving equal groups, arrays, and measurement quantities'.
• Operational details: the goal is to CHOOSE and use an efficient representation for a given problem — an array, repeated addition, a jump on a number line, or a recalled fact — and to recognise whether a story is multiplication or division. Push from counting-all toward using known facts.
• Checkpoint: model and solve in context. Tier A (6): solve a simple equal-groups problem with an array or repeated addition. Tier B (6–7): choose a sensible representation and solve both a grouping and a sharing story. Tier C (7): solve using a known fact rather than counting all, and explain why that's quicker.
bestPractices: Give real, contextual problems (equal groups, arrays, simple sharing) and let children choose the representation — array, repeated addition, number-line jumps, or a known fact — rather than prescribing one method.
Explicitly move children from 'count everything in ones' toward 'use a fact or a group structure', highlighting the efficiency gain so they are motivated to leave counting-all behind.
Include both multiplication and division stories (and both division structures) so problem-recognition — deciding which operation a story needs — is practised, not just computation.
Use the bar model and array to represent the structure of a word problem before calculating, so meaning drives the method.
Connect back to known 2, 5, 10 facts so problem solving rehearses and applies fluency rather than relying on re-counting.
keyRepresentations: Arrays (structure of equal-groups/array problems)
Repeated addition and number-line jumps
Bar model (representing the problem structure)
Known multiplication/division facts applied to context
commonMisconceptions: Counting every object in ones instead of using groups or a known fact — not progressing in efficiency.
Not recognising which operation a word problem needs (multiplication vs division; sharing vs grouping).
Modelling with unequal groups and still treating it as multiplication.
Grabbing the numbers and operating without representing the problem's structure first.
Muddling the roles of the numbers (number of groups vs group size) when setting up the calculation.

learn.summary: For ages 6–7 (UK Y2, US Grade 2–3): solving multiplication and division word problems by CHOOSING and using an efficient representation — an array, repeated addition, number-line jumps, or a recalled fact — and recognising whether a story calls for multiplication (combining equal groups) or division (splitting into equal parts), and within division whether it is sharing or grouping. The developmental goal is to move children from counting everything in ones toward using group structure or known facts, and to represent a problem's structure before calculating.

activities.title: Problem playground: model the story, then solve
feedback: If a child writes 5 + 2 = 7 for '5 bags of 2', act out the five groups with objects, count the total, and connect it to 2+2+2+2+2 and 5×2 so the groups-of structure is felt.

If a child shares 15 among 3 but ends with unequal piles or a miscount, model round-robin 'one for each' dealing and check at the end that the piles are equal — the sharing idea is there, the execution needs tightening.
If an array for 4 × 3 is ragged or has the wrong count, align rows and columns neatly, count rows × per-row, and connect the tidy array back to the numbers 4 and 3.
Correct answers to anchor on: 5 bags of 2 = 10 apples (2+2+2+2+2, or the fact 5×2); 15 shared among 3 = 5 each; 15 in bags of 3 = 5 bags; a 4-by-3 array totals 12.
activities.rationale: Choosing and applying a method across both multiplication and division stories (including both division structures) practises problem-recognition, not just computation, and keeps meaning ahead of calculation. Manipulable modelling lets children see whether their representation matches the story.
sourceClaims: Y2: solve problems involving multiplication and division using materials, arrays, repeated addition, mental methods and facts, including problems in contexts.
3.OA.3 use multiplication and division within 100 to solve word problems involving equal groups, arrays and measurement quantities.
learnerActions: Read a contextual equal-groups or sharing story (e.g. '5 bags with 2 apples in each — how many altogether?').
First decide: is this a multiplication story (combining equal groups) or a division story (splitting into equal parts — by sharing or by grouping)? State your choice before solving.
Choose how to model it: build an array, lay equal jumps on a number line, write it as repeated addition, or use a known fact.
Solve and check that your model actually matches the story (equal groups, the right group size and number of groups).

Repeat with a sharing story (e.g. 'Share 15 sweets equally among 3 children'), a grouping story (e.g. '15 sweets are put into bags of 3 — how many bags?') and an array task (e.g. 'Draw an array for 4 × 3').
activities.intendedInsight: A word problem's structure (equal groups, array, or sharing/grouping) determines which operation and representation fit; meaning should drive the method rather than grabbing the numbers and operating blindly.

activities.title: Count-all vs known fact: the efficiency race
feedback: If a child still counts every object, point out the time/effort difference they just saw and prompt: 'Which fact could land this answer straight away?'
Check that both methods reach the same total. If they agree, that agreement confirms the fact. If they differ, recount, because counting in ones can go wrong too.
Keep any demo total tied to a fact the child actually knows — e.g. if 24 is used, link it to the 2-times fact 2×12, or choose a 5- or 10-fact — so the recall step is genuinely available to them.
activities.rationale: Explicitly highlighting the efficiency gain motivates the shift from counting-all toward using facts — the developmental move this topic exists to produce. A side-by-side comparison makes the gain concrete; the demonstration shows relative speed rather than a proven intervention.
sourceClaims: Y2: solve problems involving multiplication and division using materials, arrays, repeated addition, mental methods and facts, including problems in contexts.
learnerActions: Take one problem whose total comes from a fact the child knows (e.g. 2×12 = 24, a 2-times fact) and solve it two ways: once by counting every object in ones, and once by using the recalled fact.
Watch the counting-all method work slowly up to the total while the known fact lands the answer at once.
Say why the fact is quicker, and try the next problem using a fact instead of counting all.
activities.intendedInsight: For a child who knows the fact, recalling it (or using group structure) is much quicker than counting everything in ones — this efficiency gain is the motivation to leave counting-all behind.

activities.title: Is it × or ÷? Sort and match the stories
feedback: If a story is matched to a wrong-operation sentence, return to acting out the situation to decide whether numbers are combined into equal groups or split into equal parts.
Praise reasoning that cites the story's structure ('there are equal groups, so it's multiplication') rather than guessing from the numbers.
activities.rationale: Matching stories to operations and spotting wrong-operation distractors rehearses and checks problem-recognition. This format exercises operation/method choice but does not itself elicit building a model, so pair it with hands-on modelling.
sourceClaims: Y2: solve problems involving multiplication and division using materials, arrays, repeated addition, mental methods and facts, including problems in contexts.
learnerActions: Read several everyday stories and sort each one: is it a multiplication (combining equal groups) or a division (splitting into equal parts) situation? For each division story, also say whether it is sharing (number of groups known) or grouping (group size known).
Match each story to the number sentence that fits it (e.g. an equal-groups story to 5 × 2, a sharing story to 15 ÷ 3).
For a tricky pair, explain what in the story tells you which operation to use.
Watch for distractors that combine the two numbers with the wrong operation (e.g. 5 + 2 or 15 − 3).
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising which operation a word problem needs — and, within division, whether it is sharing or grouping — is a distinct skill from doing the arithmetic.

activities.title: Market-stall problems: talk through your method
feedback: If a child names a method without justifying it, ask them to point to what in the story makes that method fit.
Follow a spoken plan by actually building or jotting the model, so the reasoning is tied to a concrete representation.
activities.rationale: Prompting children to reason aloud about method choice supports problem-recognition and metacognition. Spoken reasoning elicits articulation and justification but does not itself produce a built model or the side-by-side speed comparison, so pair discussion with hands-on modelling and with the count-all vs known-fact comparison to ground the efficiency insight.
learnerActions: A character (e.g. a market-stall seller) poses an everyday equal-groups buying problem and asks 'how would you work it out?'
Say aloud which operation and representation you would use and why.
Try a follow-up that changes the numbers (e.g. 'If there were 6 bags of 2, how many apples then?') and explain how your method adapts.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to articulate and justify a chosen strategy deepens understanding of why a representation fits a problem.

constraints: Include both multiplication and division stories, and both division structures (sharing and grouping), so problem-recognition is practised — not just computation.
Represent the problem's structure (array, bar model, or number line) before calculating, so meaning drives the method.
Connect back to known 2, 5, 10 facts so problem solving rehearses and applies fluency rather than relying on re-counting; keep any demonstrated fact within the facts the child actually knows.
Let children choose the representation rather than prescribing one method.
Matching/multiple-choice sorting rehearses and checks problem-recognition but does not by itself teach how to construct a model; pair it with hands-on modelling.

A fixed illustrated worked example (tap-to-reveal array and fact) can show one case but cannot provide the varied, decision-rich practice of choosing and applying a method; use it as a scaffold, not the main task.
These problems are modelled with flat arrays, bars and number lines; a 3D presentation is not expected to add conceptual value for this topic — a design judgement here, not a general rule.
Keep the bar model/array as a tool for the structure of the word problem, not as decoration added after the answer.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original 'race to 24' moment is retained as a motivating device; '24' is illustrative, not tied to the worked examples (which total 10, 5 each, and 12). Any concrete total used should match a fact the child actually knows (e.g. 24 = 2×12, a 2-times fact).
The second cited source (CCSS 3.OA.3) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its support as unconfirmed.

The 'efficiency race' and the framing that counting-all is slower are pedagogically motivating but not empirically established comparative efficacy; presented as a demonstration of relative speed, not a proven intervention.
Note 2.OA.4 (array totals via equal addends) was mentioned in the pedagogy as a building-block standard but is not in the row's sources[] list; it is not cited as a sourceClaim.

'Grouping' is treated as one of the two division structures (quotitive), distinct from the equal-groups structure of multiplication; the binary × vs ÷ sorts were reworded to avoid mislabelling multiplication as 'grouping'.

probeDeeper: Which of these is a sharing problem and which is a groups problem?
Could you use a times-table fact instead of drawing it all?
How does your array show 4 × 3?
If there were 6 bags of 2, how many apples then?
assess.correctAnswer: 10 apples (5 groups of 2, or 2+2+2+2+2, or the known fact 5×2); 5 each (15 shared into 3 groups); a 4-by-3 array totalling 12 — choosing a fitting representation and reaching the right total.

errorPatterns.pattern: operation confusion — for '5 bags of 2' writes 5 + 2 = 7, combining the numbers rather than making equal groups
errorPatterns.nextMove: act out the groups with objects, count the total, and connect it to 2+2+2+2+2 and 5×2 so the groups-of structure is felt
errorPatterns.revealedBy: adds or subtracts the two numbers instead of grouping

errorPatterns.pattern: shares unequally or loses track — deals 15 among 3 but ends with unequal piles or miscounts
errorPatterns.nextMove: model round-robin dealing 'one for each' and check the piles are equal at the end — the sharing idea is there, the execution needs tightening
errorPatterns.revealedBy: unequal shares or a wrong count in the sharing task

errorPatterns.pattern: array mismatched to the factors — draws 4 × 3 as a ragged or wrong-count arrangement
errorPatterns.nextMove: align the rows and columns neatly and count rows × per-row; connect the tidy array back to the numbers
errorPatterns.revealedBy: array rows/columns don't line up with 4 and 3

responseLevels.gap: Combines the two numbers with the wrong operation, or cannot represent the situation at all.
responseLevels.full: Chooses a fitting strategy for both grouping and sharing problems, represents each accurately (array / repeated addition / known fact), and reaches correct totals.
responseLevels.partial: Solves the equal-groups problem but is unreliable on sharing, or reaches answers only by drawing every object with no move toward known facts.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Solve these, and show your working with objects, an array, or a jotting. (1) There are 5 bags with 2 apples in each — how many apples altogether? (2) Share 15 sweets equally among 3 children — how many each? (3) Draw an array to work out 4 × 3. (Watch which strategy they choose and whether it fits the problem.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The multiplication and the division sit side by side, so the task reveals whether the child selects the right structure (grouping/repeated addition versus sharing) and can represent it. A struggling child adds or subtracts the two numbers (5+2, 15−3), builds groups of the wrong size, or draws an array that doesn't match the factors. Watching the working — not the answer alone — shows whether the strategy is sound.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Odd and even numbers
topic.description: Recognise odd and even numbers
evidence: Identify whether a given number is odd or even
Explain that even numbers can be divided into 2 equal groups
Spot the pattern: even numbers end in 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8
topic.assessmentPrompt: If you give {{name}} a number like 37 or 84, can they quickly tell you whether it's odd or even — and explain how they know?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 6–7 (UK Y2, US Grade 2). Recognising odd and even numbers — a first structural property of number, tied to the 2s table and divisibility by 2.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y2 'recall and use multiplication and division facts for the 2, 5 and 10 multiplication tables, including recognising odd and even numbers'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.OA.3 'determine whether a group of objects (up to 20) has an odd or even number of members, e.g. by pairing objects or counting them by 2s; write an equation to express an even number as a sum of two equal addends'.
• Operational details: define even/odd by the PAIRING test — even = can be split into pairs with none left over (= 2×something); odd = exactly one left unpaired. Connect to the 2s table (even numbers ARE the multiples of 2) and to the ones-digit rule (ends in 0,2,4,6,8 = even). Note 0 is even.
• Checkpoint: classify by structure. Tier A (6): pair up counters and say odd or even for numbers to 10. Tier B (6–7): classify numbers to 20 and state the ones-digit rule. Tier C (7): explain even as 'two equal groups / 2×n' and why 0 is even.
bestPractices: Define odd/even by pairing objects (or making two equal rows), not by memorised endings first — even means everything pairs up with none left over; odd leaves exactly one.
Connect even numbers to the 2s multiplication table and to '2 × something' / two equal addends, so odd/even is understood as a multiplicative/divisibility property, not an arbitrary label.
Derive the ones-digit rule (ends in 0,2,4,6,8) from the pairing pattern rather than teaching it as a bare fact, and apply it to larger numbers.
Explicitly address that 0 is even (zero objects pair perfectly — none left over) and that odd/even has nothing to do with how big a number is.
Use the hundred square to see even/odd as alternating columns, reinforcing the pattern visually (links to the 2s skip-count pattern).
keyRepresentations: Pairing counters into twos (leftover = odd)
Two equal rows / the 2s array (even = two equal groups)
Ten-frame (full pairs vs one lonely counter)
Hundred square with even numbers shaded (alternating columns)
commonMisconceptions: Thinking odd/even is about a number's SIZE rather than divisibility by 2.
Forgetting that 0 is even.
Judging by the first (leading) digit instead of the ones digit.
Believing a number could be both odd and even, or neither.
Not connecting even numbers to the 2s table / '2×n' — treating the ending rule as unrelated to multiplication.

learn.summary: For ages 6–7 (UK Y2 / US Grade 2), teach odd and even as a structural property of number: even means a count can be split fully into pairs (or two equal groups) with none left over (= 2×something); odd leaves exactly one unpaired. Build the meaning by pairing physical or on-screen counters, connect it to the 2s table and the ones-digit pattern (ends in 0,2,4,6,8), and make clear that 0 is even and that odd/even has nothing to do with a number's size.

activities.title: Pairing machine: pair the counters and spot the leftover
feedback: When a number pairs cleanly, name it: 'Every counter has a partner — that's EVEN, two equal groups of the same size.'
When one is left over, point to it: 'That single counter with no partner is exactly what ODD means.'
On a ten-frame: 'See the filled pairs — if one cell sits alone with no partner, the number is odd.'
After several tests, highlight the shaded hundred square: 'See how even numbers fall in the same columns and all end in 0, 2, 4, 6, 8? That pattern comes from the pairing.'
For 0: 'No counters, so nothing is left over — zero pairs perfectly, so 0 is even.'
If a learner splits 7 into 3 and 4 and calls it even, line the two piles up one-to-one: 'The groups have to match exactly. One counter has no partner, so 7 is odd.'
activities.rationale: Odd/even is defined by the action of pairing, so letting children run the test themselves lets the leftover (the meaning of odd) be seen directly, and lets the digit rule be discovered from the pattern rather than memorised. A ten-frame, an on-screen pairing control with live hundred-square shading, and a two-equal-rows toggle are optional ways to make the pairing mechanism and its link to the 2s table concrete; equivalent work with real counters achieves the same.
sourceClaims: 2.OA.3 determine whether a group (up to 20) is odd or even by pairing or counting by 2s; write an even number as a sum of two equal addends.
learnerActions: Choose a quantity of counters (start with numbers to 10, then extend to 20).
Pair the counters up into twos — physically with real counters, or by tapping a 'pair up' control if using a screen model.
Optionally lay the counters on a ten-frame to see full pairs versus one lonely counter.
Decide: if every counter has a partner, the number is EVEN; if exactly one counter is left on its own, the number is ODD.
Test number after number and watch the result build on a hundred square (even numbers shaded) so the alternating-column / ends-in-0,2,4,6,8 pattern appears.
Use a '2×n' / two-equal-rows view to see each even number as two equal groups, linking it to the 2s table.
Test 0: zero counters, zero left over — so 0 is even.
activities.intendedInsight: Even means everything pairs up with none left over (two equal groups / 2×n); odd means exactly one is left unpaired. The ones-digit rule and the 2s table both come from this pairing structure, not from an arbitrary ending.

activities.title: Introduce with a paired vs leftover picture
feedback: Point to the leftover object: 'This one has no partner — that is what makes the set odd.'
On the hundred square: 'The shaded numbers all end in 0, 2, 4, 6, 8.'
activities.rationale: A fixed image can introduce the paired-vs-leftover contrast and the hundred-square pattern clearly. It cannot be re-run across many different numbers by the learner, so it works best as a first introduction or support alongside hands-on pairing where children test numbers themselves.
learnerActions: Look at a picture that contrasts a set whose objects all pair up (even) with a set that has one object left over (odd).
Tap or point to an even set to reveal its neat pairs; tap an odd set to reveal the single leftover.
Look at a hundred square with even numbers shaded to see the alternating pattern.
activities.intendedInsight: A set that pairs up completely is even; a set with one left over is odd — and even numbers fall in a regular pattern.

activities.title: Sort numbers and check the edge cases
feedback: For 0: 'Zero counters leave nothing over, so 0 is even.'

If a learner uses the first digit (e.g. calls 23 even because of the 2), redirect: 'Look at the ones digit — the tens always pair up, so the ones decide whether one counter is left over. 23 ends in 3, so it is odd.'
For two-digit numbers: 'Tens always pair up, so just check the ones digit.'
activities.rationale: Deliberate edge cases (0, large numbers, a leading-digit distractor) target the common errors that odd/even depends on size or the first digit. A sort can check and practise classification, but it can be answered by the digit rhyme alone without the pairing meaning, so it works best after that meaning is secure and alongside a show-or-explain step.
learnerActions: Sort a mix of numbers (including 0 and two-digit numbers to 20) into 'odd' and 'even' boxes.
Answer: is 0 odd or even? Explain why.
Find the number that breaks a stated rule, and resist a distractor that judges by the leading (first) digit instead of the ones digit.
activities.intendedInsight: The classification holds for every whole number, including0. In base ten, each ten can be paired fully, so the ones digit determines whether a counter remains unpaired; a number’s size or leading digit does not decide its parity.

activities.title: Predict before you pair: does adding one change it?
feedback: Strong reasoning sounds like: 'It will be odd, because the new one has no partner.'
If a learner cannot predict and only reports after counting, revisit pairing: 'Each pair needs two. One extra counter has nobody to pair with, so the total becomes odd.'
Confirm by pairing: '6 made 3 pairs; the 7th counter is left over, so 7 is odd.'
activities.rationale: Asking for the reason before observing distinguishes genuine pairing understanding from reciting the last-digit rule, which is the key diagnostic distinction for this topic.
learnerActions: Start with 6 counters (even). Before touching them, predict whether adding ONE more will keep it even or make it odd — and say why.
Add the counter and pair them up to check your prediction.
Explain the result using pairing: the new counter either finds a partner or is left alone.
activities.intendedInsight: Adding one counter to an even number leaves one unpaired, making it odd; the reason stated before checking shows whether a learner understands pairing or is only reading off a label afterwards.

constraints: Define odd/even by pairing (or making two equal rows) first; introduce the ones-digit rule as something derived from the pairing pattern, not as a bare fact to memorise.
Insist that the two groups be EQUAL and match one-to-one: splitting 7 into 3 and 4 does not make it even. Line the piles up so the unpaired counter is visible.
Explicitly address that 0 is even (zero counters, none left over) and that odd/even is independent of a number's size.
A paired-vs-leftover picture is an introduction/support: it cannot be run across many numbers by the learner, so pair it with hands-on testing.

A sorting/choice check can teach and check classification but may be answered by the digit rhyme alone; use it after the pairing meaning is secure, and include a show-or-explain step to confirm understanding.
Do not accept the last-digit rule as proof of understanding — ask the learner to show the pairing and explain why one is left over.
Recognition or labelling tasks do not by themselves show that a learner can construct and justify the pairing; include predict-and-explain or show-with-counters tasks.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original source asserted that a dialogue 'offers little a talking partner uniquely adds' and that '3D adds nothing' for this planar property; these comparative/necessity claims are not established by the available sources and have been dropped rather than propagated. Spoken explanation (e.g. the predict-and-explain task) is in fact used here during teaching.

The original marked an on-screen pairing tool as the uniquely 'ideal' format; this has been softened to an optional way to make the mechanism concrete, since the sources do not establish comparative efficacy of one medium over hands-on counters.

The Y2 DfE curriculum statement ('recognising odd and even numbers' within the 2, 5 and 10 tables) is topic/coverage context only; it has been removed from activity sourceClaims because it asserts no teaching method, and is retained here solely as curriculum context. The 2s-table link remains as design rationale.
One source (CCSS 2.OA.3) is marked verified:false in the row; it is cited because it directly describes the pairing/counting-by-2s method, but its verification is unconfirmed.

Self-audit: pairing arithmetic checked — 8 = 4 pairs (even), 7 = 3 pairs + 1 leftover (odd), 6 = 3 pairs (even), adding 1 to 6 gives 7 (odd), 23 ends in 3 so is odd. The '3 and 4' split of 7 is correctly identified as unequal and therefore NOT evidence of evenness. The leading-digit distractor (e.g. 23 judged by the '2') is corrected to the ones-digit rule in the activity.

assess.poeTask: Give the child 6 counters (even) and ask them to predict, before touching them, whether adding ONE more counter will keep it even or make it odd — and to say why. Then add the counter and pair them up to check. The value is the reason stated before observing: a child who understands pairing predicts 'odd, because the new one has no partner'; a child on the digit-rule alone often cannot predict and only reads off afterwards.
probeDeeper: You paired them up. What does having one left over tell you about 7?
Is 10 odd or even? Can you tell without laying out ten counters?
If I add one more counter to an even pile, does it stay even? Why?
Someone split 7 into 3 and 4 and said it's even. What would you tell them?
assess.correctAnswer: 7 is odd, 8 is even. A child reasoning correctly pairs the counters up (or splits into two equal groups): 8 makes 4 pairs with none left over, so it is even; 7 makes 3 pairs with one left over, so it is odd — even means it can be shared into two equal groups (or all paired) with nothing left, odd leaves one.

errorPatterns.pattern: decides odd/even by counting-to-say only — knows the last-digit rule but cannot connect it to pairing; thinks 'even' just means 'a number you say when counting by twos'
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT accept the digit rule as proof — have the child pair the counters physically and name 'even = everyone has a partner, odd = one left alone'; connect it back to why the digits work only after the pairing meaning is secure.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child gives the right label but, asked to show it, cannot make the pairs relevant or says 'because it just is / because it ends in 8'

errorPatterns.pattern: thinks a number is even if it can be split into two groups AT ALL, ignoring that the groups must be EQUAL (splits 7 into 3 and 4 and calls it even)
errorPatterns.nextMove: insist the two groups match one-to-one; line the piles up side by side so the leftover in 7 is visibly unpaired.
errorPatterns.distractor: 7 is even (I can make two groups: 3 and 4)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child divides 7 into two unequal piles and declares it even 'because there are two groups'

errorPatterns.pattern: believes larger numbers are 'more even' or that odd/even alternates unreliably for big numbers — unsure whether e.g. 10 is even because 'it's a big number'
errorPatterns.nextMove: show that only the pairing of the LAST counter matters; group in tens (always even) and check the ones, so the rule scales.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child hesitates or guesses on two-digit numbers, treating the property as tied to size not structure

responseLevels.gap: labels by rote or guesses; cannot demonstrate with counters; or calls unequal-split numbers even.
responseLevels.full: shows even = full pairing / two equal groups and odd = one left over, explains the leftover as the defining feature, and extends the reasoning to larger numbers via the last digit.
responseLevels.partial: correctly pairs the counters and identifies odd/even for the presented numbers but relies on the last-digit rule for others with no link to pairing — cannot explain why the rule works.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are 7 counters. Is 7 odd or even? Now here are 8 counters — is 8 odd or even? For each one, show me with the counters how you can tell.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Many children label numbers odd/even purely by the last digit rhyme without any idea of WHY. Demanding they SHOW it with counters separates a memorised digit-rule from the pair/equal-share meaning. The child who only knows 'ends in 0,2,4,6,8' cannot demonstrate the leftover, and stumbles on the reason tier.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Reading ×, ÷, and = Symbols
topic.description: Read, write, and interpret the symbols ×, ÷, and = in multiplication and division number sentences
evidence: Read 3 × 4 = 12 aloud as 'three times four equals twelve'
Write a multiplication sentence to match an array
Read 12 ÷ 3 = 4 aloud correctly
topic.assessmentPrompt: If you write '6 × 4 = 24' or '15 ÷ 3 = 5' on paper, can {{name}} tell you what the times sign, division sign, and equals sign each mean?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 6–7 (UK Y2, US Grade 3). Reading, writing and interpreting the ×, ÷ and = symbols in multiplication and division number sentences — the notation that records the concepts (LANGUAGE topic).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y2 'calculate mathematical statements for multiplication and division within the multiplication tables and write them using the multiplication (×), division (÷) and equals (=) signs'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 3.OA.1/3.OA.2 interpret products and quotients; the equals sign as relational is emphasised across CCSS-M (e.g. 3.OA.4 finding the unknown that makes an equation true).
• Operational details: bind each symbol to a meaning and a representation — × = 'groups of' / an array, ÷ = sharing or grouping, = 'is the same value as' (NOT 'the answer comes next'). The relational meaning of = is the load-bearing idea: children must accept 12 = 3×4 and 3×4 = 2×6 as valid. Translate freely between story, picture and symbol sentence.
• Checkpoint: read, write and balance. Tier A (6): write × and = to match an array (3×4=12). Tier B (6–7): write a division sentence for a sharing story and read it aloud correctly. Tier C (7): judge whether sentences like 12 = 3×4 and 10 = 2×5 are true, showing = means 'same value'.
bestPractices: Attach every symbol to its meaning and a representation: × read as 'groups of' shown by an array, ÷ read as 'shared into / grouped into' shown by counters, = spoken as 'is the same value as'.

Directly confront the equals-sign misconception: use a balance model and present sentences with the answer on the LEFT (12 = 3×4) and equalities with no operation on the right (3×4 = 2×6) so = cannot be misread as 'write the answer here'.
Have children translate in all directions — story → array → symbol sentence and back — so the notation is a record of meaning, not a detached ritual.
Read sentences aloud precisely, attending to order for division (12÷3 is 'twelve divided by three', not 'three into twelve' muddled), since ÷ is not commutative.
Contrast × with + explicitly (3×4 is not 3+4) to prevent symbol confusion.
keyRepresentations: Number sentences mapping symbols to arrays/groups
Balance / pan-scale model for the equals sign (relational meaning)
Story ↔ array ↔ symbol translation triples
Symbol reference (×, ÷, = with spoken names and meanings)
commonMisconceptions: Reading = as 'the answer is / write the result here' (operational) rather than 'is the same value as' (relational) — the single most damaging notation error, blocking later algebra.
Rejecting true sentences like 12 = 3×4 or 3×4 = 2×6 because 'the sum isn't on the right'.
Confusing × with + (treating 3×4 as 3+4).
Writing division in the wrong order (since ÷ is not commutative, 12÷3 and 3÷12 are different).
Reading a symbol sentence with no attached meaning — manipulating symbols without knowing what they represent.

learn.summary: For ages 6–7 (UK Year 2, roughly US Grade 1), teach children to read, write and interpret the ×, ÷ and = symbols in multiplication and division number sentences. Bind each symbol to a meaning and a representation: × as 'groups of' shown by an array, ÷ as 'shared/grouped into' shown by counters, and = as 'is the same value as' shown by a level balance. The load-bearing idea is the relational meaning of =: children must accept 12 = 3×4 and 3×4 = 2×6 as valid, so = is never misread as 'write the answer here'. Children should translate freely between story, picture and symbol sentence and read sentences aloud precisely, respecting that ÷ is not commutative.

activities.title: Build-and-balance: linking pictures, symbol sentences and equal value
feedback: If a child writes 3 + 4 for an array of 3 rows of 4, show the repeated equal groups and contrast: 3 × 4 is three groups of four (12), while 3 + 4 is just 3 and 4 together (7).

If a child swaps × and ÷ (reading 3 × 4 as 'three divided by four', or choosing ÷ for the array), anchor each symbol to its action: × builds equal groups into a total, while ÷ breaks a whole up into equal parts; pair each symbol with its picture repeatedly.
If a child can read 3 × 4 = 12 aloud but cannot produce a sentence for a picture, scaffold with 'how many rows? how many in each? so what times what?' to move from picture to words to symbols.

When a child is uneasy that 12 = 3×4 'is backwards', place 12 identical cubes on one pan and 3 groups of 4 of the same cubes on the other (or use a screen balance) and let them see the beam sit level — same value, either way round.
If a child balances 3×4 against 2×6, invite them to count each side (12 and 12) and state that equal value is why = links them.

When 3×4 is set against 3+4 (built from identical cubes) and the beam tips, ask the child to say which side is heavier and by how much (12 cubes against 7, so 5 more), reinforcing that = requires genuine sameness.
activities.rationale: Attaching every symbol to both a spoken meaning and a representation, and using a balance so = is felt as sameness, targets a well-documented and damaging notation error (reading = as 'write the answer'), which the cited sources describe as a barrier to later algebra. A live balance and auto-forming picture make the sameness and the symbol–meaning bond concrete; a linked build-and-record surface and a pan-balance are two optional interaction examples that make the mechanism vivid without being the only way to teach it.
sourceClaims: Y2: calculate mathematical statements for multiplication and division within the tables and write them using the ×, ÷ and = signs.
The equals sign must be taught as relational ('same value as') not operational ('write the answer'); the operational misconception is a well-documented barrier to later algebra.
learnerActions: Make an array (for example 3 rows of 4 counters) and write the multiplication sentence that matches it: 3 × 4 = 12.
Share a set of counters into equal groups (for example 12 counters shared into 3 groups of 4) and write the matching division sentence: 12 ÷ 3 = 4.
Go the other direction too: given a sentence like 2 × 5 = 10, build the array or grouping picture that matches it.

Place expressions on each side of a two-pan balance and check whether it sits level: show 12 as 12 identical cubes on the LEFT pan and 3 × 4 as 3 groups of 4 of the same cubes on the right (or use a screen balance), and check that the beam sits level.
Using the same identical cubes, try 3 × 4 against 2 × 6 (it should balance) and 3 × 4 against 3 + 4 (it should tip), and say in words why each result makes sense.
Say each symbol aloud as you work: × as 'times / groups of', ÷ as 'divided by', = as 'is the same value as'.
activities.intendedInsight: Each symbol records a meaning and a picture, and = means 'the two sides have the same value' — not 'the answer comes next'. A true equation can be written with the product on the left (12 = 3×4) or with an expression on each side (3×4 = 2×6).

activities.title: Symbol reference you build and talk about
feedback: If a child names a symbol but not its meaning, ask them to show the matching picture too, so name, meaning and picture always travel together.
Caption the = picture with 'same value as' and revisit it whenever a child defaults to 'the answer'.
activities.rationale: A concise symbol reference supports a notation topic and keeps spoken names bound to meanings and pictures. On its own it supports recall and self-checking but does not exercise the relational balance or translation, so it works best alongside the build-and-balance activity rather than replacing it.
learnerActions: For each of ×, ÷ and =, record its spoken name, its meaning, and a small picture: × = 'groups of' with an array; ÷ = 'shared into / grouped into' with counters; = 'is the same value as' with a level balance.
Point to each symbol and say its name and meaning aloud before using it in a sentence.
Use the reference to check yourself while writing a sentence for a new picture.
activities.intendedInsight: Notation is a record of meaning: knowing the name, meaning and picture for each symbol lets you read and write sentences deliberately rather than by rote.

activities.title: Read, write and judge sentences aloud
feedback: If a child reads 12 ÷ 3 as 'three into twelve' muddled with order, slow down and separate: the first number is the whole being divided.
If a child rejects 12 = 3 × 4 as 'not allowed', return to the balance idea: both sides have value 12, so = fits.
For a false equation such as 10 = 2 × 4, have the child compute each side (10 and 8) and state that unequal values mean = does not hold.
activities.rationale: True/false judgements on reversed and operation-free equalities are especially diagnostic of the relational-equals idea, and reading aloud with correct order exposes ÷ order errors. Judging truth and producing sentences goes beyond recognition toward independent reading and writing.
sourceClaims: The equals sign must be taught as relational ('same value as') not operational ('write the answer'); the operational misconception is a well-documented barrier to later algebra.
3.OA.1/3.OA.2 interpret products and quotients; CCSS-M emphasises the equals sign as relational (the unknown that makes an equation true, 3.OA.4).
learnerActions: Read 3 × 4 = 12 aloud as 'three times four equals twelve' and 12 ÷ 3 = 4 as 'twelve divided by three equals four'.
Write a division sentence for a sharing story and read it back correctly, keeping the order right: 12 ÷ 3, not 3 ÷ 12.
Judge whether sentences are true: is 12 = 3 × 4 true? is 10 = 2 × 5 true? is 3 × 4 = 2 × 6 true? Explain each answer using 'same value'.
Fill in a missing symbol in a sentence (for example 3 __ 4 = 12) and justify the choice.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading order matters for ÷ because it is not commutative, and deciding whether an equation is true tests whether = is understood as 'same value'.

activities.title: Convince the doubter
feedback: Prompt the child to back up their justification with a count of each side (both are 12) or a balance check rather than just asserting it.
If the child cannot explain, return to building the two sides and comparing their values.
activities.rationale: Having to justify a true equation against a mistaken claim gives mild Socratic value and surfaces the child's reasoning. This is a supplement to, not a substitute for, the hands-on balance work where the sameness is directly experienced.
sourceClaims: The equals sign must be taught as relational ('same value as') not operational ('write the answer'); the operational misconception is a well-documented barrier to later algebra.
learnerActions: Respond to a character who insists '3 × 4 = 2 × 6 can't be right' and explain, using value or a balance, why it is correct.
Respond to a character who reads = as 'the answer goes next' and show them 12 = 3 × 4 to correct the idea.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to justify why an unusual-looking equation is true cements the relational meaning of = more firmly than just accepting it.

constraints: The relational meaning of = ('is the same value as') is the load-bearing idea; never let = be presented or read as 'the answer comes next'. Deliberately include equations with the product on the left (12 = 3×4) and with an expression on each side (3×4 = 2×6).
Keep division order explicit: ÷ is not commutative, so 12 ÷ 3 and 3 ÷ 12 are different; the first number is the whole being divided.
Explicitly contrast × with + (3 × 4 is three groups of four = 12, not 3 + 4 = 7) to prevent symbol confusion.
A symbol-reference display supports recall and self-checking but does not exercise the balance or translation; use it alongside the build-and-balance work, not instead of it.
True/false and fill-in-symbol items check reading and judging, but children must also PRODUCE a sentence for a picture; recognition-only tasks do not show independent construction.

A flat/planar treatment suits this abstract notation; no claim is made that any one medium is required — paper, counters and a screen model can each serve. A physical pan balance and a screen balance offer different experiences of the same sameness idea.

Interaction examples such as auto-forming pictures, typing a sentence to build a picture, dragging expressions onto pans, and a live tipping beam are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory features.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three cited sources are marked unverified in the source row (the CCSS-M Grade 3 claim and the NCETM/relational-equals claim). The relational-equals teaching principle is widely discussed in mathematics education (e.g. Carpenter, Franke & Levi), but comparative efficacy or necessity of any specific activity or medium is not established by these sources.

The original research asserted '3D adds no value', framed the balance tool as uniquely able to fix the relational-equals misconception, and called the operational-equals error 'the single most damaging notation error'; these comparative/necessity/superlative claims are not established by the cited sources and have been softened to scoped proposals and the source-supported 'barrier to later algebra'.
Restored two source error-pattern responses that an earlier draft had dropped: the ×/÷ swap reteach and the 'can read but not generate' scaffold are in the build-and-balance feedback.

Self-audit of arithmetic in examples: 3 × 4 = 12, 2 × 6 = 12, 2 × 5 = 10, 12 ÷ 3 = 4 all check out; 3 + 4 = 7 (distinct from 3 × 4). The false example 10 = 2 × 4 used in feedback evaluates to 8 ≠ 10, correctly illustrating a false equation.

probeDeeper: Which picture goes with a ÷ sentence? Why?
Read this: 12 = 3 × 4 — is that allowed?
Say a 'times' sentence for 2 rows of 5.
What does the = sign tell you?
assess.correctAnswer: For the array: 'three times four equals twelve' (3 × 4 = 12). For the sharing: 'twelve divided by three equals four' (12 ÷ 3 = 4). Reads × as 'times/multiplied by', ÷ as 'divided by', and = as 'equals / is the same as'.

errorPatterns.pattern: swaps × and ÷ — reads or writes one where the other is meant; the two symbols aren't distinguished
errorPatterns.nextMove: anchor each symbol to its action — × builds equal groups into a total, ÷ breaks the whole up — pairing symbol with picture repeatedly
errorPatterns.revealedBy: reads 3 × 4 as 'three divided by four', or picks ÷ for the array

errorPatterns.pattern: reads = only as 'makes the answer' — uneasy with sentences like 12 = 3 × 4 that aren't written answer-on-the-right
errorPatterns.nextMove: read = as 'is the same as / balances' and show true equations written both ways round
errorPatterns.revealedBy: rejects or mis-reads an equation not in 'sum = answer' form

errorPatterns.pattern: can read but not generate — reads 3 × 4 = 12 aloud but can't produce a sentence to match the picture
errorPatterns.nextMove: scaffold 'how many rows? how many in each? so…' to move from picture to words to symbols
errorPatterns.revealedBy: fluent reading, but stuck when asked to say/write a sentence for the array or sharing picture

responseLevels.gap: Swaps × and ÷, or reads = only as 'the answer is'; cannot match a symbol sentence to a picture.
responseLevels.full: Reads ×, ÷, = accurately, generates a correct number sentence for both a grouping and a sharing picture, and treats = as 'is the same as'.
responseLevels.partial: Reads the standard sentences correctly but hesitates to generate one for a picture, or is unsettled by equations not written answer-on-the-right.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Look at this array (3 rows of 4) and this picture of 12 sweets shared into 3 groups of 4. Say out loud a number sentence that goes with each picture, using the words 'times', 'divided by', and 'equals'. Then read these back to me: 3 × 4 = 12 and 12 ÷ 3 = 4.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Because the child must PRODUCE a sentence for a picture and READ symbols aloud, the task shows whether the symbols carry meaning. A child who has it maps × to the grouping picture and ÷ to the sharing picture and reads both fluently. A child without it swaps × and ÷, reads = only as 'makes the answer', or can read the symbols but cannot generate a sentence for the picture.
