topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Sharing and grouping problems
topic.description: Model practical equal-sharing and grouping problems up to about 30 with diagrams, physical objects and virtual materials (dragging on-screen objects into equal groups or arrays), and solve them using skip counting or repeated addition
evidence: Solve 'share 18 stickers equally among 3 friends' by dragging on-screen stickers into 3 groups and say each friend gets 6
Solve 'how many bags of 5 apples can we make from 20?' with real apples or counters and skip count the bags
Draw a diagram of 4 tables with 4 chairs each and check the total of 16 with an on-screen array
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to share 18 stickers equally among 3 friends, can they work it out by sorting them into groups — either with the real stickers or on a tablet?

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: What Multiplication Means
topic.description: Interpret products of whole numbers (e.g. 5 × 7 as the total number of objects in 5 groups of 7)
evidence: Explain that 4 × 6 means 4 groups of 6 objects
Draw a picture or array to represent a multiplication expression
Match a multiplication expression to a word problem involving equal groups
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees '5 × 7' written down, can they explain it means 5 groups with 7 in each group — not just recite the answer '35'?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 8–9y; interpret products of whole numbers: 5 × 7 means 5 groups of 7 (equal-groups structure made explicit and named).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y3 pupils develop reliable methods and 'solve problems, including missing number problems, involving multiplication', building on Y2 recall of 2/5/10 tables and the equal-groups meaning of ×.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 3.OA.1 — 'Interpret products of whole numbers, e.g., interpret 5 × 7 as the total number of objects in 5 groups of 7 objects.'
• Operational details — the first factor is the number of groups, the second the group size (adopt one convention explicitly, but show children the answer is the same either way — a bridge to commutativity). Move deliberately from repeated addition (7+7+7+7+7) to the compact product 5×7, so × is seen as a shorthand for equal groups, not a brand-new operation. Use the three canonical models in parallel: equal groups (collections), arrays (rows×columns), and number-line hops of equal size.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8): given 4 × 6, say/draw 4 groups of 6 and give the total. Tier B (age 8–9): match a × expression to the correct equal-groups word problem and to an array. Tier C (age 9): write a × expression for a picture AND explain what each factor represents (groups vs group size).
bestPractices: Bridge explicitly from repeated addition: write 7+7+7+7+7 alongside 5×7 so the product is felt as a compression of equal groups, not a new fact to memorise.
Use the three-model triangle — equal groups, array, equal-hops on a number line — and have children translate one representation into the others; fluency in switching is the concept.
Insist on language: read 5 × 7 as 'five groups of seven', and always name what each factor means, so children do not treat × as a meaningless symbol between two numbers.
Follow CPA: concrete counters into hoops → pictorial array/bar → abstract expression, keeping the equal-groups meaning visible at each step.
Contrast equal-groups situations with unequal-groups ones (3+5+4 is NOT multiplication) so children abstract the 'equal' in equal groups.
keyRepresentations: Equal groups (counters in hoops / bags of sweets) — the primary meaning of a product
Rectangular array (rows × columns) — makes the total structured and countable, and previews commutativity and area
Number line with equal-sized hops — links × to skip counting and to scaling
Bar model / repeated-addition strip — 5 equal bars of 7 bridging + to ×
commonMisconceptions: Reading 5 × 7 as '5 and 7' or adding the factors (5+7=12) rather than seeing groups.
Confusing which factor is the number of groups vs the group size, then drawing 7 groups of 5 for '5 groups of 7' — harmless for the product but a sign the structure isn't understood.
Believing the groups need not be equal — counting any collection as multiplication.
Thinking × always makes a 'much bigger' number and being surprised by ×1 or (later) ×0 and fractional factors.
Treating × as an unrelated new operation rather than a shorthand for repeated equal addition.

learn.summary: For 8–9 year olds, build the meaning of a product as equal groups: 5 × 7 means 5 groups of 7, totalling 35. Move deliberately from repeated addition (7+7+7+7+7) to the compact product, naming what each factor represents (number of groups vs group size), and translate between equal-groups collections, rectangular arrays, and equal-sized number-line hops. The central idea to establish is that the groups must be equal, and that × is a shorthand for repeated equal addition, not a brand-new operation.

activities.title: Equal-groups builder: set the groups and the group size
feedback: If a child makes the groups unequal, point out the arrangement can't be written as one × expression until every group matches — this is the 'equal' in equal groups.
When a child writes 5 × 7, have them point to the five hoops and to the seven counters inside one hoop, naming each factor's job.
If a child reads 5 × 7 as '5 and 7' or expects 5+7=12, set the array and the sum 7+7+7+7+7 side by side and count the total (35) together to show it is not simple addition of the two numbers.
activities.rationale: Letting quantity drive a linked visual — hoops, array, and repeated-addition sum updating together — is intended to let 'groups of' be felt rather than told, and surfacing the equal-groups constraint directly addresses the misconception that any collection counts as multiplication. Live recolouring/relinking of the three representations is an optional interaction example that makes the mechanism concrete, not a required feature.
sourceClaims: Equal-groups, array, and number-line models should be used in parallel and translated between to build the meaning of multiplication (CRA/CPA progression).
learnerActions: Choose how many groups and how many in each group (for example, 5 groups of 7), then place that many counters into each hoop.
Watch an array of rows × columns assemble beside the hoops and a running repeated-addition sum (7+7+7+7+7) build underneath, all three reading the same total.
Collapse the long sum into the product by writing it as 5 × 7, and read it aloud as 'five groups of seven'.
Deliberately drag one extra counter into a single hoop so the groups become unequal, and notice the arrangement can no longer be written as a single product until all groups match again.
Vary the two quantities and say, each time, which number is the number of groups and which is the size of each group.
activities.intendedInsight: A product is equal groups counted efficiently: the total recomputes as you change how many groups and how many per group, and the groups must be equal for a single multiplication to describe them. Repeated addition and the product are two forms of the same quantity.

activities.title: Concrete to pictorial to symbol with real counters
feedback: If a child draws 6 groups of 4 for 'four baskets of six', agree the total is the same (24) but map the story precisely: 4 baskets (groups), each holding 6.
If a drawing is correct but the equation is hesitant, label the array's rows and columns and read both factors off the picture to bridge drawing to symbols.
If the number-line hops are unequal, point out each hop must be the same size (6) precisely because the groups are equal.

For the unequal example, ask what single number is in every group as the groups stand; show that there isn't one, so no single × expression describes these groups. (If a child notices the 12 counters could be shared out again into 3 groups of 4, agree: that is a new, equal grouping, so it can be written as 3 × 4.)
activities.rationale: A concrete-pictorial-abstract progression keeps the equal-groups meaning visible at each step, and explicitly contrasting equal with unequal groups helps children abstract the 'equal' requirement. Paper, counters, drawn arrays and a number line are welcome concrete media here, and the number-line hops realise the third canonical model.
sourceClaims: Equal-groups, array, and number-line models should be used in parallel and translated between to build the meaning of multiplication (CRA/CPA progression).
learnerActions: Put physical counters into hoops or bags to make, say, 4 groups of 6, and count the total.
Redraw the same situation as a rectangular array of 4 rows of 6 (or 6 rows of 4) and as a repeated-addition strip of 4 equal bars of 6.
Show the same four groups of six as four equal hops of 6 along a number line (0 → 6 → 12 → 18 → 24), landing on the total.
Write the matching expression and label which factor is the number of groups and which is the group size.
Contrast with an unequal collection such as 3 + 5 + 4 and explain why, as the groups stand, it cannot be written as a single multiplication.
activities.intendedInsight: The same equal-groups quantity can be shown concretely, pictorially, on a number line and symbolically, and only equal groups can be written as a single product; unequal groups cannot.

activities.title: Labelled reference diagram with reveal callouts
feedback: If a child can state the total but not what each factor means, direct them back to the specific callout for that factor.
Accept any wording for the 'why 5 × 7' question that expresses 'seven added five times' or 'five equal groups of seven'.
activities.rationale: A static labelled diagram with tap-to-reveal callouts is a clean vocabulary anchor. It names the structure well but does not let the child vary the numbers, so it supports reference and language rather than building the varying-quantity intuition; pair it with a manipulable activity.
learnerActions: Study a labelled picture of 5 groups of 7 (or a 5×7 array) and reveal callouts naming each part: '5 = number of groups', '7 = size of each group', '35 = total'.
Answer the prompt 'Why can we write 5 × 7 instead of 7+7+7+7+7?' in your own words.
Use the diagram as a reference while naming the factors in a new expression.
activities.intendedInsight: Each factor in a product has a distinct meaning — number of groups versus group size — and the product is the total of equal groups.

activities.title: Match, sort and consolidate (checking understanding)
feedback: If a child matches a '4 + 6' story to 4 × 6, build the four groups of six, count 24, and set it beside 4 + 6 = 10 so the difference between joining two numbers and making four equal groups is visible.
If a match is right but the reason is 'there's a 4 and a 6', ask them to point to the four groups and the six in each before accepting it.
activities.rationale: Matching and sorting tasks are highly checkable and good for consolidation and diagnosis, including a deliberate add-the-factors wrong option (a '4 + 6' story). A sort can check or reinforce classification of situations as equal-groups or not, but does not by itself elicit the child's own construction or explanation, so use it after hands-on construction.
learnerActions: Link an expression such as 4 × 6 to its array, its equal-groups picture, and a matching word problem.
Build or order the repeated-addition sum (6+6+6+6) that corresponds to a given product.
Decide whether a given story shows equal groups (multiplication) or just two numbers joined (addition), explaining the choice.
Spot and reject a tempting wrong match, such as a '4 + 6' story offered for 4 × 6, explaining why it does not fit.
activities.intendedInsight: Interpreting a product means connecting an expression to its equal-groups structure, its array, its repeated-addition form and a real situation — and distinguishing it from merely adding the two numbers seen.

activities.title: Explain equal groups to a puzzled partner
feedback: If the explanation only restates the numbers, ask the partner's follow-up 'how many groups, and how many in each?' to push toward structure.
If a story has unequal groups, ask whether every bag has the same number, and have them adjust it.
activities.rationale: Spoken explanation and responsive questioning can surface a child's own language for 'groups of' and probe factor meaning. A conversation on its own cannot display a recomputing array or collection, so use talk alongside a picture or array that shows the total.
learnerActions: Take the role of explaining to a younger friend (or a market stall-holder counting bags of apples) what 5 × 7 means.
Answer the partner's probing questions: 'How many bags, and how many in each?' and 'What does the 5 mean here?'
Tell a short story that matches a given product such as 3 × 5, naming the groups and the group size.
activities.intendedInsight: Putting equal-groups meaning into your own words can reveal and strengthen understanding of which factor is the number of groups and which is the group size.

constraints: Adopt one convention for reading the factors (first = number of groups, second = group size), but show that the total is the same either way as a bridge to commutativity; do not treat a right total with swapped factors as a product error.

Groups must be equal for a situation to be written as a single product; unequal collections as given (e.g. 3+5+4) cannot be described by one product and should be used as explicit non-examples, while acknowledging that regrouping the counters into equal groups (e.g. 3 groups of 4) creates a new equal-groups situation.

Reference diagrams and recognition/matching/sorting tasks check or anchor vocabulary and classification; they do not by themselves elicit independent construction or explanation, so pair them with activities where the child builds groups and writes the expression.
Spoken-explanation activities are a supplement: keep a visible array or collection alongside so the total and structure are shown, not only described.
Keep repeated addition visible next to the product at each step so × is experienced as a compression of equal addition, not a separate memorised fact.
Avoid implying × always makes a 'much bigger' number; this prepares for later ×1, ×0 and fractional factors without surprise.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit: 5 × 7 = 35 and 4 × 6 = 24 confirmed; repeated-addition forms (7 five times; 6 four times) are consistent, and the number-line hops 0→6→12→18→24 equal 24. 4 + 6 = 10 correctly contrasted with 4 × 6 = 24 in the misconception feedback.

Swapping factors (6 groups of 4 vs 4 groups of 6) gives the same total but a different match to a story; this is a matching/structure issue, not a wrong product — preserved as such, not framed as an arithmetic error.
Efficacy wording in the rationales uses intended/may because the activities are unvalidated proposals.

The equal-sized number-line hop model is now instantiated as a learner action and feedback item within the concrete-to-pictorial activity; it remains lighter than the equal-groups and array strands, so a dedicated skip-counting activity could further strengthen the three-model triangle.

Two of the three cited sources (3.OA.1 CCSS and the NCETM/CPA guidance) are marked verified:false in the source row; the DfE National Curriculum claim is marked verified:true. Cited claims support general teaching principles only and do not establish that these specific activities were tested or are comparatively more effective. The 3.OA.1 claim was not cited on any activity because it names the objective rather than any activity's specific teaching mechanism.

The non-preferred 3D option was omitted because its content was a ranking rationale (that a third spatial dimension adds no new information for planar equal-groups work) rather than a distinct teaching activity; this is a scoped observation, not an established universal law.
Quiz-step vocabulary (including 'distractor') and internal artefact-type labels were removed from learner-facing text per the brief.

probeDeeper: Draw me 4 × 6 — what does each part of your drawing show?
Is 4 × 6 the same total as 4 + 6? Why not?
Tell me a story that matches 3 × 5.
If each basket had 6 eggs and there were 5 baskets, how would the expression change?
assess.correctAnswer: 4 × 6 (and 6 + 6 + 6 + 6) — it's 4 groups of 6, so it's 6 added four times, total 24. 4 + 6 would just be one 4 and one 6 joined, not four groups of six.

errorPatterns.pattern: adds the two numbers — reads a multiplication story as 'combine the numbers I see' (4 + 6 = 10) rather than four groups of six
errorPatterns.nextMove: build the four groups of six with counters or an array, count the total, and set it beside 4 + 6 so the difference between joining two numbers and making equal groups is visible
errorPatterns.revealedBy: chooses 4 + 6, or answers 10

errorPatterns.pattern: mis-maps which factor is the number of groups and which is the group size — draws 6 groups of 4 for 'four baskets of six'
errorPatterns.nextMove: agree the total is the same, then map the story precisely — 4 baskets (groups) each holding 6 — and discuss how the two factors play different roles in context
errorPatterns.revealedBy: draws 6 rows of 4 (right total, wrong match to the story)

errorPatterns.pattern: draws equal groups correctly but can't connect them to the expression — can't say which number is the groups and which the size
errorPatterns.nextMove: label the array's rows and columns and read off both factors, bridging drawing to symbols — the group idea is there, only the link to notation is missing
errorPatterns.revealedBy: a correct drawing paired with a wrong or hesitant equation

responseLevels.gap: Interprets the multiplication story additively (4 + 6) or spots the two numbers without the groups-of structure.
responseLevels.full: Explains 4 × 6 as four groups of six, draws or reads an array to match, and connects the equal-groups structure to both the repeated-addition form and a word problem.
responseLevels.partial: Identifies 4 × 6 and can draw equal groups, but is shaky about which factor is the number of groups versus the group size, or links to the expression only with support.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here's a problem: 'There are 4 baskets with 6 eggs in each basket.' Which of these could you write for it — 4 × 6, or 4 + 6, or 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 — and tell me why it means the same as the story.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who grasps multiplication as equal groups picks 4×6 (and the repeated-addition form) and explains it as four groups of six. A child with only a vague sense picks 4 + 6 (adds the two numbers they see), or picks 4×6 but justifies it by 'there's a 4 and a 6' rather than the groups-of structure. The 'why it means the same as the story' tier separates structural understanding from number-spotting.

sources.claim: Y3 pupils solve problems including missing-number problems involving multiplication, building on the equal-groups meaning established in Y2.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (KS1–2), Year 3 Number — multiplication and division

sources.claim: 3.OA.1 requires interpreting products of whole numbers, e.g. 5 × 7 as the total number of objects in 5 groups of 7.
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 3, Operations & Algebraic Thinking (3.OA.A.1)

sources.claim: Equal-groups, array, and number-line models should be used in parallel and translated between to build the meaning of multiplication (CRA/CPA progression).
sources.source: IES/What Works Clearinghouse & NCETM guidance on multiplicative reasoning and the CPA approach

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: What Division Means
topic.description: Interpret whole-number quotients (e.g. 56 ÷ 8 as the number of objects in each share or the number of equal groups)
evidence: Explain that 56 ÷ 8 can mean sharing 56 into 8 equal groups or making groups of 8
Draw a picture to represent a division expression
Match a division expression to a word problem involving equal sharing or grouping
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain that '56 ÷ 8' could mean 'if 56 things are shared between 8 people, how many does each person get?' — not just recite the answer '7'?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 8–9y; interpret whole-number quotients: 56 ÷ 8 can mean the number in each share (partitive/sharing) OR the number of equal groups of 8 (quotitive/grouping).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y3 'solve problems, including missing number problems, involving … division', building on Y1–Y2 sharing and grouping and the fact that division is NOT commutative.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 3.OA.2 — 'Interpret whole-number quotients of whole numbers, e.g., interpret 56 ÷ 8 as the number of objects in each share when 56 objects are partitioned equally into 8 shares, or as a number of shares when 56 objects are partitioned into equal shares of 8 objects each.'
• Operational details — the load-bearing idea is that ONE division expression models TWO different actions: sharing (partitive: 56 shared among 8 → how many each) and grouping (quotitive: 56 put in groups of 8 → how many groups). Both give 7, but the story and the drawing differ. Teach both explicitly and have children label which is which; this dual meaning is the single hardest and most neglected point. Keep division tied to multiplication and to its two prerequisite actions from Y1.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8): share 12 counters among 3 plates and among groups of 3; give both answers. Tier B (age 8–9): match a ÷ expression to a sharing story AND a grouping story and draw each. Tier C (age 9): write a ÷ expression for a picture and state whether it shows sharing or grouping, and why the answer means different things.
bestPractices: Teach BOTH structures deliberately and by name — partitive/sharing ('how many in each?') and quotitive/grouping ('how many groups?') — using the same numbers so children see one ÷ expression modelling two actions.

Use contrasting stories for the same expression (56÷8: '56 sweets shared between 8 children' vs '56 sweets into bags of 8') and have children draw each differently — the drawings expose which structure they hold.
Anchor division to multiplication from the start (56÷8 relates to 8×?=56) so division is not learned as an isolated procedure.
Follow CPA: physically share/group counters → draw the sharing/grouping → write the ÷ expression, keeping the action visible.
Introduce remainders informally through the same actions (15 shared among 4 leaves 3 over) so the meaning of a remainder is grounded before written methods.
keyRepresentations: Sharing model — dealing counters one-by-one into a fixed number of plates (partitive: answer = per plate)
Grouping model — repeatedly taking a fixed group size until the pile is gone (quotitive: answer = number of groups)
Array / rows×columns — shows ÷ as the inverse of × (56 in 8 rows → 7 per row)
Number line — equal backward hops of 8 from 56 to 0 (grouping) counts the number of jumps
commonMisconceptions: Believing division has only one meaning (sharing), so grouping/quotitive word problems are misread or mis-drawn.
Thinking division is commutative — that 56÷8 and 8÷56 are the same — by analogy with ×.
Sharing unequally or forgetting shares must be equal.
Believing the answer must always be smaller and being confused by remainders or by dividing a smaller by a larger number.
Divorcing ÷ from × and treating it as a standalone symbol rather than the inverse operation.

learn.summary: For ages 8–9: interpret whole-number quotients so that one division expression (e.g. 56 ÷ 8 = 7) models TWO different actions — partitive/sharing ('56 shared among 8 → how many each?') and quotitive/grouping ('56 put into groups of 8 → how many groups?'). Both reach 7, but the story, the drawing, and what the 7 counts differ. Teach both structures explicitly by name, keep division tied to multiplication (8 × ? = 56), follow a concrete→pictorial→abstract progression, and introduce remainders informally through the same actions.

activities.title: Share-and-group the same pile
feedback: If a learner says only the sharing action 'is really dividing', have them act out both with counters — deal-one-each versus make-a-group-then-another — and point out both reach 7 and both are written 56 ÷ 8.
If a learner writes 8 ÷ 56, anchor that the whole amount (56) is the thing being broken up, so it is written first (the dividend); connect to starting with the whole set before sharing.

If a learner reaches 7 both ways but cannot explain the difference, have them label each drawing — 'number of groups' versus 'size of each group' — and narrate the two stories; do not reteach the operation, just make the roles explicit.
When a remainder appears (e.g. 58 ÷ 8 = 7 r2), ask why some counters are left over: can they still give every one of the 8 plates one more counter, or make another full bag of 8?
activities.rationale: Division's dual meaning can be made concrete by performing both actions on the same quantity and comparing. A sharing mode and a grouping mode on identical counters let a learner watch two different processes land on the same quotient, making partitive-versus-quotitive concrete and letting remainders emerge naturally. This aligns with teaching both structures by name and with a concrete-pictorial-abstract progression. A live surface that re-deals or re-groups and relabels the answer can make this tangible, but counters and plates/bags on a table achieve the same comparison.
sourceClaims: 3.OA.2 requires interpreting quotients as both the number in each share (partitive) and the number of shares/groups (quotitive).
Division should be taught through both partitive (sharing) and quotitive (grouping) structures using concrete-pictorial-abstract progression.
learnerActions: Start with one pile of 56 counters.
First, SHARE: deal the counters one at a time, round-robin, into 8 plates until the pile is empty. Count how many landed on each plate (7).
Then, GROUP: from a fresh pile of 56, repeatedly scoop a group of 8 counters into a bag until the pile is empty. Count how many bags you made (7).
Write 56 ÷ 8 = 7 beside BOTH actions, then say aloud what the 7 means in each: '7 on each plate' versus '7 bags'.

Repeat both actions with 58 counters. When sharing, deal only full rounds (one to every plate) and stop when there are too few left to give all 8 plates one more. When grouping, stop when fewer than 8 counters remain. Notice the 2 leftover counters that cannot complete another round of equal shares or another group of 8. These are the remainder (58 ÷ 8 = 7 r2).
activities.intendedInsight: One division expression encodes two different questions. Doing both actions on the same quantity shows that 56 ÷ 8 lands on 7 either way, yet the 7 means 'number in each share' when sharing and 'number of groups' when grouping. Leftovers that cannot complete a share or a group are a remainder.

activities.title: Two panels, same expression
feedback: If a learner thinks the two pictures are different sums, point out both total 56 and both are written 56 ÷ 8 — only what the 7 counts changes.
Reinforce the labels: 'sharing — answer = how many in each share' and 'grouping — answer = how many groups'.
activities.rationale: A clear two-panel contrast with reveal-the-label callouts is a strong anchor for the dual-meaning vocabulary. A fixed diagram cannot let the learner perform the actions and discover the equivalence, so it works best alongside hands-on sharing/grouping rather than instead of it.
sourceClaims: 3.OA.2 requires interpreting quotients as both the number in each share (partitive) and the number of shares/groups (quotitive).
learnerActions: Look at two side-by-side pictures: LEFT shows 8 plates of 7 counters; RIGHT shows 7 bags of 8 counters.
For the left picture, state what the answer counts ('how many on each plate'); for the right, state what it counts ('how many bags').
Write the single expression 56 ÷ 8 = 7 under both and answer: 'Both say 56 ÷ 8 = 7 — so what does the 7 count in each?'
Name each structure: left = sharing/partitive, right = grouping/quotitive.
activities.intendedInsight: The same expression and the same answer attach to two distinct meanings; naming each structure fixes the vocabulary of sharing versus grouping.

activities.title: Arrays and number lines: division as the inverse of multiplication
feedback: If a learner treats 56 ÷ 8 as unrelated to multiplication, point to the array: the same 8 rows of 7 give both 8 × 7 = 56 and 56 ÷ 8 = 7.
If a learner miscounts hops on the number line, check that every hop is exactly 8 and that they count the hops, not the points landed on (56→48→40→32→24→16→8→0 is 7 hops).
activities.rationale: Arrays make the inverse relationship between multiplication and division visible, and equal backward hops on a number line represent the quotitive/grouping meaning as repeated subtraction. These anchor division to multiplication — a load-bearing idea in the original research — rather than teaching it as a standalone procedure.
learnerActions: Arrange the 56 counters as an ARRAY — 8 rows of 7 (or 7 rows of 8) — and write 8 × 7 = 56 alongside 56 ÷ 8 = 7 to see division as the inverse of multiplication.
Read the same array both ways: 8 rows of 7 counters, or 7 columns of 8 counters, each totalling 56.
On a NUMBER LINE, start at 56 and make equal backward hops of 8 until you reach 0; count the hops (7) — this is the number of groups of 8, the grouping/quotitive meaning.
Say how 8 × 7 = 56, 56 ÷ 8 = 7 and 56 ÷ 7 = 8 are all related through the same array.
activities.intendedInsight: An array makes division visible as the inverse of multiplication (8 × 7 = 56 ↔ 56 ÷ 8 = 7), and equal backward hops on a number line model the grouping meaning as repeated subtraction. Both keep division connected to multiplication rather than treated as an isolated symbol.

activities.title: Sort and match the stories
feedback: A tempting wrong match is a story like '6 shared among 24' or '6 ÷ 24' — use it to catch the belief that division is commutative, then return to the whole-gets-broken-up idea.
If a learner only ever picks 'sharing', revisit the hands-on grouping action to establish that making equal groups of a fixed size is also division.
activities.rationale: Sorting and matching are highly checkable and can pinpoint the single-meaning misconception and the commutativity error. This consolidates and reveals understanding rather than building it, so it is best used after learners have performed both actions. It elicits classification and explanation, not independent construction of the actions themselves.
learnerActions: Sort a set of word problems into two bins: 'sharing' and 'grouping'.
For 24 ÷ 6, choose which written story matches it as a GROUPING situation (making groups of 6) and explain your choice.
Explain why a story such as '6 shared among 24' (i.e. 6 ÷ 24) is NOT the same as 24 ÷ 6 — division is not commutative.
For each story you sort, say what each number stands for — the whole, the number of groups or the group size, and the answer.
activities.intendedInsight: Classifying and matching stories surfaces whether a learner holds only the sharing meaning and exposes the commutativity error (treating 24 ÷ 6 and 6 ÷ 24 as the same).

activities.title: The baker's choice
feedback: If the learner cannot state the difference, pair the talk with counters so the two physical processes are visible while they explain.
Prompt: 'In your story, what does the 6 tell you — the number of groups, or how many in each group?'
activities.rationale: Spoken explanation and story-making can prompt a learner to put the structure into words and expose confusion. Discussion is proposed to work best when coupled to concrete sharing/grouping, since talk alone does not have the learner carry out the two physical actions; it is not a substitute for them.
learnerActions: Take the role of helping a baker split 56 rolls.
Decide and say aloud: do you want 8 boxes with the same number in each (sharing), or boxes that each hold 8 (grouping)?
Describe what changes between the two choices and what the answer 7 means in each.
Invent your own grouping story for 24 ÷ 6 and tell it to a partner.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the choice out loud prompts a learner to distinguish sharing from grouping and to say what each number represents, strengthening the language of the two structures.

constraints: Teach both structures deliberately and by name — partitive/sharing ('how many in each?') and quotitive/grouping ('how many groups?') — using the SAME numbers so one expression models two actions.
Keep division tied to multiplication (56 ÷ 8 relates to 8 × ? = 56, and arrays show the inverse relationship) so it is not learned as an isolated procedure.
Follow concrete → pictorial → abstract: physically share/group, then draw/array/number-line, then write the expression, keeping the action visible.
Division is NOT commutative: 56 ÷ 8 and 8 ÷ 56 are different. Address this explicitly, including using a correctly reversed-story distractor (e.g. 6 ÷ 24 as the reversal of 24 ÷ 6).

Sorting, matching, and multiple-choice tasks verify and reveal understanding (including recognition-only responses) but do not by themselves have the learner independently perform the sharing and grouping actions; use them after hands-on work.
A fixed two-panel diagram anchors vocabulary but cannot be manipulated to let the learner discover the equivalence; pair it with hands-on actions.
Introduce remainders informally through the same actions (leftovers that cannot complete a share or a group) before any written method.
Shares must be equal; guard against sharing unequally and against the belief that a quotient must always be smaller or that one cannot divide a smaller number by a larger one.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit: 56 ÷ 8 = 7 is correct both as 8 shares of 7 and as 7 groups of 8; 58 ÷ 8 = 7 remainder 2, consistent with the leftover-counters description; 24 ÷ 6 = 4 (used for classification/story-making). Array check: 8 rows of 7 = 56, giving 8 × 7 = 56, 56 ÷ 8 = 7 and 56 ÷ 7 = 8. Number-line check: 56→48→40→32→24→16→8→0 is 7 hops of 8.

The source's diagnostic treats the 8 as the number of shares/groups in the sharing Story A and as the group size in the grouping Story B; this is preserved consistently in the activities and feedback.

The original row's grouping distractor for 24 ÷ 6 was given as an '8 ÷ 24 story', which does not reverse 24 ÷ 6 and cannot illustrate commutativity; it was an error and has been corrected to the proper reversal 6 ÷ 24. The erroneous original value is recorded here only, not offered to learners.

The array (division as the inverse of multiplication) and number-line (equal backward hops = number of groups) representations from the original key representations were missing from the candidate's activities; they have been restored as a dedicated activity to preserve the tie-to-multiplication idea.

Source claims for CCSS 3.OA.2 and NCETM are marked verified:false in the row; the DfE claim is marked verified:true. No efficacy or comparative-necessity claims are asserted beyond what the standards/guidance state.

The original research asserted the dual meaning 'is only felt' by the interactive mode, that 'no static picture can' build it, and that the concept 'lives in the two physical processes which talk can't render'; these categorical necessity/modality claims have been softened to scoped proposals, since catalog fit ratings do not establish such necessity.

probeDeeper: In Story A, what does the 8 tell you? In Story B, what does the 8 tell you?
Draw 56 ÷ 8 for the sharing story.
Could 56 ÷ 8 ever leave something over? When?
Make up your own grouping story for 24 ÷ 6.
assess.correctAnswer: Yes — both are 56 ÷ 8. In Story A you know the number of groups (8 children) and find the size of each share (7 each); in Story B you know the group size (8 per bag) and find the number of groups (7 bags). Same division, two meanings.

errorPatterns.pattern: only sharing counts as division — thinks division means sharing into a known number of groups, so making groups of 8 (Story B) isn't 'really' dividing
errorPatterns.nextMove: act out both with counters — deal-one-each (sharing) versus make-a-group-then-another (grouping) — showing both reach 7 and both are 56 ÷ 8
errorPatterns.distractor: Only Story A is 56 ÷ 8; Story B is a different sum.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says only Story A is 56 ÷ 8 and treats Story B as a different operation

errorPatterns.pattern: reverses the dividend and divisor — writes 8 ÷ 56 for these stories
errorPatterns.nextMove: anchor that the whole (56) gets broken up, so it is the dividend; connect to the equal-sharing model where you start with the whole set
errorPatterns.revealedBy: records the division the wrong way round

errorPatterns.pattern: solves both to 7 but the quotient's meaning is opaque — can't say the 8 is the number of groups in A and the group size in B
errorPatterns.nextMove: label each drawing (number of groups vs size of group) and narrate the two stories — do not reteach the operation, just make the roles explicit
errorPatterns.revealedBy: correct answers with no account of what each number represents

responseLevels.gap: Recognises only one meaning of division (usually sharing) and treats grouping as a different operation, or reverses the ÷ sentence.
responseLevels.full: Explains both the sharing and grouping meanings of 56 ÷ 8, says what each number represents in each, and matches stories to the expression.
responseLevels.partial: Solves both stories to 7 but cannot articulate that the 8 is the number of groups in one and the group size in the other.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are two stories. Story A: '56 sweets shared equally among 8 children — how many each?' Story B: '56 sweets put into bags of 8 — how many bags?' Can they BOTH be written as 56 ÷ 8? Explain how each one is 56 ÷ 8.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands division holds BOTH the sharing (partitive) and grouping (quotitive) meanings and can say what the 8 and the 7 stand for in each. A child with only one model insists just one story 'is really dividing' (usually the sharing one), or reaches 7 for both but can't explain why the 8 plays a different role in each. The two-story tier forces the dual structure into the open.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Times tables (age 8+)
topic.description: Recognise and use repeated reasoning to generalise: extend patterns in times tables and equivalent fractions, derive unknown facts from known facts efficiently, describe general rules
evidence: Notice that all fractions equivalent to 1/2 have a numerator that is half the denominator
Use the pattern 3×4=12, 3×40=120, 3×400=1200 and explain the generalisation
Derive 8×7 from 8×5=40 plus 8×2=16 and describe the strategy as a general approach
topic.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} notices a pattern — like that multiplying by 4 is the same as doubling twice — do they use that generalisation to solve similar problems more efficiently?

pedagogy.summary: At 8-9, repeated reasoning becomes explicit generalisation WITH justification: noticing that every fraction equivalent to 1/2 has a numerator half its denominator, seeing 3×4=12, 3×40=120, 3×400=1200 as one scaling pattern and saying WHY, and naming 'derive from a known fact' (8×7 = 8×5 + 8×2) as a general strategy rather than a one-off. CCSS MP8 stresses moving from noticed repetition to a general method while checking reasonableness. Teaching should press beyond 'I see a pattern' to 'why must it happen, and will it always?' — grounding the scaling pattern in place value and the fraction pattern in a visual model.
bestPractices: Lay out a scaling chain (3×4, 3×40, 3×400) and ask the child to explain WHY the product scales by 10 each time using place value, not just append zeros
Show families of equivalent fractions on a bar/number line so the numerator-half-denominator rule for 1/2 is seen to hold and can be tested
Name the derive-from-known-facts move as a reusable general strategy and ask the child to describe it in their own words
Insist on a test case for any stated rule ('does it still work for 3×4000? for 4/8?') to separate a justified generalisation from a guess
keyRepresentations: Place-value scaling chain (×10 shifts) for 3×4 → 3×40 → 3×400
Fraction wall / number line for families of equivalent fractions
Array / area-model split for deriving ×7 from ×5 + ×2
Multiplication grid showing column patterns
commonMisconceptions: Uses 'add a zero' for ×10 scaling with no place-value reason, so it fails on decimals
Notices a pattern but treats it as coincidence, unable to say why it must hold or whether it always will
Over-generalises the 1/2 rule to other fractions, or applies it without testing
Derives a fact but does not recognise the derive-from-known-facts move as a general strategy for other facts

learn.summary: For ages 8-9, press repeated reasoning into justified generalisation: not just noticing that 3×4=12, 3×40=120, 3×400=1200 scale by ten, but saying WHY (place value shifts the digits one place) and testing whether a rule always holds. Similarly, families of equivalent fractions (1/2, 2/4, 3/6) reveal a numerator-half-denominator pattern that should be tested on new cases, not trusted on sight. Name 'derive from a known fact' (8×7 = 8×5 + 8×2) as a reusable strategy the child can describe in their own words. The target is the justification and the extension, not just correct numbers.

activities.title: Scaling machine with a 'why' window
feedback: If the child only says 'add a zero', show the scaling on a place-value chart so the digits visibly shift one column, and contrast a decimal case where 'add a zero' gives the wrong answer: 1.2 × 10 is 12, but writing a zero on the end gives 1.20, which is still 1.2. Use the chart to show that 3×0.4 = 1.2 is a tenth of 12 because the digits shift one column right

If the child gives 120 and 1200 but shrugs at 'will it always work?', don't just assert the rule — ask 'why does times-ten make it ten times bigger?' and work the next case (3×4000 = 12000) together so a justified generalisation forms
Affirm reasoning that connects the shift to place value and confidently extends to 3×4000 for the same reason
activities.rationale: CCSS MP8 stresses moving from noticed repetition to a general method while evaluating reasonableness; grounding the scaling in place value (rather than 'add a zero') supplies the justification and reveals why it generalises. An interactive scaling tool lets the child produce cases and test an extension live, but a place-value chart or written scaling chain achieves the same reasoning on paper.
sourceClaims: MP8: students move from repeated calculations to general methods and shortcuts, and evaluate the reasonableness of results
Pupils should derive facts from known facts, recognise/use structure, and explain why patterns hold using representations that reveal the structure
learnerActions: Start from 3×4 = 12, then produce 3×40 and 3×400 by scaling up by ten each step
For each step, explain WHY the product gets ten times bigger using place value (40 is ten times 4, so the answer is ten times bigger; the digits shift one place left) rather than saying 'add a zero'
Predict 3×4000 and state whether the same reason guarantees it will work, then check
Now test the idea going the OTHER way: 0.4 is a tenth of 4, so is 3×0.4 a tenth of 12? Work it out and explain why the place value, not an added zero, decides this
activities.intendedInsight: The product scales by ten BECAUSE place value shifts the digits one column, so the pattern must keep working (including for 3×4000). Reasoning from place value (not just appending zeros) also handles decimal cases like 3×0.4 = 1.2 — here 0.4 is a tenth of 4, so the product is a tenth of 12, with the digits shifting one column right. The add-a-zero shortcut cannot explain this, and it gives wrong answers for decimals (1.2 × 10 is 12, not 1.20).

activities.title: Equivalent-fraction family tester
feedback: If the child claims a fraction is equivalent to 1/2 on the verbal rule alone when it isn't, check it on the fraction wall/number line (same whole) so the mismatch is visible
If the child says 5/9 is equivalent because 5 is roughly half of 9, prompt them to compare 5/9 and 1/2 exactly on the bar and see they don't line up
Affirm when the child tests a candidate fraction (e.g. confirms 4/8 lines up, 5/9 does not) rather than trusting the rule outright
activities.rationale: EEF guidance recommends explaining why patterns hold using representations that reveal structure; a bar/number line makes the equivalence testable and guards against over-generalisation. A live generator makes testing immediate, but a drawn fraction wall supports the same checking.
sourceClaims: Pupils should derive facts from known facts, recognise/use structure, and explain why patterns hold using representations that reveal the structure
learnerActions: Line up 1/2, 2/4, 3/6 on a fraction bar or number line (same whole) and notice that each numerator is half its denominator
State the candidate rule 'a fraction equals 1/2 when the numerator is half the denominator'
Invent a new fraction and test whether the rule holds by checking it against the bar/number line, not by eyeballing
Try a trap case: is 5/9 equivalent to 1/2 because 5 is 'about half' of 9? How could you be sure?
activities.intendedInsight: A noticed rule must be tested before it is trusted; the numerator-half-denominator pattern for 1/2 can be confirmed on a model, and over-applying it (e.g. to 5/9) is caught by checking rather than guessing.

activities.title: Derive-from-known-facts as a named strategy
feedback: If the child treats 8×7 = 8×5 + 8×2 as a single trick for one fact, ask them to describe it as a general approach and apply it to a new fact
Use an array/area model split into 8×5 and 8×2 parts so the child sees why the parts add to the whole
Watch for the common wrong split 8×5 + 2 (adding 2 instead of 8×2 = 16, which gives 42 not 56); check the split against the model
activities.rationale: EEF recommends deriving facts from known facts and recognising structure; naming the strategy and transferring it to a new fact turns a single derivation into a general method, consistent with MP8's move from repetition to general strategy. An area/array model makes the factor split visible.
sourceClaims: MP8: students move from repeated calculations to general methods and shortcuts, and evaluate the reasonableness of results
Pupils should derive facts from known facts, recognise/use structure, and explain why patterns hold using representations that reveal the structure
learnerActions: Work out 8×7 from facts you already know: 8×5 = 40 and 8×2 = 16, then add to get 56
Explain why splitting 7 into 5 + 2 lets you reuse known facts (an array or area model split into an 8×5 part and an 8×2 part)
Describe the move in your own words as a general strategy for any hard table fact
Try the same strategy on another fact (e.g. 6×7 or 9×6) and say which known facts you'd lean on
activities.intendedInsight: Deriving an unknown fact by splitting a factor and reusing known facts is a reusable general strategy, not a one-off; the child should recognise and name it so they can apply it to other facts.

activities.title: Prove it holds every time
feedback: If the child treats a pattern as coincidence and won't commit to whether it always holds, ask 'why must it happen?' and test the next case together
Praise a reason grounded in structure (place value, the fraction model) over 'it just works'
activities.rationale: MP8 emphasises expressing regularity as a general method and checking reasonableness; insisting on a reason and a test case is how a child moves from 'I see a pattern' to 'it must always happen'.
sourceClaims: MP8: students move from repeated calculations to general methods and shortcuts, and evaluate the reasonableness of results
learnerActions: After extending a scaling chain or stating a fraction rule, answer: how could you convince someone the pattern works every time, not just for these three cases?
Produce a test case for any stated rule ('does it still work for 3×4000? for 4/8?') and report what you find
Distinguish a justified generalisation ('it must, because place value shifts') from a guess ('it just seems to')
activities.intendedInsight: A pattern noticed is not a pattern proven; a reason it must hold, plus a fresh test case, separates a reliable generalisation from a coincidence.

activities.title: Check your generalisation (quick questions)
feedback: If the child picks 5/9 as equivalent to 1/2, send them back to the fraction model to test it
If the child selects 8×5 + 2, point out the second part must be 8×2 = 16, not 2 (so the total is 56, not 42)
Always ask the 'why does it work?' follow-up; a correct pick without a reason is not yet a generalisation
activities.rationale: Recognition questions can check whether a generalisation has formed, but selecting an answer is not the same as constructing a justification; pairing every item with a 'why' step keeps the focus on reasoning. This supplements, not replaces, the construct-and-test activities.
learnerActions: Continue the scaling chain: given 3×4=12 and 3×40=120, give 3×400 and 3×4000
Pick which fractions are equivalent to 1/2 from a set that includes near-misses (e.g. 5/9)
Choose the correct derivation of 8×7 and reject the wrong split 8×5 + 2 in favour of 8×5 + 8×2 = 56
For each choice, say WHY it is correct, not just which answer
activities.intendedInsight: Selecting correct continuations and derivations, paired with a stated reason, confirms the child is generalising with justification rather than pattern-matching.

constraints: The learning target is the justification and the extension, not just correct products or correct fraction picks; accept an answer only when the child can say WHY and whether it always holds.

Recognition/selection questions can check whether a generalisation exists but do not elicit the child's own construction or justification; always pair them with a 'why does it work?' step and treat them as a supplement to construct-and-test work.

A static annotated scaling chain or fraction wall can show and explain the pattern, but cannot let the child generate and test new cases; use it as a reference scaffold, not as the place where testing happens.

Discussion on its own supplies no concrete case or model for the child to test a generalisation against; pair any talk with numbers, a place-value chart, a fraction model, or an array so claims can be checked.
'Add a zero' is an unjustified shortcut that misfires on decimals; require a place-value reason instead.
Scaling chains and fraction families are flat relationships, so a 3D representation is not needed to show their structure.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Arithmetic checked: 8×5=40, 8×2=16, 40+16=56 (8×7); 3×40=120, 3×400=1200, 3×4000=12000, 3×0.4=1.2; the wrong split 8×5+2=42 is only ever presented as an error to reject, never as a valid answer.

Place-value reasoning for ×10 (digits shift one place left on whole numbers) is sound; 3×0.4 is the scaling-DOWN direction (0.4 is a tenth of 4, so the product is a tenth of 12 = 1.2), which is where the 'add a zero' shortcut fails — the activity now flags this is the opposite direction rather than the same leftward shift.
The 5/9 case is a genuine non-equivalence (5 is not half of 9), used to prompt checking rather than eyeballing; 4/8 is a confirming case (4 is half of 8).

The non-preferred 'conversation' and '3D' entries were low-fit in the source; their genuine affordance limits are preserved as narrowly scoped constraints without asserting any universal 'only X can teach this' claim.

probeDeeper: Ask 'you scaled 3×4 up by tens — does the same idea work going the other way, 3×0.4? why or why not?' to test the limits of the generalisation
Counterexample tuned to this topic: 'is 5/9 equivalent to 1/2 because 5 is about half of 9? how could you be sure?' to check the child tests rather than eyeballs
Ask 'you got 8×7 from 8×5 + 8×2 — could you describe that as a general trick for any hard table fact?' to see if the strategy is generalised
Ask 'how could you convince someone the pattern works every time, not just for these three?' to surface justification
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for 120 and 1200 with a place-value justification ('40 is ten times 4, so the answer is ten times bigger; the digits shift a place') and confidence it extends to 3×4000 = 12000 for the same reason. The WHY and the extension, not just the numbers, are the target.

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses 'add a zero' with no place-value reason, so cannot justify why the product scales and it would misfire on decimals
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the scaling on a place-value chart so digits shift one column; contrast a decimal case where 'add a zero' fails
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Asked why, the child says only 'you add a zero' and cannot connect it to ×10 or place value

errorPatterns.pattern: Notices the pattern but treats it as a coincidence, unable to say it must always hold
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT just assert the rule; ask 'why does times-ten make it ten times bigger?' and test the next case together so a justified generalisation forms
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child gives 120 and 1200 but, asked 'will it always work?', shrugs or won't commit to 3×4000

errorPatterns.pattern: Over-generalises the equivalent-fraction pattern (applies the 1/2 numerator-half-denominator rule to fractions it doesn't fit) without testing
errorPatterns.nextMove: Check the claim on a fraction wall/number line; test candidate fractions rather than trusting the verbal rule
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child claims a fraction is equivalent to 1/2 on the rule alone when it isn't, or won't test

responseLevels.gap: Produces the products by 'add a zero' but cannot justify, treats patterns as coincidence, and over-applies fraction rules without testing
responseLevels.full: Extends the scaling chain with a place-value justification, states the derive-from-known-facts move as a general strategy, and tests fraction generalisations — explaining WHY a rule must hold and transferring it unprompted
responseLevels.partial: States the pattern and can extend it when prompted, but justifies weakly ('you add a zero') and does not reliably test whether a rule always holds

assess.diagnosticPrompt: You know 3 × 4 = 12. What are 3 × 40 and 3 × 400? Explain WHY the pattern works — and would it still work for 3 × 4000?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The products can be produced by 'adding a zero' with zero understanding. What discriminates is the place-value reason and whether the child is sure it generalises. A child with repeated-reasoning insight explains why it must scale and extends confidently; one without recites 'add a zero' and cannot justify or is unsure about 3×4000.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Times tables
topic.description: Recall and use multiplication and division facts for the 2, 5, and 10 multiplication tables
evidence: Quickly answer 5 × 3 = 15 from memory
Quickly answer 20 ÷ 5 = 4 from memory
Recite the 2, 5, and 10 times tables fluently
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} quickly recall times table facts from the 2s, 5s, and 10s — like '5 × 6 = 30' or '20 ÷ 2 = 10' — forwards and backwards?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 6–7 (UK Y2, US Grade 2–3). Recall and use multiplication AND division facts for the 2, 5 and 10 tables — the first fact set, built on the 2s/5s/10s skip counting.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y2 'recall and use multiplication and division facts for the 2, 5 and 10 multiplication tables, including recognising odd and even numbers'; non-statutory 'connect the 2, 5 and 10 tables to each other' and 'use commutativity and inverse relations (4×5=20 and 20÷5=4)'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 3.OA.7 'fluently multiply and divide within 100 … by end of Grade 3 know from memory all products of two one-digit numbers' (the 2s/5s/10s are the earliest-secured, from 2.OA skip counting).
• Operational details: derive rather than only chant — 10s from place value, 5s as half of the 10s, 2s as doubles. Crucially include the DIVISION facts and out-of-sequence recall (not just reciting). Use commutativity and the inverse to get four facts from one (2×5, 5×2, 10÷5, 10÷2).
• Checkpoint: quick recall + inverse. Tier A (6): recall 2s and 10s facts in order. Tier B (6–7): recall any 2, 5 or 10 fact out of order and its division fact. Tier C (7): explain that the 5s are half the 10s and state the full fact family for 5×4.
bestPractices: Build the three tables on structure, not rote: 10s from place value, 5s as exactly half of the matching 10s fact, 2s as doubles — so a forgotten fact can be re-derived.
Teach the DIVISION facts alongside the multiplication facts as fact families (5×4=20 → 20÷5=4, 20÷4=5), and use commutativity so learning one fact delivers its partner — halving the memory load.
Rehearse out of sequence and in mixed contexts once the count is secure, so recall is genuine fluency rather than a chant that only works from the start.
Exploit hundred-square and multiplication-square patterns (5s and 10s in columns, 2s in even columns) to make the facts a connected web — building on the skip-counting patterns already learned.
Connect the three tables to each other and to odd/even (the 2s table = even numbers) so the fact sets reinforce rather than compete.
keyRepresentations: Multiplication square / times-table grid (patterns and commutative symmetry)
Hundred square with 2s, 5s, 10s shaded (columns/even-number pattern)
Arrays for each fact (and the fact family)
Number line with equal jumps (bridge from skip counting)
commonMisconceptions: Being able to chant the table from the start but not recall a fact out of order — mistaking the chant for fluency.
Knowing the multiplication fact but not the corresponding division fact.
Treating 5×4 and 4×5 as separate facts to memorise (not using commutativity).
Confusing 'the 2 times table' with 'counting in 2s starting anywhere' — or muddling doubling with adding 2.
Not connecting 5s to 10s (missing that 5s are half the 10s), so each table is learned in isolation.

learn.summary: For ages 6–7 (UK Y2, US Grade 2–3): recall and USE multiplication AND division facts for the 2, 5 and 10 tables, out of order and as fact families, built on structure rather than rote chanting. Derive 10s from place value, 5s as exactly half of the matching 10s fact, and 2s as doubles, so a forgotten fact can be re-derived. Teach division facts alongside multiplication (5×4=20 → 20÷5=4, 20÷4=5) and use commutativity so one learned fact delivers its partner. Connect the three tables to each other and to odd/even (the 2s = even numbers).

activities.title: Shade the table: derive the 5s from the 10s
feedback: If a child treats the 5s and 10s as unrelated, pair the two shaded columns side by side and ask 'what is half of 40?' to reveal 5×4 = 20.
If a child doubles wrongly or adds 2 instead, show 2×6 as two groups of 6 (or 6 doubled = 12), distinct from 6+2 = 8.
Reinforce the end-digit pattern as a self-check: 5s end in 5 or 0; 10s end in 0.
Optional live display: when the learner taps a grid cell, pop out the array for that fact and write its whole fact family so the derivation stays visible.
activities.rationale: Building facts on structure (place value, halving, doubling) lets a learner re-derive a forgotten fact and connects the tables rather than learning each in isolation; a visible, manipulable grid makes the 'half the 10s' relationship directly observable, and the number line links it to the skip-counting already secured.
sourceClaims: Y2: recall and use multiplication and division facts for the 2, 5 and 10 tables, including odd/even; connect the tables and use commutativity and inverse relations.
Tables should be derived from structure (10s from place value, 5s as half of 10s, 2s as doubles) and learned with their division facts as fact families, not by rote chanting alone.
learnerActions: On a multiplication grid or hundred square, shade the 10s column (10, 20, 30, 40, 50…) and read them as place-value facts: 10×3 = 3 tens = 30.

Beside it, shade the 5s (5, 10, 15, 20, 25…) and line each 5s value up against the matching 10s value. On a multiplication grid this is the 5s column; on a hundred square the 5s fill two columns, the numbers ending in 5 and those ending in 0.
Notice and say aloud that each 5s value sits exactly halfway to the 10s value: 5×4 = 20 is half of 10×4 = 40.

Shade the 2s (on a multiplication grid, the 2s column; on a hundred square, every column ending in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8) and state that the answers in the 2s table are even numbers, and that 2×n is the double of n.
Pick one fact per table and write it as a derivation: '10×6 = 60, so 5×6 = 30 (half), and 2×6 = 12 (double of 6).'
Optionally, show the same facts as equal jumps on a number line (counting in 2s, 5s or 10s) to connect the shaded columns back to the skip-counting the child already knows.
activities.intendedInsight: The 2, 5 and 10 tables are a connected web, not three separate lists: 10s come from place value, 5s are half the matching 10s, 2s are doubles — so any fact can be rebuilt if forgotten.

activities.title: Four facts from one array: multiplication and its inverse
feedback: If division lags, return to the SAME array and count the rows/columns to show 20÷5 and 20÷4 directly.
If a child treats 5×4 and 4×5 as two separate things to memorise, rotate the array a quarter turn to show it is the same 20.
Use a fact-family triangle (20 at top, 5 and 4 below) so the child can cover any one number and state it from the other two.
activities.rationale: Fact families on a single array link multiplication with its inverse division and exploit commutativity, directly targeting the common gap where multiplication is fluent but division or the commutative partner is not.
sourceClaims: Tables should be derived from structure (10s from place value, 5s as half of 10s, 2s as doubles) and learned with their division facts as fact families, not by rote chanting alone.
Y2: recall and use multiplication and division facts for the 2, 5 and 10 tables, including odd/even; connect the tables and use commutativity and inverse relations.
learnerActions: Build or look at an array for one fact, e.g. 5 rows of 4 (= 20).
Write the two multiplication facts the array shows using commutativity: 5×4 = 20 and 4×5 = 20.
Write the two division facts from the same array: 20÷5 = 4 and 20÷4 = 5.
Repeat for several 2/5/10 facts, each time producing the full fact family of four facts from one picture.
Say why 20÷5 = 4 'has to be' true given 5×4 = 20 (sharing 20 into 5 equal rows gives 4).
activities.intendedInsight: One array holds a whole fact family; using commutativity and the inverse means learning one fact delivers its partners, so division facts are not extra memorising.

activities.title: Mixed quick-recall, out of order, with a derive-it fallback
feedback: Correct answers for the prompts above: 5×3 = 15, 10×4 = 40, 2×7 = 14; 20÷5 = 4, 30÷10 = 3, 14÷2 = 7.
On a miss, respond with the array AND the derive-it prompt (find the ten fact and halve it; double for twos), not just the right number.

For a near-miss count error such as 5×3 answered as 20, note that 20 still ends in 0, so the basic end-digit check (5s end in 5 or 0) will not catch it. Use the derive-it route instead (10×3 = 30, half of 30 is 15), or the sharper pattern that 5 times an odd number ends in 5. Then re-count one step at a time to check. The correct answer is 15.
Do NOT drill under heavy time pressure if a child reconstructs by skip-counting; keep skip-counting as a backup while spaced, meaningful retrieval moves facts into memory.
Optional quick-fire mode: present facts in random order with instant array feedback on misses.
activities.rationale: Out-of-order mixed × and ÷ practice distinguishes true recall from skip-count reconstruction and exposes lagging division facts; pairing every miss with a structural derivation keeps fluency resting on recoverable structure.
sourceClaims: Y2: recall and use multiplication and division facts for the 2, 5 and 10 tables, including odd/even; connect the tables and use commutativity and inverse relations.
learnerActions: Once skip-counting is secure, answer facts asked OUT of sequence, mixing × and ÷: 5×3, 10×4, 2×7, then 20÷5, 30÷10, 14÷2.
For each, notice whether you knew it instantly or had to count, and say which.
On any fact you did not just know, use the derive-it route aloud: for a 5s fact, find the matching 10s fact and halve it; for a 2s fact, double the number.
Keep skip-counting available as a backup check, not as the main method.
activities.intendedInsight: Genuine fluency is recall out of order (including division), not a chant that only works from the start; when memory fails, a structured derivation recovers the fact.

activities.title: Trade-a-fact oral rehearsal
feedback: Keep the derive-it prompt handy so a miss ends with a reconstructed fact, not just the answer.
If division is slower than multiplication, pair every × question with its ÷ inverse so the family is rehearsed together.
activities.rationale: Oral rehearsal adds low-stakes retrieval practice and reinforces fact families; a spoken partner does not itself display the shaded columns or arrays that make the halving relationship visible, so it works best alongside the grid and array tasks rather than replacing them.
sourceClaims: Tables should be derived from structure (10s from place value, 5s as half of 10s, 2s as doubles) and learned with their division facts as fact families, not by rote chanting alone.
learnerActions: Take turns with a partner: one asks a 2, 5 or 10 fact (× or ÷), the other answers, then they swap.
On a miss, the asker prompts the derivation: 'What's the ten fact? Now halve it' for 5s, or 'double it' for 2s.
Include inverse pairs deliberately, e.g. ask 5×6 then immediately 30÷5.
activities.intendedInsight: Spoken back-and-forth rehearsal gives extra meaningful retrieval and keeps the derive-it route verbal and quick.

constraints: Secure skip-counting in 2s, 5s and 10s is a prerequisite; if a child can only reconstruct every fact by counting from the start, strengthen that skip-counting first rather than drilling under time pressure.
Answer-giving/recall checks measure whether facts are fluent but do not by themselves build the structure; use them alongside the deriving and fact-family tasks, not in place of them.
A fixed poster or static grid is a good pattern reference but cannot run out-of-order recall practice or generate arrays on demand; combine it with spoken or interactive mixed-fact practice.
Out-of-order, mixed × and ÷ recall is the target; a chant that only works from the beginning of the table is not yet fluency.
Keep the halving relationship explicit: 5×n is half of 10×n (e.g. 5×4 = 20 is half of 40), and 2×n is the double of n, distinct from n+2.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic in prompts/feedback: 5×3 = 15, 10×4 = 40, 2×7 = 14, 20÷5 = 4, 30÷10 = 3, 14÷2 = 7, 5×4 = 20, 5×6 = 30, 2×6 = 12, 10×6 = 60 — all verified correct. The near-miss example '5×3 = 20' is presented explicitly as an error to correct (correct value 15), never as a valid option.
The source claim that '5s are half the 10s' and '2s are doubles' is mathematically sound and retained as the derivation backbone.

CCSS 3.OA.7 (verified:false) states the fluency objective but was not cited as method-level support for out-of-order practice; its comparative/efficacy weight should not be overstated. NCETM mastery guidance is also marked unverified in the row.

Original row asserted that a talking partner 'adds little' and that 3D 'adds no conceptual value'; these comparative/necessity claims are not established by the available sources and have been removed or recast as narrow affordance-and-limit statements.
The number-line-with-equal-jumps representation from the original row was restored as an optional action in the shading activity to preserve the stated bridge from skip counting.

probeDeeper: How did you work out 5 × 3 — did you know it or count it?
What's 5 × 6? How could 5 × 5 help?
Which of these tables feels easiest? Why?
assess.correctAnswer: 15, 40, 14; 4, 3, 7 — answered from memory (or by very rapid skip-count), with the division facts as secure as the multiplication.

errorPatterns.pattern: reconstructs every fact by skip-counting — to answer 5 × 3 counts '5, 10, 15' rather than recalling; accurate but slow
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT drill under time pressure — recall builds from repeated meaningful use; keep skip-counting as a backup while spaced retrieval moves facts into memory
errorPatterns.revealedBy: audible or finger counting-up before each answer

errorPatterns.pattern: division facts lag multiplication — fluent on 5 × 3 but stalls on 20 ÷ 5; the ÷ fact isn't linked to the same fact family
errorPatterns.nextMove: teach fact families on one array/triangle — 5 × 4 = 20, so 20 ÷ 5 = 4 and 20 ÷ 4 = 5
errorPatterns.revealedBy: quick on ×, slow or guessing on ÷

errorPatterns.pattern: near-miss count error — says 5 × 3 = 20 (miscounts a step) or muddles the 5s and 10s
errorPatterns.nextMove: anchor the pattern (5s end in 5 or 0; 10s end in 0) and re-count to self-check
errorPatterns.revealedBy: an answer one step off, or a 5s/10s mix-up

responseLevels.gap: Cannot produce the facts, or only by counting from the start each time with errors.
responseLevels.full: Answers 2/5/10 multiplication and division facts from memory (or near-instantly), using fact families to link × and ÷.
responseLevels.partial: Recalls 2s/5s/10s multiplication but reconstructs by skip-counting, or the division facts lag behind.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: I'll ask some facts quickly — answer as fast as you can, and I'll watch whether you count to get there. 5 × 3? 10 × 4? 2 × 7? Now the division ones: 20 ÷ 5? 30 ÷ 10? 14 ÷ 2? (Watch whether recall is instant or reconstructed by skip-counting, and whether the division facts are as secure as the multiplication.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Asking multiplication and its inverse division side by side, and watching HOW the child answers, separates true recall from skip-count reconstruction, and reveals the common gap where multiplication is fluent but the matching division facts are not.
