topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Division as Unknown Factor
topic.description: Understand division as an unknown-factor problem (e.g. find 32 ÷ 8 by finding the number that makes 32 when multiplied by 8)
evidence: Explain that 32 ÷ 8 = ? is the same as 8 × ? = 32
Use a known multiplication fact to find a division answer
Describe the relationship between multiplication and division as inverse operations
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} work out '32 ÷ 8' by asking 'what do I multiply 8 by to get 32?' — using times table knowledge rather than a separate division method?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 8–9y; understand division as an unknown-factor problem: 32 ÷ 8 = ? is the same as 8 × ? = 32 — division and multiplication are inverse operations.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y3 'write and calculate mathematical statements for multiplication and division using the multiplication tables'; Y2 established using the inverse and that ×÷ are related; children use known × facts to answer ÷.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 3.OA.6 — 'Understand division as an unknown-factor problem, e.g., find 32 ÷ 8 by finding the number that makes 32 when multiplied by 8.'
• Operational details — the goal is that children STOP treating ÷ as a separate skill and reach for a known × fact instead: to find 32÷8 they ask 'eight times what is 32?'. This is the engine of division fluency and rests on fact families / the multiplication–division inverse. Use the array/rectangle (one side known, other unknown) and the fact-family triangle (8, 4, 32 generating 8×4=32, 4×8=32, 32÷8=4, 32÷4=8) as the core models.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8): rewrite 32÷8=? as 8×?=32 and solve using a known fact. Tier B (age 8–9): given a fact-family triangle, write all four related ×÷ facts. Tier C (age 9): explain WHY knowing 6×7=42 instantly gives both 42÷6 and 42÷7, using the inverse relationship.
bestPractices: Teach the fact-family triangle (three numbers → two × and two ÷ facts) so children experience × and ÷ as one linked system, not two.
Reframe every division as a missing-factor question aloud: '32÷8' → 'eight times what is 32?' — make this verbal move the default strategy.
Use the array with one dimension hidden: 32 dots in 8 rows, cover the columns, and ask how many per row — the unknown factor is literally the missing side.
Practise the inverse both directions with the same trio so children check division by multiplying back (8×4=32 confirms 32÷8=4).
Deliberately connect to fluency: as × tables are memorised, harvest the ÷ facts for free rather than learning them separately.
keyRepresentations: Fact-family triangle (the 8/4/32 trio generating all four ×÷ statements)
Array/rectangle with one side unknown — division as finding the missing dimension
Bar model — whole 32 split into 8 equal parts, each part the unknown factor
Number line — how many 8-hops reach 32 (unknown number of jumps)
commonMisconceptions: Seeing ÷ and × as unrelated, so learning division facts from scratch instead of deriving them from known products.
Writing the fact family wrongly by treating ÷ as commutative (32÷4 and 4÷32 as the same).
Getting the missing-factor direction confused (solving 8×?=32 as 8×32).
Not using multiplication to check division answers, so errors go uncaught.
Believing the unknown must be the largest number in the trio.

learn.summary: For ages 8–9, build the understanding that division is an unknown-factor problem: 32 ÷ 8 = ? is the same question as 8 × ? = 32, because multiplication and division are inverse operations. The core move is to reframe every division aloud as a missing-factor multiplication ('eight times what makes 32?') and to use known times-table facts to derive division answers rather than learning division separately. Core models are the fact-family triangle, the array with one dimension hidden, the bar model, and the number line of equal hops.

activities.title: Fact-family array: grow the eights until you reach 32
feedback: If a learner grows past 32 (e.g. to 40, which is 5 columns), ask them to look at the total and step back one column to land exactly on 32.
When all four statements appear, prompt: 'Point to the multiplication you used and the division it just answered — how are they the same picture?'
If they treat 8×4 and 32÷8 as separate problems, cover the columns again and ask them to predict the division answer before revealing.
activities.rationale: Letting the learner physically grow groups of 8 and watch the missing dimension and the four fact-family statements appear together ties division concretely to a known multiplication, directly targeting the misconception that × and ÷ are unrelated. The slider/shutter updating together is an optional interaction example that makes the inverse concrete; a hidden-dimension array drawn on paper with counters works similarly.
sourceClaims: 3.OA.6 requires understanding division as an unknown-factor problem (find 32÷8 by finding the number that makes 32 when multiplied by 8).
Fact families and the multiplication–division inverse should be used so division facts are derived from known products, supporting fluency.
learnerActions: Face the question '32 ÷ 8 = ?' alongside a grid showing 8 rows whose columns are hidden behind a shutter.
Instead of dividing, add columns of 8 one at a time, tracking the running total: 8, 16, 24, 32.
Stop when the total reaches 32 and count how many columns you added (4).
Reveal the full array and read off all four related facts together: 8×4=32, 4×8=32, 32÷8=4, 32÷4=8.
Say aloud what you just did: 'I found 32÷8 by asking how many 8s make 32.'
activities.intendedInsight: Division answers the question 'how many of this factor fit into the whole?' — it is multiplication with a missing factor, and the same array simultaneously shows the multiplication and its inverse division.

activities.title: Fact-family triangle: four facts from three numbers
feedback: If a learner writes '4÷32', point out that division is not commutative: the whole (32) is the amount being divided, so it comes first — the family gives 32÷4 and 32÷8, not 4÷32.

If a learner writes '32÷32', explain that the fact family for 8, 4 and 32 uses all three different numbers; the whole 32 is divided by one of its factors (8 or 4), not by itself, so 32÷32 is not one of these four facts.

If a learner assumes the hidden number must be the largest in the trio, show the triangle: here the whole 32 sits at the top and is the largest, yet when a base corner is hidden the missing number is a smaller factor (4 or 8) — the unknown is only the biggest when the top number itself is covered.
If they can state 8×4=32 but stall on 32÷4, prompt: 'The triangle has the same three numbers — which number is now hidden?'
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal or lift-the-flap triangle is a clean, memorable anchor for the four related facts and the inverse idea that learners can carry as a mental model. It consolidates structure but does not let learners vary the trio and watch the inverse hold across many cases, so pair it with the array activity.
sourceClaims: Fact families and the multiplication–division inverse should be used so division facts are derived from known products, supporting fluency.
Y3 pupils write and calculate mathematical statements for multiplication and division using the tables they know, using the inverse relationship established in Y2.
learnerActions: Draw or view a triangle with the product 32 at the top and the factors 8 and 4 at the base corners.
Cover one corner (say the 4) and say how you would find the hidden number using the other two.
Write all four related facts from the trio: 8×4=32, 4×8=32, 32÷8=4, 32÷4=8.
Repeat with a new trio, e.g. 6, 7, 42, writing all four statements (6×7=42, 7×6=42, 42÷6=7, 42÷7=6).
activities.intendedInsight: Three different numbers in a fact family (like 8, 4 and 32) give two multiplications and two divisions, so knowing one product gives you both divisions for free. When the two factors are the same (like 4, 4 and 16), there is just one multiplication and one division.

activities.title: Rewrite and check: division as missing factor
feedback: If a learner chooses a reversed form like 4÷32, ask which number is the whole being divided — that must come first in the division, so it should be 32÷4.
If a learner inverts to 8×32, prompt: 'Does 8 times 32 give 32? 8×32 is 256. We need the number that, times 8, makes 32 — that is 4.'

If a learner fills 8×?=32 by adding (e.g. '8 and 24 more makes 32'), restate it as 'how many eights are in 32?' and count equal groups — 8, 16, 24, 32 is four hops — so they build groups of 8, not a sum.
Praise multiplying back as a check: 'You confirmed 32÷8=4 by showing 8×4=32 — that catches mistakes.'
activities.rationale: These crisply checkable tasks consolidate the strategy and target the commutativity, wrong-direction, and additive misconceptions with specific prompts (4÷32, 8×32, adding to reach 32). This format verifies and consolidates the idea rather than building it from scratch, and does not show the array's missing side, so it follows the manipulation activities.
sourceClaims: Y3 pupils write and calculate mathematical statements for multiplication and division using the tables they know, using the inverse relationship established in Y2.
learnerActions: Rewrite each division as a missing-factor multiplication, e.g. 32÷8=? ↔ 8×□=32, then solve using a known fact.
Match each division fact to the multiplication fact that solves it.
Check each division answer by multiplying back (8×4=32 confirms 32÷8=4).
Spot the trap: decide whether '32÷8 = 8×32' is correct, and explain your reasoning.
activities.intendedInsight: Rewriting ÷ as missing-× and checking by multiplying back makes the inverse relationship a reliable, self-correcting strategy.

activities.title: Maths-detective talk: which fact helps?
feedback: If a learner starts counting or sharing, redirect: 'Before counting — what times 8 gives that number?'
If they explain the inverse clearly for 42, invite them to transfer it to a fresh trio to show it generalises.
activities.rationale: A Socratic partner can nudge the missing-factor move and make the verbal reframing habitual, which the pedagogy names as the default strategy. The underlying structure is best carried by the array/triangle, so dialogue supports but does not replace manipulation.
learnerActions: When given a division, answer the prompt 'which times-table fact you already know could help here?' before computing.
State the division as a spoken missing-factor question: '32÷8' becomes 'eight times what gives 32?'
Explain in your own words why knowing 6×7=42 instantly gives both 42÷6=7 and 42÷7=6.
activities.intendedInsight: Verbalising the missing-factor question makes reaching for a known multiplication the default first move for any division.

constraints: The rewrite-and-match-and-check format mainly verifies and consolidates; it does not elicit construction of the array model or show the missing dimension, so use it after hands-on work, not as the first exposure.
The static triangle anchors the four facts but does not let learners vary the trio and watch the inverse hold across many cases — pair it with the variable array.
Dialogue prompts support the verbal missing-factor habit but should accompany, not replace, manipulation of the array and triangle.

Division is not commutative: the whole (e.g. 32) must be the number being divided, so guard against the commutativity error 4÷32; also guard against 32÷32, which reuses one number and is not part of the 8/4/32 family.
The slider/shutter and tap-to-reveal are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete; the same learning can be done with counters, drawn arrays, and paper triangles.
Keep the missing-factor direction explicit: 8×?=32 is solved by finding the factor (4), not by computing 8×32 (=256) or by adding to reach 32.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One source claim (3.OA.6) is marked verified:false and two NCETM/standards claims are unverified in the original row; treat cited standards wording as legacy, not re-checked.

The original assessment reteach note 'the answer to a division is always SMALLER-or-equal to what you started with when sharing among many' is only true for dividing by a whole number greater than 1 and could mislead if generalised; it was not carried into learner-facing actions. Prefer rebuilding the fact triangle (product on top, factors at corners) to fix wrong-direction errors.
Arithmetic self-check: 8×4=32, 32÷8=4, 32÷4=8, 8×32=256, 5×8=40, and 6×7=42 with 42÷6=7, 42÷7=6 all verified correct as used in activities and feedback.

probeDeeper: You used 8 × 4 = 32. How does knowing that multiplication tell you the division answer?
If I change it to 32 ÷ 4, which fact helps now — and what will the answer be?
Write the whole fact family for 8, 4 and 32. Which two are multiplications and which two are divisions?
Someone says 32 ÷ 8 must be 8 × 32. Why is that not right?
assess.correctAnswer: 4. The child reframes 32 ÷ 8 as 'eight times WHAT makes 32?' — 8 × 4 = 32, so 32 ÷ 8 = 4 — because division asks for the missing factor, and multiplication and division are inverse operations that undo each other.

errorPatterns.pattern: finds the answer only by dealing out / repeated subtraction and cannot connect it to a multiplication fact — sees ÷ and × as unrelated procedures
errorPatterns.nextMove: lay out the same 32 in a 8×4 array; show the ONE array answers both 8×4=? and 32÷8=?; build a fact-family triangle so the inverse link is explicit.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child solves 32÷8 by sharing counters but, asked which times-table fact helps, shrugs or starts a fresh count

errorPatterns.pattern: inverts the unknown-factor relationship — for 32÷8 reaches for '32 × 8' or picks the wrong fact family member
errorPatterns.nextMove: anchor on 'the answer to a division is always SMALLER-or-equal to what you started with when sharing among many' and rebuild the fact triangle: the product 32 sits at the top, 8 and the missing 4 at the corners.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child names a multiplication whose product is not 32 (e.g. 8×32) or multiplies the two given numbers

errorPatterns.pattern: reads the missing-factor equation 8 × ? = 32 but then adds to reach 32 (8 + 24) rather than multiplies
errorPatterns.nextMove: restate the box as 'how many EIGHTS in 32', count the eights (8,16,24,32 = four jumps) on a number line to bind it to groups, not addition.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child says '8 and then 24 more makes 32' when filling the box

responseLevels.gap: reaches an answer only by sharing/counting or gets it wrong; treats × and ÷ as unconnected; cannot supply a linked multiplication.
responseLevels.full: reframes the division as an unknown-factor multiplication, justifies it via the inverse relationship, generates the full fact family, and transfers to a new division using the same product.
responseLevels.partial: states 8 × 4 = 32 gives 4 for this item but cannot generalise — does not produce the reciprocal division (32÷4) from the same fact or articulate 'division finds the missing factor'.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a division: 32 ÷ 8 = ?. Solve it, but instead of sharing or counting, use a multiplication fact you already know. Which multiplication did you use, and why does that give you the answer to the division?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child can get 4 by skip-counting or sharing without seeing the inverse relationship; the demand to name the multiplication fact and explain WHY it answers the division exposes whether they hold division as an unknown-factor problem. A child who only knows division as 'sharing out' can compute but cannot state the linked multiplication as a reason.

topic.name: Factor Pairs & Commutativity
topic.description: Recognise and use factor pairs and commutativity in mental calculations
evidence: List all factor pairs of a given number (e.g. 24: 1×24, 2×12, 3×8, 4×6)
Use commutativity to reorder a multiplication for easier mental calculation
Explain what a factor pair is and how commutativity helps
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to multiply '4 × 15', can they spot that splitting it into '4 × 5 × 3 = 20 × 3 = 60' is a clever shortcut — using factor pairs to make it easier?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 8–9y; recognise and use factor pairs and commutativity in mental calculations (e.g. list factor pairs of 24; reorder a product for easier calculation).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y4 'recognise and use factor pairs and commutativity in mental calculations'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.OA.4 — 'find all factor pairs for a whole number in the range 1–100 … recognize that a whole number is a multiple of each of its factors' (leads into prime/composite); 3.OA.5 commutativity as a strategy.
• Operational details — a factor pair is two numbers that multiply to give a target (24: 1×24, 2×12, 3×8, 4×6). The two skills interlock: commutativity means 3×8 and 8×3 are the SAME pair, so you find pairs systematically and stop when they meet in the middle (avoiding duplicates). Factor pairs are found via known table facts and the ×÷ inverse ('what times what makes 24?'). The mental-calculation payoff: reorder/regroup using pairs (e.g. 25×16 = 25×4×4 = 100×4 = 400). Represent each pair as a rectangle (24 dots as 1×24, 2×12, 3×8, 4×6 rectangles) so factors ARE the possible rectangle dimensions — the direct bridge to arrays/area and later to primes (a prime makes only the 1×n rectangle).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8): find factor pairs of a small number with an array (12). Tier B (age 8–9): list ALL factor pairs of a number to ~50 systematically, using commutativity to avoid repeats. Tier C (age 9): use factor pairs to simplify a mental calculation and explain why you stop searching at the square root.
bestPractices: Search for factor pairs systematically — 1, 2, 3, … in order, pairing each with its partner — and use commutativity to know you've found them all when the pair 'meets in the middle'.
Represent each factor pair as a rectangle of the target number, so a factor is literally a side length and children see the finite set of rectangles a number allows.
Find factors through known table facts and the ×÷ inverse, reinforcing that factor-finding is division/known-fact work.
Use factor pairs and commutativity as mental-calculation tools (reorder/regroup for easy pairs like ×5×2=×10), not just as a listing exercise.
Seed prime/composite intuition: numbers with only the 1×n rectangle (one factor pair) hint at primes; square numbers have a repeated factor (the square).
keyRepresentations: Rectangle/array for each factor pair — factors as side lengths of all rectangles of that number
Systematic factor-pair list (1×24, 2×12, 3×8, 4×6) with the 'meet in the middle' stopping point
Factor 'rainbow' arcs pairing 1–24, 2–12, 3–8, 4–6 — shows commutativity and completeness
×÷ fact family — factor-finding as division
commonMisconceptions: Listing 3×8 and 8×3 as different pairs (not applying commutativity), inflating the count.
Missing factor pairs by searching unsystematically, especially the middle ones.
Confusing factors with multiples (factors go INTO the number; multiples are in its times table).
Forgetting 1 and the number itself are always a factor pair.
Not knowing when to stop — continuing past the square root and re-finding pairs in reverse.

learn.summary: Teaching factor pairs and commutativity to 8–9 year-olds: a factor pair is two whole numbers that multiply to a target (24: 1×24, 2×12, 3×8, 4×6). Commutativity means 3×8 and 8×3 are the SAME unordered pair, so pairs are searched systematically from 1 upward and the search stops when the two factors 'meet in the middle' (near the square root). Each pair corresponds to a rectangle the number can form, which bridges to arrays/area and previews primes (a whole number greater than 1 with only the 1×n rectangle). Factor pairs also pay off as a mental-calculation tool via reordering/regrouping (e.g. 25×16 = 25×4×4 = 100×4 = 400). Manipulable rectangle-building is the core; static diagrams, checking tasks, and Socratic questioning serve distinct supporting roles.

activities.title: Rectangle hunt: build every rectangle of a number
feedback: If a rectangle has gaps, it is not a valid arrangement — the dimensions only count as a factor pair when every counter fills a complete rectangle.
When a learner records 3×8 and 8×3 separately, show the same rectangle rotated: same counters, same two factors, so it is one pair, not two.
If a learner is unsure when to stop, point out that once the two sides of the rectangle cross over (near 4 and 6 for 24), every larger factor has already appeared as the partner of a smaller one.
With 23, prompt: 'Can you make any rectangle other than a single line? What does that tell you about 23?'
activities.rationale: Building rectangles makes the abstract list a felt, discovered structure, ties factor-finding to arrays/area (the total count equals the number), and lets completeness and the stopping point emerge from running out of rectangles rather than from a memorised rule. Contrast with a prime previews prime/composite ideas. Optional live feedback (logging dimensions, drawing rainbow arcs, rotating a rectangle to show 3×8 = 8×3) makes the mechanism concrete but is not required — paper, tiles, or dots work.
sourceClaims: Representing factor pairs as rectangles/arrays and searching systematically (stopping at the square root) supports completeness and previews prime/composite numbers.
4.OA.4 requires finding all factor pairs for a whole number 1–100 and recognising multiples, leading into prime/composite.
learnerActions: Take 24 counters (or squared paper, tiles, or dots) and arrange them into complete, gap-free rectangles, recording the dimensions of each as a factor pair.
Work systematically: ask 'does 1 fit? does 2 fit? does 3 fit?...' in order, logging each rectangle you can make (1×24, 2×12, 3×8, 4×6).
After making 3×8, try to make 8×3 and observe it is the SAME rectangle turned a quarter-turn — record it as one pair already found, not a new one.
Keep going (5 does not fit; 6 gives 6×4, the same rectangle as 4×6) and notice that no NEW rectangles appear once the two sides meet in the middle; explain why you can stop there.
Repeat with 23 counters and discover only a single 1×23 line forms — a whole number greater than 1 that makes only a single 1×n line is prime.
Draw a 'factor rainbow': arcs pairing 1–24, 2–12, 3–8, 4–6 to show each pair and completeness.
activities.intendedInsight: Factors are the possible side-lengths of all rectangles a number can form; commutativity collapses 3×8 and 8×3 into one pair; a systematic search can stop where the factors meet in the middle because every larger factor has already appeared as the partner of a smaller one; and a whole number greater than 1 that makes only the 1×n rectangle is prime.

activities.title: Factor pairs as a mental-calculation tool
feedback: Check the regrouping preserves the product: 25×4×4 uses the same factors as 25×16 (because 16 = 4×4), so the answer must match (400).
If a learner cannot find a factor, prompt them to use a known table fact or division: 'what number times 4 gives 16?'
activities.rationale: The curriculum goal names mental calculation explicitly; applying factor pairs to real regrouping connects the skill to its payoff and reinforces factor-finding as division/known-fact work.
sourceClaims: Y4 pupils recognise and use factor pairs and commutativity in mental calculations.
learnerActions: Rewrite a multiplication by regrouping convenient factors: turn 25×16 into 25×4×4, then compute 100×4 = 400.
Find a factor pair that makes a product easy (e.g. pairing ×5 with ×2 to make ×10), and explain why reordering is allowed.
Find factors using known times-table facts and the multiplication/division inverse: 'what times what makes 24?'
activities.intendedInsight: Commutativity (changing the order) and regrouping (choosing which factors to multiply first, e.g. 25×(4×4) = (25×4)×4) let you use factor pairs to turn a calculation into easier steps, so factor-finding is a practical mental-maths tool, not just a listing exercise.

activities.title: Prove the list is complete (systematic-search reasoning)
feedback: If the justification is 'I think that's all', model checking each counting number in order from 1 up to the point where the factor pairs meet (e.g. 1 to 6 for 36), recording each result so completeness is demonstrated, not guessed.
For the odd-count question, show that a square's two equal factors (5×5 for 25) count as one factor, so the total is odd.
activities.rationale: A Socratic 'how do you know?' exchange can build the systematic-search and completeness habit and targets the 'stop too early' and 'don't know when to stop' errors. It works alongside, not instead of, the visual rectangle work.
sourceClaims: Representing factor pairs as rectangles/arrays and searching systematically (stopping at the square root) supports completeness and previews prime/composite numbers.
learnerActions: List all factor pairs of a number such as 36, then explain how you know none is missing.
Respond to a challenge — 'Have we found them all? How do you know?' — by describing your sweep from 1 and your stopping point.

Explain why 24 has an even count of factors (8) but a square number like 25 has an odd count (3: 1, 5, 25), because one pair uses the same factor twice (5×5, the square root), so that factor is counted only once.
activities.intendedInsight: Completeness comes from a systematic sweep that pairs each small factor with its partner and stops where they meet, not from feeling finished; in a square number, one pair uses the same factor twice (e.g. 6×6 for 36), so that factor is counted once and the number of factors is odd.

activities.title: Check and sort: factors, pairs, and multiples
feedback: 24 has four distinct factor pairs. If a learner answers eight, they are counting reversed versions (8×3 as separate from 3×8) — these are the same pair.
If a learner lists a multiple (e.g. 48) as a factor of 24, remind them a factor goes INTO 24; a multiple is 24 times something.
Always include 1 and the number itself (1×24) — these form a pair every whole number has.
activities.rationale: Short checkable tasks can verify the duplicate/commutativity and factor-versus-multiple distinctions. A sort or fill-in checks classification but does not itself build the rectangle intuition or elicit the hands-on discovery of the stopping point, so it best follows the hands-on work.
sourceClaims: 4.OA.4 requires finding all factor pairs for a whole number 1–100 and recognising multiples, leading into prime/composite.
learnerActions: Fill in the missing factor pair of 36 given a partial list.
Sort numbers into 'factor of 24', 'multiple of 24', 'both' (24 itself) or 'neither' to distinguish the two ideas.
State how many DISTINCT factor pairs 24 has (four: 1×24, 2×12, 3×8, 4×6), treating each unordered pair once.
activities.intendedInsight: Factors divide into the number while multiples lie in its times table; distinct factor pairs are counted once because commutativity makes reversed versions the same pair.

constraints: Count a factor pair once: 3×8 and 8×3 are the same unordered pair. The common error of listing them separately (giving 24 '8 pairs') must be corrected in teaching, not presented as a valid option.

Checking/sorting tasks verify understanding and check classification; they do not by themselves build the rectangle intuition or let a learner discover the meeting-in-the-middle point, so they are well placed after hands-on exploration (not a universal requirement).

A static factor-rainbow diagram is a useful reference and can show completeness and commutativity, but it does not let the learner search for pairs or discover the meeting-in-the-middle point themselves.

Physical counters, tiles, or dots have slight thickness and stand in for the ideal flat rectangle; treat the arrangement as a representation of the number's structure where side-lengths = factors and the total count = the number — this legitimately bridges to arrays and area, so preserve (do not deny) the array/area interpretation.
Factor pairs are planar (two factors, rectangles). A three-factor/volume (cuboid) treatment belongs to a different topic and should not be introduced here.
Always include the 1×n pair; every number has 1 and itself as a factor pair.
The 'one rectangle = prime' observation applies only to whole numbers greater than 1; 1 forms only 1×1 but is not prime.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original materials describe stopping 'at the square root'. For these learners this is framed concretely as 'the two sides of the rectangle meet in the middle'; the exact square-root rule is the underlying reason and can be stated by older/more confident learners.
Source claims for CCSS-M 4.OA.4 and the NCETM guidance were marked unverified in the original row; do not treat them as independently confirmed.

The original counted 24 as having four distinct factor pairs; one legacy error-pattern distractor stated '24 has 8 factor pairs' — this is included only as a misconception to correct, never as a correct answer.

The original framed primes as 'numbers with just one rectangle'; this converse is inaccurate for 1, so the learner-facing wording was qualified to whole numbers greater than 1 while keeping the correct direction (a prime makes only the 1×n rectangle).

probeDeeper: How did you know 5 is not a factor of 24?
You wrote 3×8. Is 8×3 a different pair or the same one — why?
How did you know when to stop checking numbers?
24 has an even number of factors but 25 has an odd number. Why might that be?
assess.correctAnswer: 1×24, 2×12, 3×8, 4×6 (and their commutative partners 24×1, 12×2, 8×3, 6×4, which are the same pairs). A child reasoning well works UP from 1 checking each number in turn, stops when the factors meet in the middle (after 4×6, since 5 doesn't divide 24 and 6 has already appeared), and uses commutativity to know 3×8 and 8×3 are one pair, not two.

errorPatterns.pattern: searches unsystematically and stops early — lists 1×24, 2×12, 4×6 and misses 3×8, with no way to know a pair is missing
errorPatterns.nextMove: model checking every counting number in order (does 1 go in? 2? 3? …) and recording each result, so completeness comes from the systematic sweep, not from feeling done.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child offers an incomplete set and, asked how they know it's complete, says 'I think that's all' with no method

errorPatterns.pattern: counts 3×8 and 8×3 as two different factor pairs, inflating the list — not treating commutativity as making them one pair
errorPatterns.nextMove: show 3×8 and 8×3 as the same array rotated a quarter turn — same rectangle, same factors; a factor PAIR is one unordered pair.
errorPatterns.distractor: 24 has 8 factor pairs (3×8 and 8×3 are different)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child lists eight 'pairs' and treats reversed versions as new

errorPatterns.pattern: does not know when to STOP — keeps testing numbers past 24 or is unsure why the search ends, missing that factors pair up around the square root
errorPatterns.nextMove: point out that once the two factors in a pair cross over (here after 4 and 6), every larger factor has already appeared as the partner of a smaller one, so the search is complete.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child keeps trying numbers like 7, 9, 10 aimlessly or asks 'how far do I go?'

responseLevels.gap: finds a few pairs by trial with gaps, no method for completeness, and/or double-counts commutative reversals.
responseLevels.full: sweeps systematically from 1, uses commutativity to pair factors and avoid duplicates, stops correctly where factors meet, and justifies that the list is complete.
responseLevels.partial: finds all four pairs but only by luck or exhaustive guessing — cannot justify completeness or explain the stopping point; may still treat reversals as distinct.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Find ALL the factor pairs of 24 — every pair of whole numbers that multiply to make 24. When you have them, tell me how you knew you had found them all and hadn't missed any.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Unsystematic children find some pairs and guess they are done; the reason tier ('how do you know you have them all?') separates a random search from a systematic sweep up to the square-root turning point. Whether they double-count 3×8 and 8×3 reveals if commutativity is being used to organise the search.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Mental multiplication and division
topic.description: Use place value, known and derived facts to multiply and divide mentally, including multiplying by 0 and 1, dividing by 1, and multiplying together three numbers
evidence: Calculate 40 × 6 = 240 mentally using place value
Explain why any number × 0 = 0 and any number × 1 = the number itself
Multiply three numbers mentally by choosing a useful pair first (e.g. 2 × 7 × 5 = 2 × 5 × 7 = 70)
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} work out things like '6 × 0', '1 × 35', or '100 ÷ 100' instantly in their head — using what they know rather than working everything out from scratch?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 8–9y; use place value, known and derived facts to multiply and divide mentally — including ×0 and ×1, ÷1, and multiplying three numbers by choosing a useful pair first.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y4 'use place value, known and derived facts to multiply and divide mentally, including: multiplying by 0 and 1; dividing by 1; multiplying together three numbers'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 3.OA.5 (properties as strategies) and 3.OA.7 (fluency using strategies); the identity/zero properties appear in the properties-of-operations table.
• Operational details — this consolidates mental strategy: (a) place value (40×6 = 4 tens ×6 = 240); (b) the special cases — ×1 leaves a number unchanged (identity), ×0 gives 0 (zero property), ÷1 leaves a number unchanged — taught with meaning (1 group of n; n groups of 1; 0 groups) not as rules; (c) associativity/commutativity to reorder three factors into an easy pair first (2×7×5 → 2×5×7 = 10×7 = 70). The habit is to LOOK for the easy route before calculating. Note ÷0 is not required here (and is undefined) — keep to ×0, ×1, ÷1.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8): 40×6 mentally via place value; state ×1 and ×0 results. Tier B (age 8–9): reorder three numbers to find an easy pair (2×9×5). Tier C (age 9): explain WHY ×0=0 and ×1/÷1 leave a number unchanged using the groups meaning.
bestPractices: Teach ×0, ×1, ÷1 through the equal-groups meaning (1 group of n = n; n groups of 1 = n; 0 groups = 0) so they're understood, not memorised as rules.
Build the habit of scanning three-factor products for the easiest pair to combine first (make a ten, or a known fact), justified by commutativity/associativity.
Use place-value reasoning for mental ×÷ with multiples of ten (40×6 = 24 tens = 240).
Verbalise the chosen strategy each time ('I'll pair the 2 and 5 to make 10') to make flexible method-choice explicit.
Keep ÷0 out of scope and, if raised, address it meaningfully (you can't make groups that share nothing / it's undefined).
keyRepresentations: Equal-groups images for the identity/zero cases (1 group of n; n groups of 1; 0 groups)
Rearrangeable factor tiles for three-number products (regroup to make a ten)
Place-value counters for × multiples of ten
Number line / known-fact chains for derived facts
commonMisconceptions: Thinking ×0 gives the other number, or ×1 doubles/changes it, when treated as rote rules.
Believing multiplication always makes a number bigger (so ×1 or later × a fraction surprises).
Not reordering three factors, so multiplying left-to-right the hard way.
Confusing ÷1 with ÷0 or thinking ÷1 halves.
Miscounting place value in 40×6 (getting 24 instead of 240).

learn.summary: For ages 8–9: multiply and divide mentally using place value, known and derived facts, including the special cases ×0, ×1 and ÷1, and multiplying three numbers by choosing a useful pair first. The goal is flexible strategy choice — looking for the easy route before calculating — with the identity/zero cases understood through the equal-groups meaning rather than memorised as rules. Note: ÷0 is out of scope and is undefined; keep to ×0, ×1, ÷1.

activities.title: Reorder three factors to find the easy pair
feedback: If a learner ploughs left to right or stalls, prompt: 'Is there a pair that makes a ten, or a fact you already know?' Then let them try pairing 2 and 5.
If they doubt that reordering is allowed, have them compute two orders (e.g. 2 × 7 × 5 and 5 × 2 × 7) and confirm both give 70.
When they verbalise the chosen strategy ('I'll pair the 2 and 5 to make 10'), affirm that naming the plan is the skill being built.
activities.rationale: Building the habit of scanning three-factor products for the easiest pair, justified by commutativity/associativity, makes flexible method-choice explicit. An optional manipulable surface — three draggable number tiles feeding one live product readout, where pairing 2 and 5 fuses them into a glowing 10 while the total never changes as tiles are shuffled — can make the invariance felt; this interaction is an example, not a requirement.
sourceClaims: Y4 pupils use place value, known and derived facts to multiply and divide mentally, including ×0 and ×1, ÷1, and multiplying three numbers.
Properties of operations (including identity and zero) are used as strategies for fluent mental calculation.
The identity/zero cases should be taught through the equal-groups meaning; reordering three factors for an easy pair uses commutativity/associativity.
learnerActions: Work out 2 × 7 × 5 in your head, saying aloud which two numbers you multiply first and why.
Try pairing 2 and 5 first to make 10, then multiply by 7 to get 70; compare this with going left to right (2 × 7 = 14, then × 5 = 70).
Check that different orders give the same total: is 2 × 7 × 5 the same as 5 × 2 × 7? Explain why you are allowed to reorder.
Repeat with 2 × 9 × 5 and 4 × 3 × 5, each time scanning for a pair that makes a ten or a known fact first.
activities.intendedInsight: Reordering factors is always allowed (commutativity/associativity) and the total stays the same — but some orderings turn a fiddly three-number product into a single known fact, so it pays to look for the friendly pair before calculating.

activities.title: Understand ×1, ×0 and ÷1 through groups
feedback: If a learner says 8 × 0 = 8 or 8 × 1 = 0, act it out with counters: 8 groups of 0 is nothing (0); 8 groups of 1 is 8. Contrast directly with adding 0.

If a learner expects ×1 to make the number bigger (believing multiplication always increases a number), use the single-group picture: one group of 8 is still 8, so multiplying by 1 changes nothing — multiplication does not always make a number larger.

If they confuse ÷1 with halving or with ÷0, return to the division picture: 8 ÷ 1 is one whole group (or groups of one), so you get everything back, 8. ÷0 is different — you cannot share 8 among zero groups, and no number of groups of 0 makes 8, so it is left undefined and out of scope.
Praise explanations that reference groups rather than restating a rule.
activities.rationale: Teaching the identity/zero cases through equal-groups meaning targets the common rote-rule confusions (×0 gives the other number; ×1 changes it) and the belief that multiplying always increases a number. Optional tap-to-reveal panels pairing each case (×1, ×0, ÷1) with its groups picture and a 'why' flap can anchor the meaning.
sourceClaims: The identity/zero cases should be taught through the equal-groups meaning; reordering three factors for an easy pair uses commutativity/associativity.
Properties of operations (including identity and zero) are used as strategies for fluent mental calculation.
learnerActions: Lay out counters to show 8 × 1 as 'one group of 8' and '8 groups of 1'; confirm both give 8.
Show 8 × 0 as '8 groups of nothing' — every group is empty, so the total is 0.
Show 8 ÷ 1 as one whole group of 8 (or sharing 8 into groups of one) and confirm the result is still 8.
Say in your own words why n × 1 = n, why n × 0 = 0, and why n ÷ 1 = n.
Contrast 8 × 0 with 8 + 0: adding 0 leaves 8, but 0 groups of 8 (or 8 groups of 0) is nothing — notice the roles are different.
activities.intendedInsight: ×1 and ÷1 leave a number unchanged because you have one whole group (or share into groups of one), and ×0 gives 0 because there are no groups (or every group is empty) — these are meanings to be seen, not rules to memorise.

activities.title: Scale with place value for multiples of ten
feedback: If a learner answers 24 (ten times too small), prompt: '4 what times 6? Four tens — so 24 tens, which is 240.'
Have them restate the known fact (4 × 6 = 24) and then re-apply the ten-times adjustment rather than reteaching from scratch when the method is sound but the number slips.
activities.rationale: Place-value reasoning for mental ×÷ with multiples of ten addresses the frequent error of multiplying the tens digit as ones. Place-value counters can make the 'tens' unit concrete; restating the underlying known fact models the known-fact chain for derived facts.
sourceClaims: Y4 pupils use place value, known and derived facts to multiply and divide mentally, including ×0 and ×1, ÷1, and multiplying three numbers.
learnerActions: Work out 40 × 6 mentally by reasoning '4 tens × 6 = 24 tens = 240'; say the 'tens' name aloud as you go.
Explain how knowing 4 × 6 = 24 helps you get 40 × 6.
Try 30 × 7 and 50 × 8 the same way, keeping the place-value name attached to each digit.
Check your answer is sensible: 40 × 6 is exactly ten times 4 × 6, so 240, not 24.
activities.intendedInsight: A known fact can be scaled by place value: 40 × 6 is ten times 4 × 6, so the answer is 240, not 24 — keeping the 'tens' label attached prevents losing the place value.

activities.title: Consolidate and check reasoning
feedback: For a correct strategy with an arithmetic slip, do not reteach — ask the learner to re-state the known fact and re-apply the adjustment.
If explanations fall back on rules, redirect to the groups picture or to checking that two orderings give the same total.
Watch for the persistent 7 × 0 = 7 and 7 × 1 = 0 confusions and address them with counters (7 groups of 0 is 0; 7 groups of 1 is 7).
activities.rationale: Checking mental results and strategy choice consolidates fluency and surfaces reasoning that a bare answer hides, including asking learners to justify ×1 = n and why reordering is allowed (properties of operations as strategies). A response format (multiple-choice for the easiest pairing, fill-in for ×0/×1/÷1, a 'why' explanation) can be used during teaching to verify and prompt justification; recognition formats verify understanding rather than, on their own, building independent strategy construction.
sourceClaims: Properties of operations (including identity and zero) are used as strategies for fluent mental calculation.
learnerActions: Decide which pair you would multiply first in 2 × 9 × 5 and say why.
Give the results for 7 × 0, 7 × 1 and 7 ÷ 1, and explain each using the groups meaning.
Answer: why does any number × 1 equal that same number?
Explain why you are free to reorder the factors in a three-number product.
activities.intendedInsight: Strategy choice and the special-case results are things you can state and justify, not just compute — being able to explain why confirms genuine understanding.

constraints: Keep ÷0 out of scope; if a learner raises it, explain meaningfully that you cannot share 8 among zero groups, and no number of groups of 0 ever makes 8 — so 8 ÷ 0 is undefined — rather than giving a number.
Teach ×0, ×1 and ÷1 through the equal-groups meaning so they are understood, not memorised; rules learned by rote without meaning can leave learners prone to the ×0 = n and ×1 = 0 confusions.
Multiplication does not always make a number larger: ×1 leaves it unchanged and ×0 gives 0. Expect and address this surprise rather than letting 'multiplying makes it bigger' stand.

Recognition-only formats (choosing the right answer, filling a blank) verify results and can prompt justification, but do not by themselves elicit independent mental strategy construction; pair them with learners computing and explaining their own method.

Tap-to-reveal panels and draggable factor tiles are optional scaffolds that make invariance and group meaning concrete; they illustrate the mechanism and are not required for the learning, and a fixed worked example can still teach the same meaning.
The additive identity (adding 0) and multiplicative zero (×0) behave differently; contrast them explicitly so learners do not carry over 'adding 0 leaves it unchanged' to multiplication.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

In the source material, two of three cited sources (CCSS-M and NCETM) are marked verified:false; treat the identity/zero and reordering teaching principles as informed guidance, not independently confirmed efficacy claims.
The source misconception 'multiplication always makes a number bigger (so ×1 surprises)' is addressed in the ×1/×0/÷1 activity feedback and as a constraint.

The source's artefact-fit note that '3D adds cost without insight' for these planar numeric strategies is a catalog ranking, not an established pedagogical law; it has been dropped rather than asserted. A screen model and physical counters offer different experiences; neither is claimed universally necessary.
The added example 4 × 3 × 5 = 60 is agent-proposed and not from the source example set; it is arithmetically correct but untested as an item.
The ÷1 feedback was clarified to state the division model (one whole group / groups of one gives everything back) consistently before contrasting with the undefined ÷0.

probeDeeper: For 2 × 7 × 5, which two did you multiply first, and why those?
What is 8 × 0 — and why? What about 8 × 1?
How does knowing 4 × 6 help you with 40 × 6?
Is 2 × 7 × 5 the same as 5 × 2 × 7? Why can you reorder them?
assess.correctAnswer: 240 (4×6 = 24, then ×10 for the tens); 70 (reorder to 2×5 = 10, ×7 = 70); 8×0 = 0; 8×1 = 8. The teacher watches for place-value scaling, using commutativity/associativity to pick an easy pair, and correct, reasoned handling of the identity/zero cases.

errorPatterns.pattern: thinks n × 0 = n (or n × 1 = 0) — confuses the roles of the additive and multiplicative identities/zero
errorPatterns.nextMove: ground in groups: 8 groups of 0 is nothing (0); 8 groups of 1 is 8; act it out with counters, contrasting with adding 0.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child says 8 × 0 = 8 or 8 × 1 = 0

errorPatterns.pattern: does not reorder the three numbers — multiplies left to right (2×7 = 14, ×5 = 70) missing the easier 2×5 pairing, or stalls
errorPatterns.nextMove: show associativity/commutativity let you pick the friendliest pair first; look for pairs making 10s.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child computes the awkward way or loses track; doesn't spot the 2×5 = 10

errorPatterns.pattern: for 40 × 6 multiplies the tens digit as ones (answer 24) forgetting the place value
errorPatterns.nextMove: reason 4 tens × 6 = 24 tens = 240; keep the 'tens' name attached to the digit.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answer ten times too small

errorPatterns.pattern: correct strategy, arithmetic slip
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach; have the child re-state the known fact and re-apply the adjustment.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: right approach, wrong number

responseLevels.gap: confuses ×0/×1, multiplies tens as ones, or cannot handle a three-number product.
responseLevels.full: scales by place value, reorders three factors to pick friendly pairs (associativity/commutativity), and reasons correctly about ×0 and ×1.
responseLevels.partial: handles place-value scaling but doesn't reorder to find easy pairs, or is inconsistent on the identity/zero cases.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the child to do these in their head, saying how: 40 × 6; then 2 × 7 × 5 (watch whether they reorder to pair 2 and 5); and slip in 8 × 0 and 8 × 1. Watch the place-value reasoning, the choice of a useful pair, and how they treat the ×0 and ×1 cases.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The three-number product reveals whether the child flexibly reorders (2×5 first) or ploughs left to right; the ×0 and ×1 items catch the persistent 8×0 = 8 and 8×1 = 0 confusions. Watching the mental strategy exposes reasoning that a bare answer hides.

evidence: Calculate 7 × 30 = 210 by reasoning 7 × 3 tens = 21 tens = 210
Explain why multiplying by a multiple of 10 adds a zero to the product
Use this skill to estimate products of larger numbers
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} quickly work out '7 × 40' or '6 × 80' by first doing the single-digit multiplication and then placing the zero — getting 280 and 480?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 8–9y; multiply a one-digit number by a multiple of 10 (10–90) using place value and properties (7×30 = 7×3 tens = 21 tens = 210).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y3–Y4 use place value and known facts to multiply mentally; underpins Y4 short multiplication and estimation.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 3.NBT.3 — 'multiply one-digit whole numbers by multiples of 10 in the range 10–90 (e.g. 9×80, 5×60) using strategies based on place value and properties of operations.'
• Operational details — the reasoning, not the trick, is the objective: 7×30 = 7×(3×10) = (7×3)×10 = 21×10 = 210 (associativity + place value). The '×10 shifts digits one place left' understanding must replace the dangerous 'just add a zero' rule (which breaks for decimals later). Use place-value counters/columns and the known fact 7×3=21 scaled by ten. This is the engine of estimation (234×5 ≈ 200×5) and a stepping-stone to × multiples of 100/1000 and to long multiplication.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8): 3×40 via 3×4 tens with counters. Tier B (age 8–9): any 1-digit × multiple of 10 mentally, explaining via the known fact and place value. Tier C (age 9): explain why the product gains a zero in terms of ten-times-larger, and use the skill to estimate a larger product.
bestPractices: Reason from the known fact scaled by ten: 7×30 = (7×3) tens = 21 tens = 210, using associativity and place value explicitly.
Teach 'ten times larger → digits shift one place left', NOT 'add a zero', so the idea survives the move to decimals.
Use place-value counters and columns so 21 tens visibly becomes 210 (regrouping ten tens into a hundred).
Connect immediately to estimation — rounding a factor to a multiple of ten to bound a larger product.
Extend the same reasoning to multiples of 100/1000 once secure, keeping the place-value story constant.
keyRepresentations: Place-value counters / columns — 21 tens regrouped to 210
Known-fact-×-ten chain (7×3=21 → 7×30=210)
Gattegno/place-value chart — the leftward digit shift for ×10
Number line in tens — skip counting by 30
commonMisconceptions: Over-relying on 'add a zero' as a rule without understanding, which later misfires with decimals (0.7×30).
Multiplying the wrong part (7×30 as 21 rather than 210) — losing the place-value scaling.
Adding an extra or too few zeros through miscounting places.
Not connecting 7×30 to the known fact 7×3, so it's computed from scratch.
Confusing multiplying by a multiple of ten with adding tens.

learn.summary: For ages 8–9: multiply a one-digit number by a multiple of 10 (10–90) by reasoning from a known fact scaled by ten — 7×30 = 7×(3×10) = (7×3)×10 = 21 tens = 210 — using place value and the associative property. The objective is the reasoning, not the 'add a zero' trick: learners should understand multiplying by 10 as making a number ten times larger so its digits shift one place left, which is why 210 ends in a zero (the ones place empties). This understanding survives the later move to decimals, where 'add a zero' fails (0.7×10 = 7, not 0.70), and powers estimation (234×5 ≈ 200×5) and multiplication by multiples of 100/1000.

activities.title: Scaling a known fact by ten with place-value counters
feedback: If a learner writes 7×30 = 21, point back to the rods: 'You took three tens seven times, not three ones. Count the tens — 21 tens is 210.'
If a learner gives 210 but only explains 'you add a zero', ask them to show it with the rods: 'Where did that zero come from? Watch the ones column empty when everything grows ten times bigger.'
If a learner miscounts zeros (e.g. 2100), have them regroup the tens carefully onto the place-value chart and reread each column.
Affirm reasoning that names the known fact: 'Yes — knowing 7×3 = 21 let you get 7×30 without starting over.'
activities.rationale: Place-value counters and regrouping make '21 tens = 210' a visible exchange rather than a memorised rule, and tie the standard's required place-value/property strategy directly to the known single-digit fact.
sourceClaims: 3.NBT.3 requires multiplying one-digit numbers by multiples of 10 (10–90) using place-value and property strategies.
Y3–Y4 pupils use place value and known facts to multiply mentally, underpinning short multiplication and estimation.
learnerActions: Build the known fact 7×3 as an array of 21 single counters (or draw them).
Replace each single counter with a rod of ten, stating aloud 'now there are 21 tens'.
Regroup the 21 tens: exchange ten tens for one hundred, repeat, ending with 2 hundreds and 1 ten.
Record the result on a place-value chart (hundreds | tens | ones) and read it as 210.
Say the full reasoning chain: '7×3 = 21, so 7×30 = 21 tens = 210, because 30 is 3 tens.'
Repeat for 5×60 (5×6 = 30, so 5×60 = 30 tens = 300) and 3×40 (3×4 = 12, so 3×40 = 12 tens = 120), each time naming the known single-digit fact first.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying by a multiple of 10 is multiplying by the single-digit fact and then by ten; the extra zero in the product is the result of every digit shifting one place left as the amount becomes ten times larger, not a zero 'stuck on the end'.

activities.title: Why 'add a zero' is not the real rule
feedback: If a learner says 0.7×10 = 0.70, show the shift on the chart: 'Sliding left makes 7, not 0.70. The zero rule breaks here — but the shift still works.'
If a learner adds too many or too few zeros for the 7×300 extension, count the place shifts together: '×100 means shifting two columns left.'
Encourage precise language: 'ten times larger' and 'shifts one place left' rather than 'add a zero'.
activities.rationale: Deliberately contrasting the whole-number case with a decimal case targets the misconception that 'add a zero' is the underlying rule, replacing it with the place-value shift that generalises.
sourceClaims: Teach multiplying by ten as a place-value shift (ten times larger) rather than 'adding a zero', which fails for decimals.
learnerActions: On a place-value chart, place 7 in the ones column, then slide it one column left to make 70; describe what happened to the digit.
Do the same with 21: slide it one column left so the ones place becomes empty and a 0 fills it, giving 210.
Now try 0.7×10 on the same chart: slide 0.7 one column left to get 7 — notice no zero was added.
State in your own words why '×10 shifts digits one place left' is safer than 'add a zero'.
(Optional extension, once the tens pattern feels secure) Predict and check 7×300 using the same idea: 7×3 = 21, shifted two places = 2100.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying by ten always shifts digits one place to the left; for whole numbers this shows up as a trailing zero, but the shift — not the zero itself — is the real rule, which is why it still works for decimals.

activities.title: Using tens facts to estimate
feedback: If a learner rounds the wrong way or forgets to scale, revisit the known-fact chain: '6×4 = 24, so 6×40 = 240.'
If a learner treats the estimate as exact, prompt: 'Is 6×43 more or less than 6×40? By about how much?'
Praise clear connections between the rounded factor and the place-value reasoning.
activities.rationale: Multiplying by multiples of ten is a useful tool for estimation (the standard itself only names place-value and property-based strategies for products in the range 10–90); applying it keeps the place-value story in a purposeful context.
sourceClaims: Y3–Y4 pupils use place value and known facts to multiply mentally, underpinning short multiplication and estimation.
learnerActions: Estimate 6×43 by rounding 43 to 40 and computing 6×40 = 240 (6×4 = 24, so 6×40 = 24 tens = 240), explaining the reasoning.

(Optional extension, once the tens case is secure) Estimate 234×5 by rounding 234 to 200 and computing 200×5 = 1000 (2×5 = 10, so 200×5 = 10 hundreds = 1000), using the same known-fact-then-scale reasoning.
Compare each estimate to the exact answer (6×43 = 258; 234×5 = 1170) and say whether the estimate is high or low and roughly by how much.
Make up one estimation of your own using a multiple of ten and justify it.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying by a multiple of ten (and, by the same reasoning, a multiple of a hundred) lets you quickly bound or approximate a larger product, which checks whether an exact answer is reasonable.

activities.title: Spot and explain the error
feedback: For '7×30 = 21': 'The 30 is three tens, so the answer must be 21 tens = 210 — ten times bigger than 21.'
For '8×40 = 32': 'That's just 8×4. Scale by ten: 32 tens = 320.'
Confirm the correct ones (5×60 = 300 and 9×80 = 720) and ask the learner to articulate the reasoning, not just the verdict.
activities.rationale: Identifying and repairing errors consolidates the reasoning and surfaces whether a learner can justify answers rather than apply a rote appendage; this is a consolidation/check activity that tests fluency rather than a substitute for building the scaling intuition with counters.
learnerActions: Decide whether each worked example is correct: 7×30 = 21; 5×60 = 300; 8×40 = 32; 9×80 = 720.
For any that are wrong, say exactly what went wrong (e.g. multiplied the tens as ones, or dropped/added a zero).
Rewrite each incorrect one with the full reasoning chain to make it correct.
Explain in words why 5×60 = 300 ends in a zero.
activities.intendedInsight: Common slips — multiplying the tens digit as ones, or miscounting zeros — can be caught by checking against the known-fact-times-ten chain.

constraints: The learning objective is the reasoning (known fact × ten via associativity and place value), not a memorised 'add a zero' step; any activity must require the learner to explain where the zero comes from.
Teach 'ten times larger → digits shift one place left' explicitly, because 'add a zero' misfires for decimals (0.7×10 = 7).
Secure the underlying single-digit fact (e.g. 7×3) first; if it is shaky, the whole derivation is unreliable.

Recognition/multiple-choice and fill-in-the-blank checks test fluency but do not by themselves build the scaling intuition; use them for consolidation alongside construction with counters and spoken reasoning.
Physical base-ten equipment and a drawn or on-screen place-value chart are both suitable; manipulatives make the regrouping of ten tens into a hundred concrete.
Extend the identical place-value story to multiples of 100/1000 only once the tens case is secure; the 7×300 step is presented as an optional extension for this reason.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 7×3=21 so 7×30=210; 5×6=30 so 5×60=300; 3×4=12 so 3×40=120; 6×4=24 so 6×40=240; 8×4=32 so 8×40=320; 9×8=72 so 9×80=720; 7×3=21 so 7×300=2100; 6×43=258; 234×5=1170; 2×5=10 so 200×5=1000 — all check out. The 'spot the error' items 7×30=21 and 8×40=32 are intentionally incorrect for learners to catch, with corrected values (210, 320) supplied in feedback.
Decimal check: 0.7×10=7 (not 0.70); the shift-left framing is correct and the 'add a zero' rule correctly fails here.
Source note: the CCSS 3.NBT.3 and NCETM claims are marked unverified (verified:false) in the original row; retained as cited without upgrading their evidence status.

Original source row legacy vocabulary describing specific interactive formats (e.g. a 'scaler' widget, tap-to-reveal, lift-the-flap) has been generalised into medium-independent learner actions while preserving the live-regrouping mechanism as an optional illustration.

The decimal example (0.7×10), the 200×5 estimation step and the 7×300 extension may exceed the typical age-band comfort zone; all are retained from the original design but flagged as needing teacher judgement/support.

probeDeeper: What does 7 × 30 have to do with 7 × 3?
Why does the answer end in a zero — where does that zero come from?
How could 6 × 40 help you estimate 6 × 43?
If you know 7 × 3 = 21, what is 7 × 300?
assess.correctAnswer: 210 and 240. The teacher watches for the child reasoning '7 × 3 tens = 21 tens = 210' — using the single-digit fact and scaling by ten — rather than a disconnected zero-adding rule.

errorPatterns.pattern: multiplies the tens digit as ones — 7×30 treated as 7×3 = 21, forgetting the ten (answer 21)
errorPatterns.nextMove: reason 7 × 3 TENS = 21 tens = 210; use base-ten equipment to show three tens taken seven times.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answer is ten times too small; child computes 7×3 and stops

errorPatterns.pattern: 'adds a zero' as a rote rule with no meaning — works here but cannot say why, and will misapply it to decimals later
errorPatterns.nextMove: tie the zero to 'ten times bigger': multiplying by 30 is multiplying by 3 then by 10, and ×10 shifts digits one place, showing up as a zero for whole numbers.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child gets 210 but explains only 'you add a zero'; cannot connect to 7×3

errorPatterns.pattern: not fluent in the underlying single-digit fact, so the whole derivation is shaky
errorPatterns.nextMove: shore up the single-digit fact before layering the tens reasoning.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child hesitates or errs on 7×3 itself

responseLevels.gap: multiplies the tens digit as ones (answer ten times too small), or has no reasoning at all.
responseLevels.full: reasons via the known fact scaled by ten ('7 × 3 tens = 21 tens'), explains the zero as the result of ×10, and uses the skill to estimate larger products.
responseLevels.partial: gets the right answer via 'add a zero' but cannot connect it to the single-digit fact or explain why the zero appears.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the child to work out 7 × 30 and 6 × 40 in their head, saying how they did it. Watch whether they use the known fact (7×3) and reason about tens, or whether they just 'add a zero' without understanding — then probe by asking what 7 × 30 has to do with 7 × 3.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Multiplying by a multiple of ten is the first place the 'add a zero' shortcut appears; watching HOW the child reasons (does the zero come from 'ten times', or is it a rote appendage?) reveals whether place-value understanding underpins the shortcut — essential because the same rule misfires later on decimals.
